abstract: A general method for deriving backpropagation algorithms for networks with recurrent and higher order networks is introduced. The propagation of activation in these networks is determined by dissipative differential equations. The error signal is backpropagated by integrating an associated differential equation. The method is introduced by applying it to the recurrent generalization of the feedforward backpropagation network. The method is extended to the case of higher order networks and to a constrained dynamical system for training a content addressable memory. The essential feature of the adaptive algorithms is that adaptive equation has a simple outer product form. Preliminary experiments suggest that learning can occur very rapidly in networks with recurrent connections. The continuous formalism makes the new approach more suitable for implementation in VLSI.

paragraphs: The paper presents a general method for deriving backpropagation algorithms for networks with recurrent connections and higher-order interactions. In these networks, activation evolves according to dissipative differential equations. Learning must therefore account for a changing network state, including the effects of feedback, rather than only a passage through successive layers.

The authors propagate the error signal by integrating a related differential equation. They first apply the method to a recurrent extension of a feedforward backpropagation network, then extend it to higher-order networks and a constrained dynamical system for training a content-addressable memory. This demonstrates how one mathematical approach can cover several kinds of network dynamics.

A central feature is that the adaptive equation retains a simple outer-product form, giving the learning update a compact structure despite the more complex activation dynamics. Preliminary experiments suggest that recurrent networks can learn very rapidly. The authors also argue that the continuous formulation is better suited to VLSI implementation. The reported speed evidence is preliminary, while the general derivation is the main methodological contribution.
summary.tldr: The paper derives continuous-time backpropagation for recurrent and higher-order networks using related differential equations and simple outer-product learning updates.

title: Generalization of Back propagation to Recurrent and Higher Order Neural Networks

paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly backpropagation reduces error after learning has already run for a long time. It considers networks both with and without hidden units. The focus is the asymptotic convergence rate: the pattern of continued improvement in the late stages of learning, rather than only whether training eventually reduces error.

The authors combine analytical calculations with numerical simulations. For the standard sigmoid transfer function, they report an error decay approximately proportional to the inverse of elapsed training time. Hidden units introduce at most logarithmic corrections to this behavior. This describes a slow tail in which further reductions in error require progressively more training.

The choice of transfer function also matters: other functions can produce slower polynomial convergence. The paper concentrates on empirical measurements that confirm the analytical results. Its contribution is to connect observed late-stage learning behavior with a mathematical account of the decay rate, while showing that this behavior depends on the response function used by the units.
summary.tldr: Numerical experiments support an approximately inverse-time decline in late-stage backpropagation error for sigmoid units.

title: Asymptotic Convergence of Backpropagation: Numerical Experiments

abstract: We study a particular type of Boltzmann machine with a bipartite graph structure called a harmo(cid:173) nium. Our interest is in using such a machine to model a probability distribution on binary input vectors. We analyze the class of probability distributions that can be modeled by such machines. showing that for each n ~ 1 this class includes arbitrarily good appwximations to any distribution on the set of all n-vectors of binary inputs. We then present two learning algorithms for these machines .. The first learning algorithm is the standard gradient ascent heuristic for computing maximum likelihood estimates for the parameters (i.e. weights and thresholds) of the modeL Here we give a closed form for this gradient that is significantly easier to compute than the corresponding gradient for the general Boltzmann machine . The second learning algorithm is a greedy method that creates the hidden units and computes their weights one at a time. This method is a variant of the standard method for projection pursuit density estimation . We give experimental results for these learning methods on synthetic data and natural data from the domain of handwritten digits.

paragraphs: This paper studies harmoniums, a type of Boltzmann machine with a bipartite structure, as models of probability distributions over binary input vectors. The first question is representational capacity. The authors show that, for any fixed positive input dimension, these machines can approximate any distribution over the possible binary vectors arbitrarily closely.

The paper then presents two learning methods. The first uses gradient ascent to seek maximum-likelihood parameter estimates. For this network structure, the authors derive a closed-form gradient that is substantially easier to compute than the corresponding gradient for a general Boltzmann machine. The structural restriction therefore provides a useful simplification while retaining broad representational capacity.

The second method constructs the model greedily, creating hidden units and determining their weights one at a time. It adapts an approach from projection pursuit density estimation. Experiments examine both learning methods on synthetic data and handwritten-digit data. The contribution combines an expressiveness result with two concrete routes for fitting the model: adjusting its parameters jointly or building hidden structure incrementally.
summary.tldr: Two-layer harmoniums can approximate any binary-vector distribution, and the paper develops gradient-based and incremental methods for learning them.

title: Unsupervised learning of distributions on binary vectors using two layer networks

abstract: The formation of propagating spiral waves is studied in a randomly connected neural network composed of integrate-and-fire neurons with recovery period and excitatory connections using computer simulations. Network activity is initiated by periodic stimulation at a single point. The results suggest that spiral waves can arise in such a network via a sub-critical Hopf bifurcation.
originalAbstract: The formation of propagating spiral waves is studied in a randomly connected neural network composed of integrate-and-fire neurons with recovery period and excitatory connections using computer simulations. Network activity is initiated by periodic stimulation at a single point. The results suggest that spiral waves can arise in such a network via a sub-critical Hopf bifurcation.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how propagating spiral patterns of activity can develop in a neural network. It uses computer simulations of randomly connected integrate-and-fire neurons. Each neuron has a recovery period, and the connections are excitatory, specifying the network conditions under which the collective activity is studied.

Activity is started by repeatedly stimulating a single point. The question is how this localized periodic input relates to a pattern that spreads through the network as a spiral. The setup links individual-neuron properties, random connections, and a simple stimulation scheme to the emergence of organized network-wide dynamics.

The simulation results suggest that spiral waves can arise through a subcritical Hopf bifurcation, a particular kind of qualitative transition in a dynamical system. This is presented as a suggested mechanism for the observed pattern formation. The contribution is therefore both an observation of spiral activity in the simulated network and a dynamical interpretation of how that activity can emerge under the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: Simulations suggest that spiral waves can emerge through a subcritical Hopf bifurcation in randomly connected excitatory integrate-and-fire networks.

title: Spiral Waves in Integrate-and-Fire Neural Networks

abstract: We investigate the effectiveness of stochastic hillclimbing as a baseline for evaluating the performance of genetic algorithms (GAs) as combinato(cid:173) rial function optimizers. In particular, we address two problems to which GAs have been applied in the literature: Koza's ll-multiplexer problem and the jobshop problem. We demonstrate that simple stochastic hill(cid:173) climbing methods are able to achieve results comparable or superior to those obtained by the GAs designed to address these two problems. We further illustrate, in the case of the jobshop problem, how insights ob(cid:173) tained in the formulation of a stochastic hillclimbing algorithm can lead to improvements in the encoding used by a GA.

In particular, we address two problems to which GAs have been applied in the literature: Koza's ll-multiplexer problem and the jobshop problem. We demonstrate that simple stochastic hill(cid:173) climbing methods are able to achieve results comparable or superior to those obtained by the GAs designed to address these two problems. paragraphs: The paper examines stochastic hillclimbing as a reference method for evaluating genetic algorithms on combinatorial optimization problems. The central question is whether relatively simple search methods can match the performance attributed to genetic algorithms. The authors investigate two problems already addressed by genetic algorithms: Koza's multiplexer problem and jobshop scheduling.

On these problems, the stochastic hillclimbing methods achieve results comparable to or better than the genetic algorithms designed for them. This makes the baseline consequential: a successful genetic algorithm needs to be assessed against an effective simpler search procedure. The reported findings concern these two problem settings and their corresponding algorithms.

The jobshop analysis also shows that constructing a hillclimbing method can reveal ways to improve the encoding used by a genetic algorithm. The comparison therefore contributes both an evaluation standard and insight into representation design. Its broader methodological point is that a baseline can help explain performance and improve the method being evaluated, rather than serving only as a score to exceed.
summary.tldr: Simple stochastic hillclimbing matches or beats genetic algorithms on two studied problems and helps improve a jobshop encoding.

title: Stochastic Hillclimbing as a Baseline Method for Evaluating Genetic Algorithms

paragraphs: Understanding a neural network's training requires describing how learning unfolds across successive updates. This paper introduces a method for calculating that training process with results directly tied to the actual number of training steps. The approach makes the passage from one stage of learning to another an explicit object of analysis.

The method avoids sophisticated machinery such as the replica trick. Its stated results include a maximal learning rate, an exact description of early stopping, and the necessary number of training steps. These are closely related questions: the rate controls update size, stopping selects a point along the process, and the step count describes how long training must proceed.

Connecting those quantities to the training trajectory gives practical choices a common analytical setting. Early stopping, in particular, becomes something that can be described through the calculated dynamics. The paper presents these results as examples of what the method can address and indicates that further training questions can be studied through the same approach.
summary.tldr: A method for calculating neural-network training dynamics links learning-rate limits, early stopping, and required training duration to actual update counts.

title: Dynamics of Training

abstract: We study a time series model that can be viewed as a decision tree with Markov temporal structure. The model is intractable for exact calculations, thus we utilize variational approximations. We consider three different distributions for the approximation: one in which the Markov calculations are performed exactly and the layers of the decision tree are decoupled, one in which the decision tree calculations are performed exactly and the time steps of the Markov chain are decoupled, and one in which a Viterbi-like assumption is made to pick out a single most likely state sequence. We present simulation results for artificial data and the Bach chorales.
originalAbstract: We study a time series model that can be viewed as a decision tree with Markov temporal structure. The model is intractable for exact calculations, thus we utilize variational approximations. We consider three different distributions for the approximation: one in which the Markov calculations are performed exactly and the layers of the decision tree are decoupled, one in which the decision tree calculations are performed exactly and the time steps of the Markov chain are decoupled, and one in which a Viterbi-like assumption is made to pick out a single most likely state sequence. We present simulation results for artificial data and the Bach chorales.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a time-series model combining a decision-tree structure with Markov dependence over time. This brings hierarchical decisions and temporal relationships into one representation. Exact calculations in the combined model are intractable, so the authors investigate variational approximations that simplify different parts of its structure.

The first approximation preserves exact Markov calculations while separating the layers of the decision tree. The second preserves exact decision-tree calculations while separating time steps in the Markov chain. These alternatives make complementary choices about which dependencies to keep intact and which to simplify, exposing the computational tradeoff created by the combined architecture.

A third approximation makes a Viterbi-like choice of a single most likely state sequence. Instead of retaining the same treatment of multiple possible sequences, it concentrates on one selected trajectory. The authors present simulations using artificial data and Bach chorales. The work provides both a combined temporal and hierarchical model and three distinct ways to make inference manageable when fully exact computation is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Hidden Markov decision trees combine hierarchical and temporal structure, with three approximations making otherwise intractable calculations manageable.

title: Hidden Markov Decision Trees

abstract: We present a probabilistic method for fusion of images produced by multiple sensors. The approach is based on an image formation model in which the sensor images are noisy, locally linear functions of an underlying, true scene. A Bayesian framework then provides for maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori estimates of the true scene from the sensor images. Maximum likelihood estimates of the parameters of the image formation model involve (local) second order image statistics, and thus are related to local principal component analysis. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method on images from visible-band and infrared sensors.
originalAbstract: We present a probabilistic method for fusion of images produced by multiple sensors. The approach is based on an image formation model in which the sensor images are noisy, locally linear functions of an underlying, true scene. A Bayesian framework then provides for maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori estimates of the true scene from the sensor images. Maximum likelihood estimates of the parameters of the image formation model involve (local) second order image statistics, and thus are related to local principal component analysis. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method on images from visible-band and infrared sensors.

paragraphs: Different imaging sensors provide different observations of the same scene. This paper combines those observations by explicitly modeling how they were formed. It assumes that each sensor image is a noisy, locally linear function of an underlying true scene, making image fusion a problem of estimating that shared hidden scene.

Within a Bayesian framework, the authors obtain either maximum-likelihood or maximum-a-posteriori scene estimates. The former seeks the scene that best explains the observations; the latter also incorporates prior information. Both follow from the same image-formation model, giving the combination of sensor measurements a probabilistic interpretation.

Estimating the image-formation parameters uses local second-order image statistics, connecting the method to local principal component analysis. This means the fusion procedure draws on statistical relationships within image regions. Demonstrations combine visible-band and infrared images. The contribution is a unified way to describe sensor noise, estimate relationships among observations, and reconstruct a scene from multiple imaging sources.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic image-formation model combines noisy sensor images into a shared scene estimate, demonstrated with visible and infrared imagery.

title: Probabilistic Image Sensor Fusion

abstract: In previous work [6, 9, 10], we advanced a new technique for direct visual matching of images for the purposes of face recognition and image retrieval , using a probabilistic measure of similarity based primarily on a Bayesian (MAP) analysis of image differ(cid:173) ences, leading to a "dual" basis similar to eigenfaces [13]. The performance advantage of this probabilistic matching technique over standard Euclidean nearest-neighbor eigenface matching was recently demonstrated using results from DARPA's 1996 "FERET" face recognition competition, in which this probabilistic matching algorithm was found to be the top performer. We have further developed a simple method of replacing the costly com put ion of nonlinear (online) Bayesian similarity measures by the relatively inexpensive computation of linear (offline) subspace projections and simple (online) Euclidean norms, thus resulting in a significant computational speed-up for implementation with very large image databases as typically encountered in real-world applications.

The performance advantage of this probabilistic matching technique over standard Euclidean nearest-neighbor eigenface matching was recently demonstrated using results from DARPA's 1996 "FERET" face recognition competition, in which this probabilistic matching algorithm was found to be the top performer. We have further developed a simple method of replacing the costly com put ion of nonlinear (online) Bayesian similarity measures by the relatively inexpensive computation of linear (offline) subspace projections and simple (online) Euclidean norms, thus resulting in a significant computational speed-up for implementation with very large image databases as typically encountered in real-world applications.

paragraphs: This paper develops a faster implementation of probabilistic image matching for face recognition and image retrieval. The underlying method evaluates similarity through a Bayesian analysis of differences between images. Earlier work used this analysis to build a dual representation related to eigenfaces, providing a probabilistic basis for deciding how closely two faces match.

The abstract reports that the earlier matching algorithm outperformed standard Euclidean nearest-neighbor eigenface matching and was the top performer in the cited face-recognition competition. That finding motivates making the probabilistic method cheaper to use. The new development targets the computational expense of evaluating nonlinear Bayesian similarity measures during matching.

The proposed replacement uses linear subspace projections computed offline and simple Euclidean norms computed online. This shifts the work into a form that reduces the cost of individual comparisons. The authors report a significant computational speedup, making the approach more practical for very large image databases. The contribution is therefore a more efficient realization of an already demonstrated probabilistic matching approach.
summary.tldr: Offline linear projections and simple online distances substantially speed up Bayesian face matching for large image databases.

title: Bayesian Modeling of Facial Similarity

abstract: Gaussian processes provide an approach to nonparametric modelling which allows a straightforward combination of function and derivative observations in an empirical model. This is of particular importance in identiﬁcation of nonlinear dynamic systems from experimental data. 1) It allows us to combine derivative information, and associated uncertainty with normal function observations into the learning and inference pro- cess. This derivative information can be in the form of priors speciﬁed by an expert or identiﬁed from perturbation data close to equilibrium. 2) It allows a seamless fusion of multiple local linear models in a consis- tent manner, inferring consistent models and ensuring that integrability constraints are met. 3) It improves dramatically the computational ef- ﬁciency of Gaussian process models for dynamic system identiﬁcation, by summarising large quantities of near-equilibrium data by a handful of linearisations, reducing the training set size – traditionally a problem for Gaussian process models.

This is of particular importance in identiﬁcation of nonlinear dynamic systems from experimental data. 1) It allows us to combine derivative information, and associated uncertainty with normal function observations into the learning and inference pro- cess. This derivative information can be in the form of priors speciﬁed by an expert or identiﬁed from perturbation data close to equilibrium. 2) It allows a seamless fusion of multiple local linear models in a consis- tent manner, inferring consistent models and ensuring that integrability constraints are met. 3) It improves dramatically the computational ef- ﬁciency of Gaussian process models for dynamic system identiﬁcation, by summarising large quantities of near-equilibrium data by a handful of linearisations, reducing the training set size – traditionally a problem for Gaussian process models.

paragraphs: Learning a nonlinear dynamic system can involve information about both its outputs and how those outputs change locally. The paper uses Gaussian processes to combine ordinary function observations with derivative observations in one empirical model. It also incorporates uncertainty associated with the derivative information, so these observations need not be treated as exact.

Derivative information can come from expert-specified priors or from perturbation experiments near equilibrium. The framework can also combine multiple local linear models consistently. Its integrability constraints ensure that the local derivative descriptions fit together as parts of a consistent function model, making the fusion more than a collection of unrelated local approximations.

The approach also addresses the computational burden of training Gaussian process models. Large amounts of near-equilibrium data can be summarized by a small number of linearizations, reducing the training set size. The authors report a dramatic efficiency improvement for dynamic system identification through this compression, connecting local system knowledge to both coherent inference and more manageable computation.
summary.tldr: Gaussian processes combine uncertain derivative information and ordinary observations to model dynamic systems consistently and more efficiently.

title: Derivative Observations in Gaussian Process Models of Dynamic Systems

paragraphs: A clustering algorithm can produce several plausible groupings of the same data because its notion of distance determines which points appear similar. A grouping may be mathematically reasonable yet fail to match what a user wants. The paper addresses this problem by learning the distance measure from examples of desired relationships.

Users supply pairs of points considered similar and, optionally, pairs considered dissimilar. The algorithm learns a metric that respects this information. This replaces repeated manual adjustment of the distance measure with an explicit learning problem: the examples express what similarity should mean for the application.

The method formulates metric learning as convex optimization, enabling efficient algorithms without the obstacle of nonglobal local optima. Empirical results show that the learned metrics can significantly improve clustering performance. The contribution is a systematic route from limited pairwise guidance to a distance measure that can support better groupings. The reported improvement is an empirical finding, while the optimization formulation supplies the stated computational advantage.
summary.tldr: A convex optimization method learns distance metrics from similar and optionally dissimilar pairs, with empirical improvements in clustering.

title: Distance Metric Learning with Application to Clustering with Side-Information

paragraphs: The paper presents a Bayesian framework for building speech-recognition models and using them to recognize speech. Called variational Bayesian estimation and clustering, or VBEC, it constructs shared-state triphone hidden Markov models. The framework brings model estimation, clustering, and predictive classification into a common Bayesian approach.

A central concern is choosing an appropriate model structure when training data are limited. The authors contrast their approach with conventional maximum-likelihood methods using criteria such as BIC or MDL. VBEC does not rely on an asymptotic assumption, meaning that its model-selection rationale does not require the large-data approximation used by those conventional criteria. The authors therefore describe its selection procedure as valid in principle even with insufficient data.

In isolated-word recognition experiments, VBEC shows an advantage over conventional methods, especially with small training sets. These results connect the model-selection argument to observed recognition performance. The claim is that the framework can find suitable structures with strong recognition performance, with the reported experimental advantage particularly relevant to situations where examples are scarce.
summary.tldr: A variational Bayesian framework selects speech-model structures without an asymptotic assumption and improves isolated-word recognition, especially with limited data.

title: Application of Variational Bayesian Approach to Speech Recognition

abstract: In Slow Feature Analysis (SFA [1]), it has been demonstrated that high-order invariant properties can be extracted by projecting inputs into a nonlinear space and computing the slowest changing features in this space; this has been proposed as a simple general model for learning nonlinear invariances in the visual system. However, this method is highly constrained by the curse of dimensionality which limits it to simple theoretical simulations. This paper demonstrates that by using a different but closely-related objective function for extracting slowly varying features ([2, 3]), and then exploiting the kernel trick, this curse can be avoided. Using this new method we show that both the complex cell properties of translation invariance and disparity coding can be learnt simultaneously from natural images when complex cells are driven by simple cells also learnt from the image.

However, this method is highly constrained by the curse of dimensionality which limits it to simple theoretical simulations. This paper demonstrates that by using a different but closely-related objective function for extracting slowly varying features ([2, 3]), and then exploiting the kernel trick, this curse can be avoided. Using this new method we show that both the complex cell properties of translation invariance and disparity coding can be learnt simultaneously from natural images when complex cells are driven by simple cells also learnt from the image.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning visual properties by finding features that change slowly as inputs vary. Earlier slow feature analysis projects inputs into a nonlinear space and extracts slowly changing directions there. This can reveal higher-order invariances, but the dimensionality of that nonlinear representation had restricted the approach to simple theoretical simulations.

The authors use a different, closely related objective for slowly varying features and apply the kernel trick. This allows the nonlinear computation to be expressed through kernel evaluations, avoiding the stated dimensionality obstacle. The change matters because it makes the slow-feature approach applicable to learning from natural images in the setting studied.

Using the new method, the authors show that translation invariance and disparity coding can be learned simultaneously as properties of complex cells. These modeled cells receive inputs from simple cells that are also learned from the images. The finding supports a learning account in which both properties emerge together from natural-image input through a hierarchy of learned visual responses.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based slow-feature method learns translation invariance and disparity coding together from natural images while avoiding the stated dimensionality obstacle.

title: Kernel-Based Extraction of Slow Features: Complex Cells Learn Disparity and Translation Invariance from Natural Images

abstract: As part of an environmental observation and forecasting system, sensors deployed in the Columbia RIver Estuary (CORIE) gather information on physical dynamics and changes in estuary habi- tat. Of these, salinity sensors are particularly susceptible to bio- fouling, which gradually degrades sensor response and corrupts crit- ical data. Automatic fault detectors have the capability to identify bio-fouling early and minimize data loss. Complicating the devel- opment of discriminatory classi(cid:12)ers is the scarcity of bio-fouling onset examples and the variability of the bio-fouling signature. To solve these problems, we take a novelty detection approach that incorporates a parameterized bio-fouling model. These detectors identify the occurrence of bio-fouling, and its onset time as reliably as human experts. Real-time detectors installed during the sum- mer of 2001 produced no false alarms, yet detected all episodes of sensor degradation before the (cid:12)eld sta(cid:11) scheduled these sensors for cleaning. From this initial deployment through February 2003, our bio-fouling detectors have essentially doubled the amount of useful data coming from the CORIE sensors.

paragraphs: Salinity sensors in the Columbia River Estuary monitoring system can gradually become fouled by biological growth. This degradation corrupts measurements needed to understand the estuary. Detecting its onset is difficult because examples are scarce and the pattern of degradation varies, making conventional discrimination between healthy and fouled sensors challenging.

The authors use novelty detection together with a parameterized model of bio-fouling. This incorporates an explicit description of the fault into the detection approach. The detectors identify both whether fouling has occurred and when it began, with reliability comparable to human experts. Early identification matters because it can reduce the amount of corrupted sensor data.

During the reported initial real-time deployment, the detectors produced no false alarms and caught every degradation episode before field staff scheduled the sensors for cleaning. Across the longer period reported in the abstract, they essentially doubled the useful data obtained from the sensors. These are deployment findings for the monitoring system studied, linking fault detection to a substantial practical improvement in data availability.
summary.tldr: Novelty detectors incorporating a bio-fouling model identified sensor degradation early and essentially doubled useful data in the reported estuary deployment.

title: Parameterized Novelty Detectors for Environmental Sensor Monitoring

abstract: We analyze classification error on unseen cases, i.e. cases that are different from those in the training set. Unlike standard generalization error, this off-training-set error may differ significantly from the empirical error with high probability even with large sample sizes. We derive a datadependent bound on the difference between off-training-set and standard generalization error. Our result is based on a new bound on the missing mass, which for small samples is stronger than existing bounds based on Good-Turing estimators. As we demonstrate on UCI data-sets, our bound gives nontrivial generalization guarantees in many practical cases. In light of these results, we show that certain claims made in the No Free Lunch literature are overly pessimistic.

paragraphs: This paper distinguishes prediction error on genuinely unseen cases from standard generalization error. Standard generalization evaluates performance under the overall data distribution, whereas off-training-set error focuses on cases absent from the training set. The authors show that this latter error can differ substantially from training error with high probability, even when the sample is large.

They derive a data-dependent bound connecting off-training-set error to standard generalization error. The argument uses a new bound on the missing mass: the probability assigned to cases that the training sample has not included. For small samples, their missing-mass bound is stronger than existing bounds based on Good–Turing estimators.

Experiments on UCI datasets show that the bound provides nontrivial generalization guarantees in many practical cases. This makes the distinction between new observations and previously unseen cases something that can be assessed using data. The authors also use the results to challenge certain pessimistic claims in the No Free Lunch literature, rather than rejecting every claim associated with that literature.
summary.tldr: A new missing-mass bound helps quantify classification error specifically on cases absent from the training set.

title: Generalization to Unseen Cases

abstract: Up to now even subjects that are experts in the use of machine learning based BCI systems still have to undergo a calibration session of about 20-30 min. From this data their (movement) intentions are so far infered. We now propose a new paradigm that allows to completely omit such calibration and instead transfer knowledge from prior sessions. To achieve this goal we first define normalized CSP features and distances in-between. Second, we derive prototypical features across sessions: (a) by clustering or (b) by feature concatenation methods. Finally, we construct a classifier based on these individualized prototypes and show that, indeed, classifiers can be successfully transferred to a new session for a number of subjects.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the repeated calibration required by machine-learning-based brain-computer interfaces. Even experienced users had to spend roughly 20–30 minutes generating calibration data before their movement intentions could be inferred. The proposed alternative uses information from earlier sessions to avoid collecting a fresh calibration session each time.

The method first defines normalized common spatial pattern features and distances between them. It then constructs representative features across sessions, either by clustering or by feature concatenation. These individualized prototypes provide the basis for a classifier, allowing information from a person's prior sessions to be carried into a new one.

The authors demonstrate successful classifier transfer to a new session for a number of subjects. This supports the possibility of omitting calibration through reuse of earlier session knowledge for those users. The result is specifically about transferring individualized information across sessions: the prototypes preserve a connection to the user's previous data, and the reported success does not establish that calibration can be omitted for every subject.
summary.tldr: Individualized feature prototypes from earlier BCI sessions enable successful classifier transfer without fresh calibration for several subjects.

title: Reducing Calibration Time For Brain-Computer Interfaces: A Clustering Approach

abstract: In many structured prediction problems, the highest-scoring labeling is hard to compute exactly, leading to the use of approximate inference methods. However, when inference is used in a learning algorithm, a good approximation of the score may not be sufﬁcient. We show in particular that learning can fail even with an approximate inference method with rigorous approximation guarantees. There are two reasons for this. First, approximate methods can effectively reduce the expres- sivity of an underlying model by making it impossible to choose parameters that reliably give good predictions. Second, approximations can respond to parameter changes in such a way that standard learning algorithms are misled. In contrast, we give two positive results in the form of learning bounds for the use of LP-relaxed inference in structured perceptron and empirical risk minimization settings. We argue that without understanding combinations of inference and learning, such as these, that are appropriately compatible, learning performance under approximate inference cannot be guaranteed.

First, approximate methods can effectively reduce the expres- sivity of an underlying model by making it impossible to choose parameters that reliably give good predictions. paragraphs: Structured prediction often needs approximate inference because finding the best labeling is computationally hard. A good approximation to the score, however, may not be a good component of a learning algorithm. This paper shows why inference quality and learning compatibility must be analyzed together.

Approximate inference can make some predictions unreachable even when the underlying model could represent them. It can also react to parameter changes in ways that mislead standard update rules. Consequently, learning may fail despite a rigorous approximation guarantee for the inference procedure considered on its own.

The authors also give positive learning bounds for linear-programming-relaxed inference in structured perceptron and empirical-risk-minimization settings. These results identify compatible combinations rather than condemning approximate inference generally. The contribution is a precise warning and a constructive alternative: a useful guarantee must describe the interaction between the learner and its inference routine, not only the quality of isolated decoding.
summary.tldr: Approximate inference can break structured learning despite score guarantees; compatible LP-relaxed combinations receive positive learning bounds.

title: Structured Learning with Approximate Inference

abstract: Continuous attractor neural networks (CANNs) are emerging as promising models for describing the encoding of continuous stimuli in neural systems. Due to the translational invariance of their neuronal interactions, CANNs can hold a continuous family of neutrally stable states. In this study, we systematically explore how neutral stability of a CANN facilitates its tracking performance, a capacity believed to have wide applications in brain functions. We develop a perturbative approach that utilizes the dominant movement of the network stationary states in the state space. We quantify the distortions of the bump shape during tracking, and study their effects on the tracking performance. Results are obtained on the maximum speed for a moving stimulus to be trackable, and the reaction time to catch up an abrupt change in stimulus.
originalAbstract: Continuous attractor neural networks (CANNs) are emerging as promising models for describing the encoding of continuous stimuli in neural systems. Due to the translational invariance of their neuronal interactions, CANNs can hold a continuous family of neutrally stable states. In this study, we systematically explore how neutral stability of a CANN facilitates its tracking performance, a capacity believed to have wide applications in brain functions. We develop a perturbative approach that utilizes the dominant movement of the network stationary states in the state space. We quantify the distortions of the bump shape during tracking, and study their effects on the tracking performance. Results are obtained on the maximum speed for a moving stimulus to be trackable, and the reaction time to catch up an abrupt change in stimulus.

paragraphs: Continuous attractor neural networks model the encoding of continuously varying stimuli. Because their neuronal interactions are translationally invariant, they can support a continuous family of neutrally stable states. This paper investigates how that neutral stability contributes to following a stimulus as it changes, connecting a property of the network’s stationary states to its dynamic behavior.

The authors develop a perturbative analysis based on the dominant movement of stationary states through the network’s state space. They also quantify changes in the shape of the activity bump during tracking and examine how those distortions affect performance. The analysis therefore considers both movement of the activity pattern and changes to its shape.

The results characterize the maximum stimulus speed the network can track and the time required to catch up after an abrupt stimulus change. These address two distinct tracking demands: sustained motion and a sudden displacement. The contribution provides quantitative descriptions of these capabilities within the model, clarifying how neutral stability and bump deformation relate to following changing inputs.
summary.tldr: A perturbative analysis links neutral stability and activity-bump distortions to tracking speed and response time in continuous attractor networks.

title: Tracking Changing Stimuli in Continuous Attractor Neural Networks

abstract: We propose a novel class of Bayesian nonparametric models for sequential data called fragmentation-coagulation processes (FCPs). FCPs model a set of sequences using a partition-valued Markov process which evolves by splitting and merging clusters. An FCP is exchangeable, projective, stationary and reversible, and its equilibrium distributions are given by the Chinese restaurant process. As opposed to hidden Markov models, FCPs allow for flexible modelling of the number of clusters, and they avoid label switching non-identifiability problems. We develop an efficient Gibbs sampler for FCPs which uses uniformization and the forward-backward algorithm. Our development of FCPs is motivated by applications in population genetics, and we demonstrate the utility of FCPs on problems of genotype imputation with phased and unphased SNP data.

FCPs model a set of sequences using a partition-valued Markov process which evolves by splitting and merging clusters. An FCP is exchangeable, projective, stationary and reversible, and its equilibrium distributions are given by the Chinese restaurant process. As opposed to hidden Markov models, FCPs allow for flexible modelling of the number of clusters, and they avoid label switching non-identifiability problems. We develop an efficient Gibbs sampler for FCPs which uses uniformization and the forward-backward algorithm. Our development of FCPs is motivated by applications in population genetics, and we demonstrate the utility of FCPs on problems of genotype imputation with phased and unphased SNP data.

paragraphs: This paper introduces fragmentation-coagulation processes as Bayesian nonparametric models for collections of sequences. Their changing state is a partition: a grouping of sequences into clusters. As the process moves along the sequence, clusters can split or merge, allowing the grouping to evolve without committing to a fixed number of clusters.

The construction is exchangeable, projective, stationary, and reversible, with equilibrium distributions supplied by the Chinese restaurant process. Compared with hidden Markov models, the authors emphasize flexible cluster counts and avoidance of label-switching non-identifiability. Representing groupings directly makes the partition central, avoiding ambiguity caused by assigning different names to otherwise equivalent clusters.

To fit these models, the paper develops an efficient Gibbs sampler using uniformization and the forward-backward algorithm. Population genetics motivates the approach, and the authors demonstrate its usefulness for genotype imputation with both phased and unphased SNP data. The work therefore joins a flexible model of changing group structure with an inference procedure and a concrete application to recovering missing genetic information.
summary.tldr: Fragmentation-coagulation processes model sequences through splitting and merging clusters, with efficient inference demonstrated on genotype imputation.

title: Modelling Genetic Variations using Fragmentation-Coagulation Processes

abstract: To learn reliable rules that can generalize to novel situations, the brain must be capable of imposing some form of regularization. Here we suggest, through theoretical and computational arguments, that the combination of noise with synchronization provides a plausible mechanism for regularization in the nervous system. The functional role of regularization is considered in a general context in which coupled computational systems receive inputs corrupted by correlated noise. Noise on the inputs is shown to impose regularization, and when synchronization upstream induces time-varying correlations across noise variables, the degree of regularization can be calibrated over time. The resulting qualitative behavior matches experimental data from visual cortex.
originalAbstract: To learn reliable rules that can generalize to novel situations, the brain must be capable of imposing some form of regularization. Here we suggest, through theoretical and computational arguments, that the combination of noise with synchronization provides a plausible mechanism for regularization in the nervous system. The functional role of regularization is considered in a general context in which coupled computational systems receive inputs corrupted by correlated noise. Noise on the inputs is shown to impose regularization, and when synchronization upstream induces time-varying correlations across noise variables, the degree of regularization can be calibrated over time. The resulting qualitative behavior matches experimental data from visual cortex.

paragraphs: Learning rules that work in unfamiliar situations requires some way to control how strongly a system adapts to its inputs. This paper proposes that noise and synchronization together could provide such regularization in neural systems. The authors develop theoretical and computational arguments for this possibility using coupled computational systems receiving noisy inputs.

In the analyzed setting, noise on the inputs imposes regularization. The important additional ingredient is correlation between noise variables: disturbances affecting different inputs can vary together. When upstream synchronization changes those correlations over time, it can also adjust the degree of regularization. Synchronization therefore supplies a possible way to regulate the effect of noise dynamically.

The resulting qualitative behavior agrees with experimental observations from visual cortex. This agreement connects the proposed computational mechanism to neural behavior without establishing that it is the brain's actual mechanism. The contribution is a plausible account of how coordinated activity could tune learning constraints, supported by theory, computation, and qualitative correspondence with the cited experimental data.
summary.tldr: Theoretical and computational results suggest that synchronization could tune neural regularization by changing correlations in input noise.

title: Synchronization can Control Regularization in Neural Systems via Correlated Noise Processes

abstract: We present the Bayesian Case Model (BCM), a general framework for Bayesian case-based reasoning (CBR) and prototype classification and clustering. BCM brings the intuitive power of CBR to a Bayesian generative framework. The BCM learns prototypes, the ``quintessential observations that best represent clusters in a dataset, by performing joint inference on cluster labels, prototypes and important features. Simultaneously, BCM pursues sparsity by learning subspaces, the sets of features that play important roles in the characterization of the prototypes. The prototype and subspace representation provides quantitative benefits in interpretability while preserving classification accuracy. Human subject experiments verify statistically significant improvements to participants' understanding when using explanations produced by BCM, compared to those given by prior art."
originalAbstract: We present the Bayesian Case Model (BCM), a general framework for Bayesian case-based reasoning (CBR) and prototype classification and clustering. BCM brings the intuitive power of CBR to a Bayesian generative framework. The BCM learns prototypes, the ``quintessential observations that best represent clusters in a dataset, by performing joint inference on cluster labels, prototypes and important features. Simultaneously, BCM pursues sparsity by learning subspaces, the sets of features that play important roles in the characterization of the prototypes. The prototype and subspace representation provides quantitative benefits in interpretability while preserving classification accuracy. Human subject experiments verify statistically significant improvements to participants' understanding when using explanations produced by BCM, compared to those given by prior art."

paragraphs: Case-based reasoning explains observations through representative examples. The Bayesian Case Model brings that idea into a Bayesian generative framework for classification and clustering. It learns prototypes: actual observations that serve as characteristic representatives of clusters, making the representation directly connected to examples in the dataset.

The model jointly infers cluster labels, prototypes, and important features. It also learns subspaces, meaning sets of features that matter for characterizing each prototype. This pursues sparsity while allowing an explanation to identify both a representative case and the aspects of that case that are relevant to its cluster.

The paper reports quantitative interpretability benefits while preserving classification accuracy. In human-subject experiments, explanations generated by the model lead to statistically significant improvements in participants' understanding compared with explanations from prior methods. These findings support the combined use of prototypes and selected features as an understandable representation. The contribution is therefore both a probabilistic modeling framework and an experimentally supported approach to explaining its learned groups through concrete cases.
summary.tldr: The Bayesian Case Model learns representative examples and relevant features, improving human understanding while preserving classification accuracy.

title: The Bayesian Case Model: A Generative Approach for Case-Based Reasoning and Prototype Classification

abstract: Subsampling methods have been recently proposed to speed up least squares estimation in large scale settings. However, these algorithms are typically not robust to outliers or corruptions in the observed covariates. The concept of influence that was developed for regression diagnostics can be used to detect such corrupted observations as shown in this paper. This property of influence -- for which we also develop a randomized approximation -- motivates our proposed subsampling algorithm for large scale corrupted linear regression which limits the influence of data points since highly influential points contribute most to the residual error. Under a general model of corrupted observations, we show theoretically and empirically on a variety of simulated and real datasets that our algorithm improves over the current state-of-the-art approximation schemes for ordinary least squares.
originalAbstract: Subsampling methods have been recently proposed to speed up least squares estimation in large scale settings. However, these algorithms are typically not robust to outliers or corruptions in the observed covariates. The concept of influence that was developed for regression diagnostics can be used to detect such corrupted observations as shown in this paper. This property of influence -- for which we also develop a randomized approximation -- motivates our proposed subsampling algorithm for large scale corrupted linear regression which limits the influence of data points since highly influential points contribute most to the residual error. Under a general model of corrupted observations, we show theoretically and empirically on a variety of simulated and real datasets that our algorithm improves over the current state-of-the-art approximation schemes for ordinary least squares.

paragraphs: Subsampling can make least squares regression faster by fitting with a selected portion of a large dataset. The difficulty addressed here is that existing subsampling methods can be vulnerable to outliers and corrupted covariates, meaning errors in the observed input variables. A smaller dataset is not necessarily useful if the selected observations allow corruption to strongly distort the fit.

The paper uses influence, a concept from regression diagnostics, to identify problematic observations. The authors show that influence can detect corrupted data points and develop a randomized approximation to this quantity. They then build a subsampling algorithm that limits the influence of individual observations, motivated by the finding that highly influential points contribute most to residual error.

Under a general model of corrupted observations, the authors provide both theoretical and empirical support for the approach. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show improvements over existing approximation schemes for ordinary least squares. The contribution links the efficiency goal of subsampling with a diagnostic of which observations can disproportionately affect the regression result.
summary.tldr: Influence-guided subsampling improves large-scale least squares estimation when observed inputs contain outliers or corruption.

title: Fast and Robust Least Squares Estimation in Corrupted Linear Models

abstract: We present a policy search method that uses iteratively refitted local linear models to optimize trajectory distributions for large, continuous problems. These trajectory distributions can be used within the framework of guided policy search to learn policies with an arbitrary parameterization. Our method fits time-varying linear dynamics models to speed up learning, but does not rely on learning a global model, which can be difficult when the dynamics are complex and discontinuous. We show that this hybrid approach requires many fewer samples than model-free methods, and can handle complex, nonsmooth dynamics that can pose a challenge for model-based techniques. We present experiments showing that our method can be used to learn complex neural network policies that successfully execute simulated robotic manipulation tasks in partially observed environments with numerous contact discontinuities and underactuation.
originalAbstract: We present a policy search method that uses iteratively refitted local linear models to optimize trajectory distributions for large, continuous problems. These trajectory distributions can be used within the framework of guided policy search to learn policies with an arbitrary parameterization. Our method fits time-varying linear dynamics models to speed up learning, but does not rely on learning a global model, which can be difficult when the dynamics are complex and discontinuous. We show that this hybrid approach requires many fewer samples than model-free methods, and can handle complex, nonsmooth dynamics that can pose a challenge for model-based techniques. We present experiments showing that our method can be used to learn complex neural network policies that successfully execute simulated robotic manipulation tasks in partially observed environments with numerous contact discontinuities and underactuation.

paragraphs: Learning control policies becomes difficult when a system has large continuous spaces and complex dynamics. The paper proposes a policy search method that learns local linear descriptions of those dynamics and repeatedly refits them. These models help optimize distributions over trajectories, providing guidance for learning policies through guided policy search.

The dynamics models vary over time and describe local behavior, avoiding the need to learn one global model of the whole system. That choice matters when dynamics are nonsmooth or discontinuous. The optimized trajectory distributions can guide policies with arbitrary parameterizations, including neural networks, so the local modeling strategy does not require the final policy to share its linear form.

The authors show that the hybrid approach needs many fewer samples than model-free methods and can handle complex, nonsmooth dynamics. Experiments demonstrate neural network policies performing simulated robotic manipulation tasks with partial observation, numerous contact discontinuities, and underactuation. These findings support local model fitting as a way to guide learning in the challenging control settings tested.
summary.tldr: Repeatedly fitted local dynamics models guide neural policy learning with fewer samples in simulated manipulation tasks involving complex dynamics.

title: Learning Neural Network Policies with Guided Policy Search under Unknown Dynamics

abstract: Bayesian nonparametric hidden Markov models are typically learned via fixed truncations of the infinite state space or local Monte Carlo proposals that make small changes to the state space. We develop an inference algorithm for the sticky hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov model that scales to big datasets by processing a few sequences at a time yet allows rapid adaptation of the state space cardinality. Unlike previous point-estimate methods, our novel variational bound penalizes redundant or irrelevant states and thus enables optimization of the state space. Our birth proposals use observed data statistics to create useful new states that escape local optima. Merge and delete proposals remove ineffective states to yield simpler models with more affordable future computations. Experiments on speaker diarization, motion capture, and epigenetic chromatin datasets discover models that are more compact, more interpretable, and better aligned to ground truth segmentations than competitors. We have released an open-source Python implementation which can parallelize local inference steps across sequences.

We develop an inference algorithm for the sticky hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov model that scales to big datasets by processing a few sequences at a time yet allows rapid adaptation of the state space cardinality. Unlike previous point-estimate methods, our novel variational bound penalizes redundant or irrelevant states and thus enables optimization of the state space. Our birth proposals use observed data statistics to create useful new states that escape local optima. Merge and delete proposals remove ineffective states to yield simpler models with more affordable future computations. Experiments on speaker diarization, motion capture, and epigenetic chromatin datasets discover models that are more compact, more interpretable, and better aligned to ground truth segmentations than competitors. We have released an open-source Python implementation which can parallelize local inference steps across sequences.

paragraphs: A nonparametric hidden Markov model must learn both temporal structure and an appropriate number of hidden states. Common approaches fix a truncation or make only small local changes to the state space. This paper develops inference for the sticky hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov model that adapts the state count while processing only a few sequences at a time.

A new variational bound penalizes redundant or irrelevant states, allowing optimization to favor a useful state space. Birth proposals use observed data statistics to introduce states that can escape local optima. Merge and delete proposals remove ineffective states, simplifying the model and reducing the cost of subsequent computation.

Experiments cover speaker diarization, motion capture, and epigenetic chromatin data. The resulting models are more compact, more interpretable, and better aligned with ground-truth segmentations than competitors. The released Python implementation can parallelize local inference across sequences. Together, the results show how actively revising model complexity can support both scalable inference and clearer temporal structure in the evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: Scalable variational inference adds, merges, and deletes hidden states to learn more compact and interpretable temporal models.

title: Scalable Adaptation of State Complexity for Nonparametric Hidden Markov Models

abstract: This paper presents the Deep Convolution Inverse Graphics Network (DC-IGN), a model that aims to learn an interpretable representation of images, disentangled with respect to three-dimensional scene structure and viewing transformations such as depth rotations and lighting variations. The DC-IGN model is composed of multiple layers of convolution and de-convolution operators and is trained using the Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes (SGVB) algorithm. We propose a training procedure to encourage neurons in the graphics code layer to represent a specific transformation (e.g. pose or light). Given a single input image, our model can generate new images of the same object with variations in pose and lighting. We present qualitative and quantitative tests of the model's efficacy at learning a 3D rendering engine for varied object classes including faces and chairs.

The DC-IGN model is composed of multiple layers of convolution and de-convolution operators and is trained using the Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes (SGVB) algorithm. We propose a training procedure to encourage neurons in the graphics code layer to represent a specific transformation (e.g. pose or light). Given a single input image, our model can generate new images of the same object with variations in pose and lighting. We present qualitative and quantitative tests of the model's efficacy at learning a 3D rendering engine for varied object classes including faces and chairs.

paragraphs: An image combines information about an object with the effects of how it is viewed and illuminated. DC-IGN aims to separate these factors into an interpretable representation. Its goal is a graphics code whose components correspond to aspects of three-dimensional scenes and transformations such as pose and lighting.

The network uses multiple convolution and deconvolution layers and is trained with Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes. The authors introduce a training procedure that encourages particular code-layer neurons to represent particular transformations. This encouragement is central to making the representation controllable, rather than merely obtaining a compact description of an image.

Given one input image, the model can generate views of the same object with changed pose or lighting. The paper evaluates this ability qualitatively and quantitatively on object classes including faces and chairs. These tests examine whether the learned representation behaves like a rendering mechanism, connecting interpretable internal factors to visible changes in the generated images.
summary.tldr: DC-IGN learns an image representation encouraged to separate pose and lighting, enabling new views of an object from one image.

title: Deep Convolutional Inverse Graphics Network

abstract: We introduce the Locally Linear Latent Variable Model (LL-LVM), a probabilistic model for non-linear manifold discovery that describes a joint distribution over observations, their manifold coordinates and locally linear maps conditioned on a set of neighbourhood relationships. The model allows straightforward variational optimisation of the posterior distribution on coordinates and locally linear maps from the latent space to the observation space given the data. Thus, the LL-LVM encapsulates the local-geometry preserving intuitions that underlie non-probabilistic methods such as locally linear embedding (LLE). Its probabilistic semantics make it easy to evaluate the quality of hypothesised neighbourhood relationships, select the intrinsic dimensionality of the manifold, construct out-of-sample extensions and to combine the manifold model with additional probabilistic models that capture the structure of coordinates within the manifold.
originalAbstract: We introduce the Locally Linear Latent Variable Model (LL-LVM), a probabilistic model for non-linear manifold discovery that describes a joint distribution over observations, their manifold coordinates and locally linear maps conditioned on a set of neighbourhood relationships. The model allows straightforward variational optimisation of the posterior distribution on coordinates and locally linear maps from the latent space to the observation space given the data. Thus, the LL-LVM encapsulates the local-geometry preserving intuitions that underlie non-probabilistic methods such as locally linear embedding (LLE). Its probabilistic semantics make it easy to evaluate the quality of hypothesised neighbourhood relationships, select the intrinsic dimensionality of the manifold, construct out-of-sample extensions and to combine the manifold model with additional probabilistic models that capture the structure of coordinates within the manifold.

paragraphs: Manifold learning seeks coordinates that describe nonlinear structure in observed data. This paper introduces LL-LVM, a probabilistic model that links the observations, their hidden manifold coordinates, and local linear maps. The model is conditioned on neighborhood relationships, so nearby points provide the organizing structure for learning.

Its central idea is to describe a nonlinear manifold through local mappings from the hidden coordinate space into the observation space. Variational optimization estimates the posterior distribution over both coordinates and maps. This gives a probabilistic form to the intuition behind locally linear embedding: preserve local geometry while discovering a broader nonlinear representation.

The probabilistic formulation also supports decisions beyond finding coordinates. It can evaluate proposed neighborhoods, select the manifold's intrinsic dimension, and extend the representation to new observations. It can additionally connect with other probabilistic models describing structure within the manifold. These capabilities make the representation part of a larger modeling framework rather than only a fixed embedding of the supplied data.
summary.tldr: LL-LVM turns local geometry preservation into a probabilistic manifold model that supports inference, model selection, and extensions to new data.

title: Bayesian Manifold Learning: The Locally Linear Latent Variable Model (LL-LVM)

abstract: Stochastic structured prediction under bandit feedback follows a learning protocol where on each of a sequence of iterations, the learner receives an input, predicts an output structure, and receives partial feedback in form of a task loss evaluation of the predicted structure. We present applications of this learning scenario to convex and non-convex objectives for structured prediction and analyze them as stochastic first-order methods. We present an experimental evaluation on problems of natural language processing over exponential output spaces, and compare convergence speed across different objectives under the practical criterion of optimal task performance on development data and the optimization-theoretic criterion of minimal squared gradient norm. Best results under both criteria are obtained for a non-convex objective for pairwise preference learning under bandit feedback.
originalAbstract: Stochastic structured prediction under bandit feedback follows a learning protocol where on each of a sequence of iterations, the learner receives an input, predicts an output structure, and receives partial feedback in form of a task loss evaluation of the predicted structure. We present applications of this learning scenario to convex and non-convex objectives for structured prediction and analyze them as stochastic first-order methods. We present an experimental evaluation on problems of natural language processing over exponential output spaces, and compare convergence speed across different objectives under the practical criterion of optimal task performance on development data and the optimization-theoretic criterion of minimal squared gradient norm. Best results under both criteria are obtained for a non-convex objective for pairwise preference learning under bandit feedback.

paragraphs: The paper studies structured prediction when feedback is limited to an evaluation of the output the learner actually chooses. At each iteration, the learner sees an input, produces a structured output, and receives its task loss. This bandit protocol makes learning possible from partial feedback about individual decisions over a sequence of interactions.

The authors formulate applications with both convex and non-convex objectives and analyze their updates as stochastic first-order methods. They evaluate natural-language-processing problems whose output spaces grow exponentially. This setting makes the learning objective especially consequential because the learner must improve from feedback on selected structures within a very large set of possibilities.

The experiments compare convergence using two criteria: best task performance on development data and smallest squared gradient norm. These assess practical prediction quality and optimization progress, respectively. A non-convex pairwise preference-learning objective achieves the best results under both criteria. The finding favors that objective in the reported evaluations, while showing why convexity alone does not settle the empirical comparison among these methods.
summary.tldr: For structured prediction with bandit feedback, a non-convex pairwise preference objective performs best under both reported convergence criteria.

title: Stochastic Structured Prediction under Bandit Feedback

abstract: In stochastic convex optimization the goal is to minimize a convex function $F(x) \doteq \E_{f\sim D}[f(x)]$ over a convex set $\K \subset \R^d$ where $D$ is some unknown distribution and each $f(\cdot)$ in the support of $D$ is convex over $\K$. The optimization is based on i.i.d.~samples $f^1,f^2,\ldots,f^n$ from $D$. A common approach to such problems is empirical risk minimization (ERM) that optimizes $F_S(x) \doteq \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\leq n} f^i(x)$. Here we consider the question of how many samples are necessary for ERM to succeed and the closely related question of uniform convergence of $F_S$ to $F$ over $\K$. We demonstrate that in the standard $\ell_p/\ell_q$ setting of Lipschitz-bounded functions over a $\K$ of bounded radius, ERM requires sample size that scales linearly with the dimension $d$. This nearly matches standard upper bounds and improves on $\Omega(\log d)$ dependence proved for $\ell_2/\ell_2$ setting in (Shalev-Shwartz et al. 2009). In stark contrast, these problems can be solved using dimension-independent number of samples for $\ell_2/\ell_2$ setting and $\log d$ dependence for $\ell_1/\ell_\infty$ setting using other approaches. We also demonstrate that for a more general class of range-bounded (but not Lipschitz-bounded) stochastic convex programs an even stronger gap appears already in dimension 2.

paragraphs: Stochastic convex optimization seeks a decision that minimizes an expected convex loss using samples from an unknown distribution. Empirical risk minimization, or ERM, instead minimizes the average loss on those samples. This paper asks how much data ERM needs to succeed and examines the related issue of uniform convergence between empirical and expected objectives.

For the standard norm-based setting with Lipschitz-bounded losses and a bounded-radius domain, the authors establish a sample requirement scaling linearly with dimension. This lower bound nearly matches standard upper bounds. It strengthens the previously known logarithmic dimensional dependence for the Euclidean setting and shows that dimension can be a substantial statistical burden for ERM.

The comparison with other approaches is central: the same optimization settings admit dimension-independent sample requirements in the Euclidean case and logarithmic dependence in the l1/linfinity case. Thus, ERM's data requirements can exceed what solving the underlying problem requires. For a broader class with bounded ranges but no Lipschitz bound, the paper demonstrates an even stronger separation already in two dimensions.
summary.tldr: ERM can require linearly dimension-dependent sample sizes even when other methods solve the same convex optimization settings with far fewer samples.

title: Generalization of ERM in Stochastic Convex Optimization: The Dimension Strikes Back

abstract: We study minimax strategies for the online prediction problem with expert advice. It has been conjectured that a simple adversary strategy, called COMB, is near optimal in this game for any number of experts. Our results and new insights make progress in this direction by showing that, up to a small additive term, COMB is minimax optimal in the finite-time three expert problem. In addition, we provide for this setting a new near minimax optimal COMB-based learner. Prior to this work, in this problem, learners obtaining the optimal multiplicative constant in their regret rate were known only when $K=2$ or $K\rightarrow\infty$. We characterize, when $K=3$, the regret of the game scaling as $\sqrt{8/(9\pi)T}\pm \log(T)^2$ which gives for the first time the optimal constant in the leading ($\sqrt{T}$) term of the regret.

paragraphs: The paper studies online prediction with expert advice as a game between a learner and an adversary. Its focus is minimax behavior: strategies that characterize the best achievable performance against a worst-case opponent. A simple adversary called COMB had been conjectured to be nearly optimal for any number of experts.

The authors establish progress on that conjecture for exactly three experts over a finite number of rounds. They show that COMB is minimax optimal up to a small additive term and construct a corresponding learner that is also nearly minimax optimal. The result addresses both sides of the game within this specific setting.

For T rounds, the game's regret is characterized by sqrt(8T/(9π)), with an additive discrepancy bounded by log(T)^2. This identifies the optimal coefficient of the leading square-root term. Previously, learners achieving the optimal leading coefficient were known only for two experts or in the limit of infinitely many experts. The contribution resolves that coefficient for the finite three-expert case.
summary.tldr: For three experts, the paper gives nearly minimax-optimal adversary and learner strategies and determines the optimal leading regret constant.

title: Near Minimax Optimal Players for the Finite-Time 3-Expert Prediction Problem

abstract: A widespread folklore for explaining the success of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) is that CNNs use a more compact representation than the Fully-connected Neural Network (FNN) and thus require fewer training samples to accurately estimate their parameters. We initiate the study of rigorously characterizing the sample complexity of estimating CNNs. We show that for an $m$-dimensional convolutional filter with linear activation acting on a $d$-dimensional input, the sample complexity of achieving population prediction error of $\epsilon$ is $\widetilde{O(m/\epsilon^2)$, whereas the sample-complexity for its FNN counterpart is lower bounded by $\Omega(d/\epsilon^2)$ samples. Since, in typical settings $m \ll d$, this result demonstrates the advantage of using a CNN. We further consider the sample complexity of estimating a one-hidden-layer CNN with linear activation where both the $m$-dimensional convolutional filter and the $r$-dimensional output weights are unknown. For this model, we show that the sample complexity is $\widetilde{O}\left((m+r)/\epsilon^2\right)$ when the ratio between the stride size and the filter size is a constant. For both models, we also present lower bounds showing our sample complexities are tight up to logarithmic factors. Our main tools for deriving these results are a localized empirical process analysis and a new lemma characterizing the convolutional structure. We believe that these tools may inspire further developments in understanding CNNs.
