paragraphs: Convolutional networks are often said to need fewer training examples because their representations are more compact than those of fully connected networks. This paper gives rigorous sample-complexity results for specified convolutional models with linear activations. The guarantees concern how many samples are needed to achieve a target population prediction error.

For an m-dimensional convolutional filter acting on a d-dimensional input, the sample upper bound scales as m/epsilon² up to logarithmic factors. The fully connected counterpart requires at least order d/epsilon² samples. This establishes an advantage when the filter dimension is much smaller than the input dimension, connecting the convolutional structure directly to a reduced sample requirement.

For a one-hidden-layer model with both an unknown m-dimensional filter and unknown r-dimensional output weights, the upper bound becomes (m+r)/epsilon² up to logarithmic factors, provided the stride-to-filter-size ratio is constant. Matching lower bounds make both results tight within logarithmic factors. The proofs use localized empirical process analysis and a lemma describing convolutional structure, with the guarantees scoped to the linear-activation models analyzed.
summary.tldr: For specified linear-activation CNNs, tight sample-complexity bounds quantify how convolutional structure can reduce training-data requirements.

title: How Many Samples are Needed to Estimate a Convolutional Neural Network?

abstract: The ever-increasing number of parameters in deep neural networks poses challenges for memory-limited applications. Regularize-and-prune methods aim at meeting these challenges by sparsifying the network weights. In this context we quantify the output sensitivity to the parameters (i.e. their relevance to the network output) and introduce a regularization term that gradually lowers the absolute value of parameters with low sensitivity. Thus, a very large fraction of the parameters approach zero and are eventually set to zero by simple thresholding. Our method surpasses most of the recent techniques both in terms of sparsity and error rates. In some cases, the method reaches twice the sparsity obtained by other techniques at equal error rates.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can be difficult to use when memory is limited because they contain many parameters. Regularize-and-prune methods address this by encouraging weights to become small and then setting selected weights to zero. This paper makes the choice of which parameters to shrink depend on their relevance to the network's output.

The authors quantify output sensitivity to individual parameters and introduce a regularization term that gradually reduces the absolute values of parameters with low sensitivity. The resulting process brings a large fraction of weights close to zero. A simple thresholding step then turns those small values into exact zeros, producing a sparse network.

The reported comparisons show better sparsity and error rates than most of the recent techniques considered. In some cases, the method achieves twice the sparsity of other techniques at the same error rate. These findings support using output sensitivity to guide pruning: the method targets parameters according to their measured influence and reports substantial sparsity gains without increasing error in those matched-error comparisons.
summary.tldr: Sensitivity-driven regularization shrinks low-influence weights before pruning, achieving strong sparsity and error results in the reported comparisons.

title: Learning sparse neural networks via sensitivity-driven regularization

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of Gaussian process (GP) optimization with an added robustness requirement: The returned point may be perturbed by an adversary, and we require the function value to remain as high as possible even after this perturbation. This problem is motivated by settings in which the underlying functions during optimization and implementation stages are different, or when one is interested in finding an entire region of good inputs rather than only a single point. We show that standard GP optimization algorithms do not exhibit the desired robustness properties, and provide a novel confidence-bound based algorithm StableOpt for this purpose. We rigorously establish the required number of samples for StableOpt to find a near-optimal point, and we complement this guarantee with an algorithm-independent lower bound. We experimentally demonstrate several potential applications of interest using real-world data sets, and we show that StableOpt consistently succeeds in finding a stable maximizer where several baseline methods fail.

paragraphs: An input that achieves a high function value may become poor after a small change. This paper studies Gaussian process optimization when an adversary can perturb the selected input. The objective is therefore to choose a point whose performance remains as high as possible after that perturbation.

This formulation addresses situations where optimization and implementation conditions differ, as well as cases where an entire region of good inputs is desirable. The authors show that standard Gaussian process optimization algorithms lack the required robustness properties. They introduce StableOpt, a confidence-bound-based algorithm designed around the robust objective, and establish how many samples it needs to find a near-optimal point.

An algorithm-independent lower bound complements that sample guarantee by characterizing limits that apply beyond the proposed method. Experiments using real-world datasets demonstrate potential applications and report that StableOpt consistently finds stable maximizers in cases where several comparison methods fail. These results support optimizing explicitly for performance under perturbation, rather than assuming that a strong unperturbed solution will also remain strong when implemented.
summary.tldr: StableOpt optimizes for inputs that retain high performance under adversarial perturbations, with sample guarantees and supporting experiments.

title: Adversarially Robust Optimization with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Error bound conditions (EBC) are properties that characterize the growth of an objective function when a point is moved away from the optimal set. They have recently received increasing attention in the field of optimization for developing optimization algorithms with fast convergence. However, the studies of EBC in statistical learning are hitherto still limited. The main contributions of this paper are two-fold. First, we develop fast and intermediate rates of empirical risk minimization (ERM) under EBC for risk minimization with Lipschitz continuous, and smooth convex random functions. Second, we establish fast and intermediate rates of an efficient stochastic approximation (SA) algorithm for risk minimization with Lipschitz continuous random functions, which requires only one pass of $n$ samples and adapts to EBC. For both approaches, the convergence rates span a full spectrum between $\widetilde O(1/\sqrt{n})$ and $\widetilde O(1/n)$ depending on the power constant in EBC, and could be even faster than $O(1/n)$ in special cases for ERM. Moreover, these convergence rates are automatically adaptive without using any knowledge of EBC. Overall, this work not only strengthens the understanding of ERM for statistical learning but also brings new fast stochastic algorithms for solving a broad range of statistical learning problems.

paragraphs: An error bound condition describes how an objective grows as a candidate solution moves away from the set of optimal solutions. Such conditions can help explain fast optimization. This paper examines their consequences for statistical learning, where the goal is to control prediction risk using a finite collection of samples.

The authors establish rates for empirical risk minimization under error bound conditions in settings involving Lipschitz continuity and smooth convex random functions. They also analyze an efficient stochastic-approximation algorithm for Lipschitz continuous random functions. That algorithm processes the samples in a single pass, connecting the statistical guarantees with a computationally economical learning procedure.

Depending on the power constant in the error bound condition, the rates range from approximately 1/√n to 1/n, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Empirical risk minimization can be faster than 1/n in special cases. Crucially, both approaches adapt to the condition without being given knowledge of it. The results explain how favorable objective structure can improve learning rates automatically.
summary.tldr: Error bound conditions yield automatically adaptive learning rates for empirical risk minimization and a one-pass stochastic algorithm.

title: Fast Rates of ERM and Stochastic Approximation: Adaptive to Error Bound Conditions

abstract: How to leverage the temporal dimension is a key question in video analysis. Recent works suggest an efficient approach to video feature learning, i.e., factorizing 3D convolutions into separate components respectively for spatial and temporal convolutions. The temporal convolution, however, comes with an implicit assumption – the feature maps across time steps are well aligned so that the features at the same locations can be aggregated. This assumption may be overly strong in practical applications, especially in action recognition where the motion serves as a crucial cue. In this work, we propose a new CNN architecture TrajectoryNet, which incorporates trajectory convolution, a new operation for integrating features along the temporal dimension, to replace the existing temporal convolution. This operation explicitly takes into account the changes in contents caused by deformation or motion, allowing the visual features to be aggregated along the the motion paths, trajectories. On two large-scale action recognition datasets, namely, Something-Something and Kinetics, the proposed network architecture achieves notable improvement over strong baselines.

paragraphs: Video recognition must combine information across time as well as within individual frames. Separating spatial and temporal convolutions is an efficient approach, but ordinary temporal convolution assumes that features at matching image locations are aligned. For moving or deforming content, the same location can refer to different visual content at different times.

The paper introduces TrajectoryNet, which replaces the existing temporal convolution with trajectory convolution. This operation aggregates features along motion paths, explicitly accounting for changes caused by movement or deformation. Its purpose is to combine temporally related content even when that content shifts position across frames, making the aggregation better suited to action recognition.

Experiments on Something-Something and Kinetics show notable improvements over strong baselines. The results support the paper's premise that how temporal features are matched matters, particularly when motion provides crucial evidence about an action. The architectural contribution is a different rule for gathering information across frames: the temporal combination follows trajectories instead of relying on alignment at fixed spatial positions.
summary.tldr: TrajectoryNet improves action recognition by combining video features along motion paths rather than fixed image locations.

title: Trajectory Convolution for Action Recognition

abstract: Video-to-video synthesis (vid2vid) aims at converting an input semantic video, such as videos of human poses or segmentation masks, to an output photorealistic video. While the state-of-the-art of vid2vid has advanced significantly, existing approaches share two major limitations. First, they are data-hungry. Numerous images of a target human subject or a scene are required for training. Second, a learned model has limited generalization capability. A pose-to-human vid2vid model can only synthesize poses of the single person in the training set. It does not generalize to other humans that are not in the training set. To address the limitations, we propose a few-shot vid2vid framework, which learns to synthesize videos of previously unseen subjects or scenes by leveraging few example images of the target at test time. Our model achieves this few-shot generalization capability via a novel network weight generation module utilizing an attention mechanism. We conduct extensive experimental validations with comparisons to strong baselines using several large-scale video datasets including human-dancing videos, talking-head videos, and street-scene videos. The experimental results verify the effectiveness of the proposed framework in addressing the two limitations of existing vid2vid approaches.

paragraphs: Video-to-video synthesis turns structured video inputs, such as poses or segmentation masks, into photorealistic video. Existing approaches described in this paper require many images of a target person or scene and generalize poorly to new targets. A model trained to render one person, for example, remains tied to that person's appearance.

The proposed framework learns to synthesize videos of previously unseen subjects or scenes using only a few target images at test time. Its key component generates network weights using an attention mechanism. This makes the example images part of how the model adapts its synthesis behavior to a new target.

The authors evaluate the framework against strong baselines on large-scale datasets covering dancing people, talking heads, and street scenes. They report that the results support its effectiveness in addressing both target-data requirements and limited generalization. The contribution is therefore a way to reuse a learned video-synthesis system across new appearances, with a few reference images supplying the target-specific information.
summary.tldr: An attention-based weight-generation module enables video synthesis for unseen subjects or scenes from a few example images.

title: Few-shot Video-to-Video Synthesis

abstract: Effective coordination is crucial to solve multi-agent collaborative (MAC) problems. While centralized reinforcement learning methods can optimally solve small MAC instances, they do not scale to large problems and they fail to generalize to scenarios different from those seen during training. In this paper, we consider MAC problems with some intrinsic notion of locality (e.g., geographic proximity) such that interactions between agents and tasks are locally limited. By leveraging this property, we introduce a novel structured prediction approach to assign agents to tasks. At each step, the assignment is obtained by solving a centralized optimization problem (the inference procedure) whose objective function is parameterized by a learned scoring model. We propose different combinations of inference procedures and scoring models able to represent coordination patterns of increasing complexity. The resulting assignment policy can be efficiently learned on small problem instances and readily reused in problems with more agents and tasks (i.e., zero-shot generalization). We report experimental results on a toy search and rescue problem and on several target selection scenarios in StarCraft: Brood War, in which our model significantly outperforms strong rule-based baselines on instances with 5 times more agents and tasks than those seen during training.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent learning requires assigning agents to tasks in ways that support coordinated behavior. Centralized reinforcement learning can solve small instances, but scaling and transferring the learned behavior to different scenarios are difficult. This paper focuses on problems with an intrinsic notion of locality, where interactions between agents and tasks are limited, for example by geographic proximity.

The proposed approach learns a scoring model and uses its scores inside a centralized optimization problem. Solving that problem at each step produces the agent-to-task assignment. Different combinations of scoring models and optimization procedures represent increasingly complex coordination patterns, making the assignment itself a structured prediction problem.

The locality assumption enables a policy learned on small instances to be reused on larger ones without additional training. Experiments cover a toy search-and-rescue problem and target selection in StarCraft: Brood War. On instances with five times as many agents and tasks as those used for training, the method significantly outperforms strong rule-based baselines, supporting its claimed ability to transfer coordination behavior across problem sizes.
summary.tldr: Learned assignment scores and centralized optimization let locally interacting agent teams transfer coordination policies to larger problems.

title: A Structured Prediction Approach for Generalization in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this work, we propose a (linearized) Alternating Direction Method-of-Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm for minimizing a convex function subject to a nonconvex constraint. We focus on the special case where such constraint arises from the specification that a variable should lie in the range of a neural network. This is motivated by recent successful applications of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in tasks like compressive sensing, denoising and robustness against adversarial examples. The derived rates for our algorithm are characterized in terms of certain geometric properties of the generator network, which we show hold for feedforward architectures, under mild assumptions. Unlike gradient descent (GD), it can efficiently handle non-smooth objectives as well as exploit efficient partial minimization procedures, thus being faster in many practical scenarios.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization where the objective is convex but the allowed solutions form a nonconvex set. Its central example requires the solution to be an output of a neural network. A generator therefore acts as a prior: optimization searches among what the network can produce, rather than over every possible value of the variable.

The authors propose a linearized version of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, or ADMM, for this setting. Their convergence rates depend on geometric properties of the generator. They also show that feedforward architectures have the required properties under assumptions described as mild, connecting the analysis to a commonly used family of networks.

The approach is motivated by generative-model applications including compressive sensing, denoising, and resistance to adversarial examples. Its practical appeal is that it can efficiently accommodate nonsmooth objectives and exploit efficient procedures for partially minimizing the problem. The authors state that these features make it faster than gradient descent in many practical scenarios. Both the rate guarantees and the speed claim have a specific scope, rather than covering every generator and objective.
summary.tldr: A linearized ADMM method optimizes with neural-generator constraints, with geometry-dependent guarantees and practical advantages for nonsmooth objectives.

title: Fast and Provable ADMM for Learning with Generative Priors

abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) in both contextual bandits and reinforcement learning allows one to evaluate novel decision policies without needing to conduct exploration, which is often costly or otherwise infeasible. The problem's importance has attracted many proposed solutions, including importance sampling (IS), self-normalized IS (SNIS), and doubly robust (DR) estimates. DR and its variants ensure semiparametric local efficiency if Q-functions are well-specified, but if they are not they can be worse than both IS and SNIS. It also does not enjoy SNIS's inherent stability and boundedness. We propose new estimators for OPE based on empirical likelihood that are always more efficient than IS, SNIS, and DR and satisfy the same stability and boundedness properties as SNIS. On the way, we categorize various properties and classify existing estimators by them. Besides the theoretical guarantees, empirical studies suggest the new estimators provide advantages.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform without deploying it to collect exploratory experience. This matters when exploration is expensive or infeasible. The paper studies the problem in both contextual bandits and reinforcement learning, focusing on how to combine strong statistical efficiency with stable and bounded estimates.

Existing estimators offer different advantages. Doubly robust methods have a local efficiency guarantee when their Q-functions are correctly specified, but misspecification can make them less efficient than importance sampling or its self-normalized form. They also lack the inherent stability and boundedness attributed to self-normalized importance sampling. Thus, one desirable statistical property does not automatically provide the others.

The authors introduce estimators based on empirical likelihood and state that they are always more efficient than importance sampling, self-normalized importance sampling, and doubly robust estimation, while retaining the self-normalized method's stability and boundedness properties. They also organize existing estimators by their properties. Empirical studies suggest practical advantages, complementing the theoretical guarantees rather than replacing them with an exclusively experimental comparison.
summary.tldr: Empirical-likelihood estimators combine stated efficiency improvements over common off-policy estimators with the stability and boundedness of self-normalized importance sampling.

title: Intrinsically Efficient, Stable, and Bounded Off-Policy Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Influence functions estimate the effect of removing a training point on a model without the need to retrain. They are based on a first-order Taylor approximation that is guaranteed to be accurate for sufficiently small changes to the model, and so are commonly used to study the effect of individual points in large datasets. However, we often want to study the effects of large groups of training points, e.g., to diagnose batch effects or apportion credit between different data sources. Removing such large groups can result in significant changes to the model. Are influence functions still accurate in this setting? In this paper, we find that across many different types of groups and for a range of real-world datasets, the predicted effect (using influence functions) of a group correlates surprisingly well with its actual effect, even if the absolute and relative errors are large. Our theoretical analysis shows that such strong correlation arises only under certain settings and need not hold in general, indicating that real-world datasets have particular properties that allow the influence approximation to be accurate.

Their first-order approximation is guaranteed to be accurate for sufficiently small changes. The authors interpret the empirical success as evidence that the studied real-world datasets have properties favorable to the approximation. The contribution is a qualified account of group-level influence: it can provide useful information beyond the small-change regime, while its correlation and numerical accuracy remain distinct questions.
summary.tldr: Influence estimates often correlate well with measured group-removal effects despite large numerical errors, but theory shows this correlation is not general.

title: On the Accuracy of Influence Functions for Measuring Group Effects

abstract: Convolutional neural networks process input data by sending channel-wise feature response maps to subsequent layers. While a lot of progress has been made by making networks deeper, information from each channel can only be propagated from lower levels to higher levels in a hierarchical feed-forward manner. When viewing each filter in the convolutional layer as a neuron, those neurons are not communicating explicitly within each layer in CNNs. We introduce a novel network unit called Cross-channel Communication (C3) block, a simple yet effective module to encourage the neuron communication within the same layer. The C3 block enables neurons to exchange information through a micro neural network, which consists of a feature encoder, a message communicator, and a feature decoder, before sending the information to the next layer. With C3 block, each neuron accounts for the channel-wise responses from other neurons at the same layer and learns more discriminative and complementary representations. Extensive experiments for multiple computer vision tasks show that our proposed mechanism allows shallower networks to aggregate useful information within each layer, and performances outperform baseline deep networks and other competitive methods.

Together, these components let each neuron account for responses from other channels at the same level. The intended result is features that distinguish inputs more effectively and complement the information represented by other channels.

Experiments across multiple computer vision tasks show that this mechanism lets shallower networks combine useful information within individual layers. The tested networks outperform baseline deep networks and other competitive methods. These findings support explicit within-layer communication as a useful architectural choice alongside the established practice of increasing network depth.
summary.tldr: C3 blocks let convolutional channels exchange information within a layer, helping shallower networks outperform deeper baselines in the reported experiments.

title: Cross-channel Communication Networks

abstract: The Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have laid the foundation for many techniques in various applications. Despite achieving remarkable performance in some tasks, the 3D viewpoint generalizability of CNNs is still far behind humans visual capabilities. Although recent efforts, such as the Capsule Networks, have been made to address this issue, these new models are either hard to train and/or incompatible with existing CNN-based techniques specialized for different applications. Observing that humans use binocular vision to understand the world, we study in this paper whether the 3D viewpoint generalizability of CNNs can be achieved via a binocular vision. We propose CNN^{2}, a CNN that takes two images as input, which resembles the process of an object being viewed from the left eye and the right eye. CNN^{2} uses novel augmentation, pooling, and convolutional layers to learn a sense of three-dimensionality in a recursive manner. Empirical evaluation shows that CNN^{2} has improved viewpoint generalizability compared to vanilla CNNs. Furthermore, CNN^{2} is easy to implement and train, and is compatible with existing CNN-based specialized techniques for different applications.

Strong performance on other tasks does not automatically supply this capability. The authors investigate whether a design inspired by binocular vision can improve viewpoint generalization while remaining compatible with the broader family of CNN-based techniques.

Their model, CNN², receives two images, resembling the paired views supplied by a left and right eye. It introduces augmentation, pooling, and convolutional layers intended to develop a sense of three-dimensionality recursively. The paired input and the modified processing layers work together as the architectural proposal; the approach retains a convolutional foundation that can fit existing application-specific methods.

Empirical evaluation finds better viewpoint generalization than vanilla CNNs. The authors also describe the model as straightforward to implement and train, with compatibility across specialized CNN techniques. These findings support binocular input as a useful design direction for the evaluated settings, without establishing that the model reaches the viewpoint understanding of human vision.
summary.tldr: CNN² processes paired images with modified convolutional components to improve viewpoint generalization over vanilla CNNs.

title: CNN^{2}: Viewpoint Generalization via a Binocular Vision

abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAE) have quickly become a central tool in machine learning, applicable to a broad range of data types and latent variable models. By far the most common first step, taken by seminal papers and by core software libraries alike, is to model MNIST data using a deep network parameterizing a Bernoulli likelihood. This practice contains what appears to be and what is often set aside as a minor inconvenience: the pixel data is [0,1] valued, not {0,1} as supported by the Bernoulli likelihood. Here we show that, far from being a triviality or nuisance that is convenient to ignore, this error has profound importance to VAE, both qualitative and quantitative. We introduce and fully characterize a new [0,1]-supported, single parameter distribution: the continuous Bernoulli, which patches this pervasive bug in VAE. This distribution is not nitpicking; it produces meaningful performance improvements across a range of metrics and datasets, including sharper image samples, and suggests a broader class of performant VAE.

paragraphs: A common variational-autoencoder setup models image pixels with a Bernoulli likelihood. The paper identifies a mismatch in this practice: a Bernoulli variable takes only the values zero and one, while the pixel data being modeled can take any value between them. The authors argue that this discrepancy materially changes the model’s behavior.

They introduce and fully characterize the continuous Bernoulli, a single-parameter probability distribution supported on the entire interval from zero to one. This provides a likelihood whose allowed values match the continuous pixel data in question. The contribution directly addresses the probabilistic model used by the VAE, rather than treating the support mismatch as an inconsequential implementation detail.

The authors report meaningful improvements across multiple datasets and evaluation metrics, including sharper generated images. Their analysis finds both qualitative and quantitative consequences from correcting the likelihood. These results show that choosing a distribution compatible with the observed data can have practical effects on VAE performance, and they motivate investigation of a broader class of effective VAE models.
summary.tldr: The continuous Bernoulli corrects a mismatch between continuous pixel values and Bernoulli likelihoods, improving reported VAE performance.

title: The continuous Bernoulli: fixing a pervasive error in variational autoencoders

abstract: Designing deep neural networks is an art that often involves an expensive search over candidate architectures. To overcome this for recurrent neural nets (RNNs), we establish a connection between the hidden state dynamics in an RNN and gradient descent (GD). We then integrate momentum into this framework and propose a new family of RNNs, called {\em MomentumRNNs}. We theoretically prove and numerically demonstrate that MomentumRNNs alleviate the vanishing gradient issue in training RNNs. We study the momentum long-short term memory (MomentumLSTM) and verify its advantages in convergence speed and accuracy over its LSTM counterpart across a variety of benchmarks. We also demonstrate that MomentumRNN is applicable to many types of recurrent cells, including those in the state-of-the-art orthogonal RNNs. Finally, we show that other advanced momentum-based optimization methods, such as Adam and Nesterov accelerated gradients with a restart, can be easily incorporated into the MomentumRNN framework for designing new recurrent cells with even better performance.

paragraphs: Designing recurrent neural networks often involves searching through many possible architectures. This paper develops a more structured route by connecting the evolution of an RNN’s hidden state to gradient descent. It then incorporates momentum into that interpretation, producing a family of recurrent architectures called MomentumRNNs.

The key change concerns the recurrent cell’s internal dynamics. Momentum becomes part of how the hidden state evolves, making optimization ideas a guide for architecture design. The authors prove theoretically and demonstrate numerically that the resulting networks alleviate vanishing gradients, the weakening of training signals as they propagate through recurrent computation.

A momentum-based LSTM variant improves convergence speed and accuracy over its LSTM counterpart across the evaluated benchmarks. The framework also applies to other recurrent cells, including orthogonal RNNs. Finally, the authors incorporate ideas from Adam and restarted Nesterov acceleration to design further cells with better reported performance. Together, these results support using established optimization mechanisms as reusable building blocks for recurrent architectures.
summary.tldr: MomentumRNN incorporates momentum into recurrent hidden-state dynamics, alleviating vanishing gradients and improving performance in the reported evaluations.

title: MomentumRNN: Integrating Momentum into Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Reconstructing seeing images from fMRI recordings is an absorbing research area in neuroscience and provides a potential brain-reading technology. The challenge lies in that visual encoding in brain is highly complex and not fully revealed. Inspired by the theory that visual features are hierarchically represented in cortex, we propose to break the complex visual signals into multi-level components and decode each component separately. Specifically, we decode shape and semantic representations from the lower and higher visual cortex respectively, and merge the shape and semantic information to images by a generative adversarial network (Shape-Semantic GAN). This 'divide and conquer' strategy captures visual information more accurately. Experiments demonstrate that Shape-Semantic GAN improves the reconstruction similarity and image quality, and achieves the state-of-the-art image reconstruction performance.

It uses that idea to divide the reconstruction problem into components that can be decoded separately.

The demonstrated task is reconstruction of viewed images from fMRI; the broader possibility of brain-reading technology serves as motivation for this specific decoding problem.
summary.tldr: Shape-Semantic GAN combines separately decoded shape and semantic brain representations to improve reconstruction of viewed images from fMRI.

title: Reconstructing Perceptive Images from Brain Activity by Shape-Semantic GAN

abstract: Biological neural networks face a formidable task: performing reliable computations in the face of intrinsic stochasticity in individual neurons, imprecisely specified synaptic connectivity, and nonnegligible delays in synaptic transmission. A common approach to combatting such biological heterogeneity involves averaging over large redundant networks of N neurons resulting in coding errors that decrease classically as the square root of N. Recent work demonstrated a novel mechanism whereby recurrent spiking networks could efficiently encode dynamic stimuli achieving a superclassical scaling in which coding errors decrease as 1/N. This specific mechanism involved two key ideas: predictive coding, and a tight balance, or cancellation between strong feedforward inputs and strong recurrent feedback. However, the theoretical principles governing the efficacy of balanced predictive coding and its robustness to noise, synaptic weight heterogeneity and communication delays remain poorly understood. To discover such principles, we introduce an analytically tractable model of balanced predictive coding, in which the degree of balance and the degree of weight disorder can be dissociated unlike in previous balanced network models, and we develop a mean-field theory of coding accuracy. Overall, our work provides and solves a general theoretical framework for dissecting the differential contributions neural noise, synaptic disorder, chaos, synaptic delays, and balance to the fidelity of predictive neural codes, reveals the fundamental role that balance plays in achieving superclassical scaling, and unifies previously disparate models in theoretical neuroscience.

summary.tldr: A tractable theory separates balance from connection disorder to explain their roles in predictive coding accuracy amid noise, chaos, and delays.

title: Predictive coding in balanced neural networks with noise, chaos and delays

abstract: The recent progress on automatically searching augmentation policies has boosted the performance substantially for various tasks. A key component of automatic augmentation search is the evaluation process for a particular augmentation policy, which is utilized to return reward and usually runs thousands of times. A plain evaluation process, which includes full model training and validation, would be time-consuming. To achieve efficiency, many choose to sacrifice evaluation reliability for speed. In this paper, we dive into the dynamics of augmented training of the model. This inspires us to design a powerful and efficient proxy task based on the Augmentation-Wise Weight Sharing (AWS) to form a fast yet accurate evaluation process in an elegant way. Comprehensive analysis verifies the superiority of this approach in terms of effectiveness and efficiency. The augmentation policies found by our method achieve superior accuracies compared with existing auto-augmentation search methods. On CIFAR-10, we achieve a top-1 error rate of 1.24%, which is currently the best performing single model without extra training data. On ImageNet, we get a top-1 error rate of 20.36% for ResNet-50, which leads to 3.34% absolute error rate reduction over the baseline augmentation.

This paper targets that evaluation bottleneck rather than treating speed and reliability as an unavoidable exchange.

The authors study the dynamics of training with augmented data and use the findings to construct a proxy task based on Augmentation-Wise Weight Sharing. Their analysis reports advantages in both effectiveness and efficiency, and the discovered policies outperform those found by existing automatic augmentation search methods.

These outcomes connect improved policy evaluation to stronger final models.
summary.tldr: Augmentation-Wise Weight Sharing speeds up augmentation-policy evaluation while finding policies that improve reported classification accuracy.

title: Improving Auto-Augment via Augmentation-Wise Weight Sharing

abstract: Temporal Graph Networks (TGNs) are powerful on modeling temporal graph data based on their increased complexity. Higher complexity carries with it a higher risk of overfitting, which makes TGNs capture random noise instead of essential semantic information. To address this issue, our idea is to transform the temporal graphs using data augmentation (DA) with adaptive magnitudes, so as to effectively augment the input features and preserve the essential semantic information. Based on this idea, we present the MeTA (Memory Tower Augmentation) module: a multi-level module that processes the augmented graphs of different magnitudes on separate levels, and performs message passing across levels to provide adaptively augmented inputs for every prediction. MeTA can be flexibly applied to the training of popular TGNs to improve their effectiveness without increasing their time complexity. To complement MeTA, we propose three DA strategies to realistically model noise by modifying both the temporal and topological features. Empirical results on standard datasets show that MeTA yields significant gains for the popular TGN models on edge prediction and node classification in an efficient manner.

This paper tackles that problem through data augmentation with an adjustable strength. The aim is to vary training inputs enough to improve learning while preserving the information that gives the graph its meaning.

The proposed Memory Tower Augmentation module, called MeTA, processes graph augmentations at multiple levels. Each level handles a different augmentation magnitude, and messages pass between levels to provide adaptively augmented inputs for each prediction. The authors also introduce three augmentation strategies that alter temporal and topological features to model noise realistically. Together, these components make augmentation strength part of the prediction process.

MeTA can be incorporated into the training of popular temporal graph models without increasing their time complexity. Experiments on standard datasets show significant improvements in predicting edges and classifying nodes. These findings support using multiple interacting augmentation levels to improve the tested models efficiently, while addressing the risk that increased modeling capacity captures incidental noise.
summary.tldr: MeTA adaptively combines temporal graph augmentations of different strengths to improve edge prediction and node classification efficiently.

title: Adaptive Data Augmentation on Temporal Graphs

abstract: Anderson mixing has been heuristically applied to reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms for accelerating convergence and improving the sampling efficiency of deep RL. Despite its heuristic improvement of convergence, a rigorous mathematical justification for the benefits of Anderson mixing in RL has not yet been put forward. In this paper, we provide deeper insights into a class of acceleration schemes built on Anderson mixing that improve the convergence of deep RL algorithms. Our main results establish a connection between Anderson mixing and quasi-Newton methods and prove that Anderson mixing increases the convergence radius of policy iteration schemes by an extra contraction factor. The key focus of the analysis roots in the fixed-point iteration nature of RL. We further propose a stabilization strategy by introducing a stable regularization term in Anderson mixing and a differentiable, non-expansive MellowMax operator that can allow both faster convergence and more stable behavior. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method enhances the convergence, stability, and performance of RL algorithms.

paragraphs: Anderson mixing had already been used heuristically to make reinforcement learning converge faster and use samples more efficiently. This paper develops a mathematical explanation for those benefits. It examines reinforcement learning through its fixed-point iterations: repeated updates that seek a solution unchanged by the update rule.

The analysis connects Anderson mixing to quasi-Newton optimization methods. It also proves that Anderson mixing enlarges the convergence radius of policy iteration schemes by an additional contraction factor. This concerns the region from which convergence can be obtained, giving a more precise account of the method’s benefits than empirical acceleration alone.

These modifications are intended to support both faster convergence and more stable behavior. Extensive experiments report improvements in convergence, stability, and reinforcement learning performance. The paper therefore contributes both an explanation of an existing acceleration idea and a modified method designed to make that idea more dependable in deep reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: The paper explains Anderson mixing’s convergence benefits in reinforcement learning and introduces regularization and MellowMax to improve stability.

title: Damped Anderson Mixing for Deep Reinforcement Learning: Acceleration, Convergence, and Stabilization

abstract: Although application examples of multilevel optimization have already been discussed since the 1990s, the development of solution methods was almost limited to bilevel cases due to the difficulty of the problem. In recent years, in machine learning, Franceschi et al. have proposed a method for solving bilevel optimization problems by replacing their lower-level problems with the $T$ steepest descent update equations with some prechosen iteration number $T$. In this paper, we have developed a gradient-based algorithm for multilevel optimization with $n$ levels based on their idea and proved that our reformulation asymptotically converges to the original multilevel problem. As far as we know, this is one of the first algorithms with some theoretical guarantee for multilevel optimization. Numerical experiments show that a trilevel hyperparameter learning model considering data poisoning produces more stable prediction results than an existing bilevel hyperparameter learning model in noisy data settings.

paragraphs: Multilevel optimization involves nested decisions: solving one optimization problem depends on the solutions of problems below it. Although applications had been discussed for decades, methods largely addressed only two levels. This paper develops a gradient-based method for problems with an arbitrary number of levels, extending an approach previously used for bilevel optimization.

The starting idea is to replace a lower-level optimization problem with a fixed sequence of steepest-descent updates. This makes the lower-level computation part of the reformulated problem. The authors extend this construction across multiple levels and prove that their reformulation approaches the original multilevel problem asymptotically. That guarantee concerns the limiting reformulation, rather than exact equivalence after any fixed number of updates.

The experiments examine a three-level hyperparameter-learning model that accounts for data poisoning. In noisy-data settings, it produces more stable predictions than an existing two-level model. This finding supports the usefulness of the additional optimization level in the tested setting, while the broader contribution is a method with theoretical support for optimization beyond two nested levels.
summary.tldr: A gradient-based method extends optimization to multiple nested levels, with an asymptotic reformulation guarantee and improved prediction stability in a tested three-level application.

title: A Gradient Method for Multilevel Optimization

abstract: (Distributionally) robust optimization has gained momentum in machine learning community recently, due to its promising applications in developing generalizable learning paradigms. In this paper, we derive generalization bounds for robust optimization and Wasserstein robust optimization for Lipschitz and piecewise Hölder smooth loss functions under both stochastic and adversarial setting, assuming that the underlying data distribution satisfies transportation-information inequalities. The proofs are built on new generalization bounds for variation regularization (such as Lipschitz or gradient regularization) and its connection with robustness.

paragraphs: Robust optimization is motivated partly by the hope that preparing for unfavorable conditions will improve performance beyond the training data. This paper studies that connection mathematically. It derives generalization bounds for robust optimization and Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization, providing guarantees that relate robust learning to performance outside the observed sample.

The results cover Lipschitz and piecewise Hölder smooth loss functions in both stochastic and adversarial settings. They assume that the underlying data distribution satisfies transportation-information inequalities. These restrictions are part of the setting in which the bounds are established: the paper connects robustness and generalization for specified loss classes and distributions rather than asserting that robustness always guarantees generalization.

The proofs build on new bounds for variation regularization, including Lipschitz and gradient regularization. Such regularization controls how a loss changes, and the analysis uses its connection with robustness to obtain the main results. The contribution therefore supplies both generalization guarantees and an analytical route to them, linking control of variation with the behavior of robust optimization.
summary.tldr: The paper derives conditional generalization guarantees for robust optimization by connecting robustness with regularization of loss variation.

title: Generalization Bounds for (Wasserstein) Robust Optimization

abstract: Latent variable models are ubiquitous in the exploratory analysis of neural population recordings, where they allow researchers to summarize the activity of large populations of neurons in lower dimensional ‘latent’ spaces. Existing methods can generally be categorized into (i) Bayesian methods that facilitate flexible incorporation of prior knowledge and uncertainty estimation, but which typically do not scale to large datasets; and (ii) highly parameterized methods without explicit priors that scale better but often struggle in the low-data regime. Here, we bridge this gap by developing a fully Bayesian yet scalable version of Gaussian process factor analysis (bGPFA), which models neural data as arising from a set of inferred latent processes with a prior that encourages smoothness over time. Additionally, bGPFA uses automatic relevance determination to infer the dimensionality of neural activity directly from the training data during optimization. To enable the analysis of continuous recordings without trial structure, we introduce a novel variational inference strategy that scales near-linearly in time and also allows for non-Gaussian noise models appropriate for electrophysiological recordings. We apply bGPFA to continuous recordings spanning 30 minutes with over 14 million data points from primate motor and somatosensory cortices during a self-paced reaching task. We show that neural activity progresses from an initial state at target onset to a reach- specific preparatory state well before movement onset. The distance between these initial and preparatory latent states is predictive of reaction times across reaches, suggesting that such preparatory dynamics have behavioral relevance despite the lack of externally imposed delay periods. Additionally, bGPFA discovers latent processes that evolve over slow timescales on the order of several seconds and contain complementary information about reaction time. These timescales are longer than those revealed by methods which focus on individual movement epochs and may reflect fluctuations in e.g. task engagement.

summary.tldr: Scalable Bayesian GPFA infers neural dimensionality and uncovers both movement preparation and slower activity associated with reaction times.

title: Scalable Bayesian GPFA with automatic relevance determination and discrete noise models

abstract: Automatically detecting anomalies in event data can provide substantial value in domains such as healthcare, DevOps, and information security. In this paper, we frame the problem of detecting anomalous continuous-time event sequences as out-of-distribution (OOD) detection for temporal point processes (TPPs). First, we show how this problem can be approached using goodness-of-fit (GoF) tests. We then demonstrate the limitations of popular GoF statistics for TPPs and propose a new test that addresses these shortcomings. The proposed method can be combined with various TPP models, such as neural TPPs, and is easy to implement. In our experiments, we show that the proposed statistic excels at both traditional GoF testing, as well as at detecting anomalies in simulated and real-world data.

paragraphs: An event sequence contains both occurrences and their timing, making unusual temporal patterns a distinct detection problem. This paper treats anomalous continuous-time sequences as observations outside the distribution described by a temporal point process. That framing connects anomaly detection to a probabilistic model of how events unfold over time.

The authors first examine goodness-of-fit tests, which assess whether observed data agree with a proposed model. They demonstrate limitations in popular statistics used for temporal point processes and introduce a new test designed to address those shortcomings. The method can work with different point-process models, including neural ones, and is described as easy to implement.

Experiments assess both conventional goodness-of-fit testing and anomaly detection on simulated and real-world data. The proposed statistic performs strongly in both roles. This matters because checking model agreement and identifying unusual sequences become parts of the same statistical approach. The contribution centers on the testing statistic and its compatibility with multiple models, making it applicable beyond one particular temporal point-process architecture.
summary.tldr: A new goodness-of-fit statistic improves detection of anomalous event sequences across temporal point-process models.

title: Detecting Anomalous Event Sequences with Temporal Point Processes

abstract: We consider Bayesian optimization of the output of a network of functions, where each function takes as input the output of its parent nodes, and where the network takes significant time to evaluate. Such problems arise, for example, in reinforcement learning, engineering design, and manufacturing. While the standard Bayesian optimization approach observes only the final output, our approach delivers greater query efficiency by leveraging information that the former ignores: intermediate output within the network. This is achieved by modeling the nodes of the network using Gaussian processes and choosing the points to evaluate using, as our acquisition function, the expected improvement computed with respect to the implied posterior on the objective. Although the non-Gaussian nature of this posterior prevents computing our acquisition function in closed form, we show that it can be efficiently maximized via sample average approximation. In addition, we prove that our method is asymptotically consistent, meaning that it finds a globally optimal solution as the number of evaluations grows to infinity, thus generalizing previously known convergence results for the expected improvement. Notably, this holds even though our method might not evaluate the domain densely, instead leveraging problem structure to leave regions unexplored. Finally, we show that our approach dramatically outperforms standard Bayesian optimization methods in several synthetic and real-world problems.

paragraphs: Some expensive optimization problems consist of connected functions, with each function consuming outputs from earlier nodes. Standard Bayesian optimization observes the final result and can overlook useful intermediate measurements. This paper models those intermediate functions explicitly so that each costly evaluation provides more information about how the overall objective behaves.

The method places Gaussian process models on the network's nodes and chooses evaluations using expected improvement under the resulting objective distribution. That distribution is non-Gaussian, so the acquisition function lacks a closed-form expression. The authors show that sample average approximation can nevertheless be used to maximize it efficiently.

They also prove asymptotic consistency: as the number of evaluations tends to infinity, the method finds a global optimum. Notably, this can hold without evaluating the domain densely, because network structure can justify leaving some regions unexplored. Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems report substantial gains over standard Bayesian optimization, supporting the value of observing and modeling intermediate outputs.
summary.tldr: Modeling intermediate outputs in expensive function networks makes Bayesian optimization more query-efficient and supports an asymptotic global-optimum guarantee.

title: Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks

abstract: A major problem in motor control is understanding how the brain plans and executes proper movements in the face of delayed and noisy stimuli. A prominent framework for addressing such control problems is Optimal Feedback Control (OFC). OFC generates control actions that optimize behaviorally relevant criteria by integrating noisy sensory stimuli and the predictions of an internal model using the Kalman filter or its extensions. However, a satisfactory neural model of Kalman filtering and control is lacking because existing proposals have the following limitations: not considering the delay of sensory feedback, training in alternating phases, requiring knowledge of the noise covariance matrices, as well as that of systems dynamics. Moreover, the majority of these studies considered Kalman filtering in isolation, and not jointly with control. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel online algorithm which combines adaptive Kalman filtering with a model free control approach (i.e., policy gradient algorithm). We implement this algorithm in a biologically plausible neural network with local synaptic plasticity rules. This network, with local synaptic plasticity rules, performs system identification, Kalman filtering and control with delayed noisy sensory feedback. This network performs system identification and Kalman filtering, without the need for multiple phases with distinct update rules or the knowledge of the noise covariances. It can perform state estimation with delayed sensory feedback, with the help of an internal model. It learns the control policy without requiring any knowledge of the dynamics, thus avoiding the need for weight transport. In this way, our implementation of OFC solves the credit assignment problem needed to produce the appropriate sensory-motor control in the presence of stimulus delay.

paragraphs: Movement control must cope with sensory information that is both noisy and delayed. Optimal feedback control addresses this by combining observations with an internal model's predictions and choosing actions that optimize relevant behavioral criteria. Translating that framework into a plausible neural learning mechanism has remained challenging.

The paper combines adaptive Kalman filtering with a model-free policy-gradient controller in an online algorithm. A neural implementation uses local synaptic plasticity rules to learn system properties, estimate state, and control behavior. Its internal model helps estimate the current state despite delayed sensory feedback.

The approach learns system identification and filtering without separate training phases or prior knowledge of noise covariances. Its controller also learns without requiring known system dynamics, avoiding the need for weight transport. This brings estimation and action learning together rather than considering filtering alone. The contribution is a biologically plausible implementation that addresses the credit-assignment problem for the studied delayed, noisy control setting: local updates support learning the computations needed to produce appropriate movements.
summary.tldr: An online neural controller combines adaptive state estimation and policy-gradient learning using local plasticity rules to handle noisy, delayed feedback.

title: Neural optimal feedback control with local learning rules

abstract: In several real world applications, machine learning models are deployed to make predictions on data whose distribution changes gradually along time, leading to a drift between the train and test distributions. Such models are often re-trained on new data periodically, and they hence need to generalize to data not too far into the future. In this context, there is much prior work on enhancing temporal generalization, e.g. continuous transportation of past data, kernel smoothed time-sensitive parameters and more recently, adversarial learning of time-invariant features. However, these methods share several limitations, e.g, poor scalability, training instability, and dependence on unlabeled data from the future. Responding to the above limitations, we propose a simple method that starts with a model with time-sensitive parameters but regularizes its temporal complexity using a Gradient Interpolation (GI) loss. GI allows the decision boundary to change along time and can still prevent overfitting to the limited training time snapshots by allowing task-specific control over changes along time. We compare our method to existing baselines on multiple real-world datasets, which show that GI outperforms more complicated generative and adversarial approaches on the one hand, and simpler gradient regularization methods on the other.

paragraphs: When data distributions drift gradually over time, a deployed model must predict beyond the time period represented in its training data. Periodic retraining makes generalization into the near future especially relevant. This paper addresses that setting with a model whose parameters depend on time, allowing its predictions to adapt to temporal change.

The proposed Gradient Interpolation loss regularizes the complexity of that time dependence. It allows the decision boundary to move while controlling how it changes according to the task. This aims to avoid overfitting the limited time snapshots available during training, while still representing changes that a strictly time-invariant predictor would not capture.

The authors compare the method with existing approaches on multiple real-world datasets. Gradient Interpolation outperforms both more complicated generative and adversarial approaches and simpler gradient-regularization methods in those experiments. The findings support controlled temporal flexibility as a useful approach to near-future prediction. The intended setting is gradually changing data and relatively short extrapolation beyond training, consistent with models that are periodically retrained.
summary.tldr: Gradient Interpolation controls how a model changes over time, improving near-future prediction under gradual distribution drift in the reported experiments.

title: Training for the Future: A Simple Gradient Interpolation Loss to Generalize Along Time

abstract: State-of-the-art Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have limited scalability with respect to the graph and model sizes. On large graphs, increasing the model depth often means exponential expansion of the scope (i.e., receptive field). Beyond just a few layers, two fundamental challenges emerge: 1. degraded expressivity due to oversmoothing, and 2. expensive computation due to neighborhood explosion. We propose a design principle to decouple the depth and scope of GNNs – to generate representation of a target entity (i.e., a node or an edge), we first extract a localized subgraph as the bounded-size scope, and then apply a GNN of arbitrary depth on top of the subgraph. A properly extracted subgraph consists of a small number of critical neighbors, while excluding irrelevant ones. The GNN, no matter how deep it is, smooths the local neighborhood into informative representation rather than oversmoothing the global graph into “white noise”. Theoretically, decoupling improves the GNN expressive power from the perspectives of graph signal processing (GCN), function approximation (GraphSAGE) and topological learning (GIN). Empirically, on seven graphs (with up to 110M nodes) and six backbone GNN architectures, our design achieves significant accuracy improvement with orders of magnitude reduction in computation and hardware cost.

paragraphs: Making a graph neural network deeper often also expands the neighborhood it must process. On large graphs, that expansion can become extremely expensive. Repeated information mixing can additionally make representations less distinctive, a problem called oversmoothing. This paper separates these two choices: how much computation happens through network layers and how much of the graph those layers can access.

For each target node or edge, the method first extracts a localized subgraph with bounded size. It then applies a graph neural network of arbitrary depth within that scope. The intended benefit depends on extracting a useful neighborhood containing critical neighbors while excluding irrelevant ones. Information mixing can then produce a meaningful local representation without spreading across the entire graph.

The authors establish improvements in expressive power through analyses of GCN, GraphSAGE, and GIN. Experiments cover seven graphs, including one with up to 110 million nodes, and six backbone architectures. They report significant accuracy improvements alongside orders-of-magnitude reductions in computation and hardware cost, supporting bounded local scope as a practical design principle.
summary.tldr: Running deep graph neural networks inside carefully selected, bounded subgraphs improves accuracy and sharply reduces computation in the reported experiments.

title: Decoupling the Depth and Scope of Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Meta learning approaches to few-shot classification are computationally efficient at test time, requiring just a few optimization steps or single forward pass to learn a new task, but they remain highly memory-intensive to train. This limitation arises because a task's entire support set, which can contain up to 1000 images, must be processed before an optimization step can be taken. Harnessing the performance gains offered by large images thus requires either parallelizing the meta-learner across multiple GPUs, which may not be available, or trade-offs between task and image size when memory constraints apply. We improve on both options by proposing LITE, a general and memory efficient episodic training scheme that enables meta-training on large tasks composed of large images on a single GPU. We achieve this by observing that the gradients for a task can be decomposed into a sum of gradients over the task's training images. This enables us to perform a forward pass on a task's entire training set but realize significant memory savings by back-propagating only a random subset of these images which we show is an unbiased approximation of the full gradient. We use LITE to train meta-learners and demonstrate new state-of-the-art accuracy on the real-world ORBIT benchmark and 3 of the 4 parts of the challenging VTAB+MD benchmark relative to leading meta-learners. LITE also enables meta-learners to be competitive with transfer learning approaches but at a fraction of the test-time computational cost, thus serving as a counterpoint to the recent narrative that transfer learning is all you need for few-shot classification.

paragraphs: Few-shot meta-learners can adapt to new tasks with little test-time computation, yet training them can require substantial memory. An entire task's support set must be processed before an optimization step, making large tasks with large images difficult to accommodate. This paper introduces LITE, an episodic training scheme designed to make such training possible on one GPU.

LITE uses a decomposition of the task gradient into contributions from its training images. It performs a forward pass over the complete training set but backpropagates through only a randomly selected subset. The authors show that this produces an unbiased approximation of the full gradient while substantially reducing memory use.

Meta-learners trained with LITE achieve new leading accuracy on ORBIT and three of four parts of VTAB+MD relative to leading meta-learners. They also become competitive with transfer-learning approaches while using a fraction of the test-time computation. These findings show how reducing training memory requirements can make the benefits of large-image meta-learning accessible without sacrificing its computationally economical adaptation.
summary.tldr: LITE reduces meta-training memory through unbiased subset backpropagation, enabling large-image tasks on a single GPU.

title: Memory Efficient Meta-Learning with Large Images

abstract: Datasets can be biased due to societal inequities, human biases, under-representation of minorities, etc. Our goal is to certify that models produced by a learning algorithm are pointwise-robust to dataset biases. This is a challenging problem: it entails learning models for a large, or even infinite, number of datasets, ensuring that they all produce the same prediction. We focus on decision-tree learning due to the interpretable nature of the models. Our approach allows programmatically specifying \emph{bias models} across a variety of dimensions (e.g., label-flipping or missing data), composing types of bias, and targeting bias towards a specific group. To certify robustness, we use a novel symbolic technique to evaluate a decision-tree learner on a large, or infinite, number of datasets, certifying that each and every dataset produces the same prediction for a specific test point. We evaluate our approach on datasets that are commonly used in the fairness literature, and demonstrate our approach's viability on a range of bias models.

paragraphs: Dataset bias can change what a learning algorithm predicts for an individual. This paper asks whether one can certify that a particular prediction would stay the same across a specified collection of biased datasets. The challenge is that this collection may contain an enormous, or even infinite, number of alternatives.

The authors focus on decision-tree learners and let users describe bias through programmable models. These descriptions can include flipped labels, missing data, combinations of different biases, and changes directed at a particular group. A symbolic technique evaluates the learner across the represented datasets, allowing the method to reason about their predictions without separately training a tree on every alternative.

The resulting certificate is pointwise: for a specific test input, every dataset covered by the bias model leads to the same prediction. Its scope therefore depends on the specified dataset changes and the input being checked. Evaluations on datasets commonly used in fairness research demonstrate that this approach is viable across a range of bias models.
summary.tldr: Symbolic analysis certifies when a decision-tree learner gives the same prediction for a test point across programmable dataset biases.

title: Certifying Robustness to Programmable Data Bias in Decision Trees

abstract: Optimal decision making requires that classifiers produce uncertainty estimates consistent with their empirical accuracy. However, deep neural networks are often under- or over-confident in their predictions. Consequently, methods have been developed to improve the calibration of their predictive uncertainty both during training and post-hoc. In this work, we propose differentiable losses to improve calibration based on a soft (continuous) version of the binning operation underlying popular calibration-error estimators. When incorporated into training, these soft calibration losses achieve state-of-the-art single-model ECE across multiple datasets with less than 1% decrease in accuracy. For instance, we observe an 82% reduction in ECE (70% relative to the post-hoc rescaled ECE) in exchange for a 0.7% relative decrease in accuracy relative to the cross entropy baseline on CIFAR-100.When incorporated post-training, the soft-binning-based calibration error objective improves upon temperature scaling, a popular recalibration method. Overall, experiments across losses and datasets demonstrate that using calibration-sensitive procedures yield better uncertainty estimates under dataset shift than the standard practice of using a cross entropy loss and post-hoc recalibration methods.

paragraphs: A classifier's confidence is useful only when it agrees with how often its predictions are correct. Neural networks can be overconfident or underconfident, even when their classification accuracy is good. This paper introduces training objectives that directly target calibration through a continuous version of the binning operation used in common calibration-error estimates.

Replacing discrete binning with soft binning makes the calibration objective differentiable, allowing it to influence network training. Across multiple datasets, the resulting losses achieve state-of-the-art single-model expected calibration error with less than a 1% decrease in accuracy. On CIFAR-100, the authors report an 82% reduction in calibration error alongside a 0.7% relative accuracy decrease against the cross-entropy baseline.

The objective can also be applied after training, where it improves upon temperature scaling in the reported experiments. Across losses and datasets, calibration-sensitive procedures yield better uncertainty estimates under dataset shift than standard cross-entropy training followed by post-hoc recalibration. The findings show an empirical tradeoff: a small accuracy decrease can accompany a substantial improvement in how faithfully confidence represents correctness.
summary.tldr: Differentiable soft-binning losses improve neural-network calibration during or after training, with small reported accuracy costs.

title: Soft Calibration Objectives for Neural Networks

abstract: Benchmarks offer a scientific way to compare algorithms using objective performance metrics.Good benchmarks have two features: (a) they should be widely useful for many research groups; (b) and they should produce reproducible findings. In robotic manipulation research, there is a trade-off between reproducibility and broad accessibility. If the benchmark is kept restrictive (fixed hardware, objects), the numbers are reproducible but the setup becomes less general. On the other hand, a benchmark could be a loose set of protocols (e.g. object set) but the underlying variation in setups make the results non-reproducible. In this paper, we re-imagine benchmarking for robotic manipulation as state-of-the-art algorithmic implementations, alongside the usual set of tasks and experimental protocols. The added baseline implementations will provide a way to easily recreate SOTA numbers in a new local robotic setup, thus providing credible relative rankings between existing approaches and new work. However, these "local rankings" could vary between different setups. To resolve this issue, we build a mechanism for pooling experimental data between labs, and thus we establish a single global ranking for existing (and proposed) SOTA algorithms. Our benchmark, called Ranking-Based Robotics Benchmark (RB2), is evaluated on tasks that are inspired from clinically validated Southampton Hand Assessment Procedures. Our benchmark was run across two different labs and reveals several surprising findings. For example, extremely simple baselines like open-loop behavior cloning, outperform more complicated models (e.g. closed loop, RNN, Offline-RL, etc.) that are preferred by the field. We hope our fellow researchers will use RB2 to improve their research's quality and rigor.

paragraphs: Robotics benchmarks face a practical tension: identical hardware and objects support reproducibility, but strict setup requirements limit participation. More flexible protocols are easier to adopt, yet differences between laboratories complicate comparisons. RB2 addresses this tension by including algorithm implementations alongside the usual tasks and experimental procedures.

Researchers can run the supplied methods in their own laboratory and compare a new approach against locally reproduced baselines. Because these local rankings may differ across setups, RB2 also provides a mechanism for pooling experimental data into a global ranking. The comparison therefore incorporates evidence from multiple laboratories rather than assuming their raw performance numbers are directly interchangeable.

The benchmark uses tasks inspired by the Southampton Hand Assessment Procedures and was run in two laboratories. In those experiments, simple open-loop behavior cloning outperforms more complicated approaches, including closed-loop models, recurrent networks, and offline reinforcement learning. These findings challenge expectations within the tested settings and illustrate why reproducible baseline implementations are useful for assessing algorithmic progress.
summary.tldr: RB2 combines reproducible local baselines with pooled rankings to compare manipulation algorithms across different robotic setups.

title: RB2: Robotic Manipulation Benchmarking with a Twist

abstract: We introduce a novel dataset for architectural style classification, consisting of 9,485 images of church buildings. Both images and style labels were sourced from Wikipedia. The dataset can serve as a benchmark for various research fields, as it combines numerous real-world challenges: fine-grained distinctions between classes based on subtle visual features, a comparatively small sample size, a highly imbalanced class distribution, a high variance of viewpoints, and a hierarchical organization of labels, where only some images are labeled at the most precise level.In addition, we provide 631 bounding box annotations of characteristic visual features for 139 churches from four major categories. These annotations can, for example, be useful for research on fine-grained classification, where additional expert knowledge about distinctive object parts is often available.Images and annotations are available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5166986
