paragraphs: WikiChurches introduces architectural style classification using 9,485 images of church buildings, with both photographs and labels sourced from Wikipedia. The task requires distinguishing categories through subtle visual features. This makes the dataset relevant to fine-grained recognition, where identifying the broad kind of object does not resolve the more detailed classification question.

Several practical difficulties occur together in the collection. The sample size is comparatively small, classes are highly imbalanced, and photographs show buildings from widely varying viewpoints. Labels also form a hierarchy, with only some images labeled at the most specific level. Evaluation therefore involves both visual variation and uneven amounts and precision of supervision.

The authors additionally provide 631 bounding boxes marking characteristic visual features for 139 churches across four major categories. These annotations could support research that uses expert knowledge about distinctive object parts. Together, the image collection, hierarchical labels, and selected feature annotations offer a benchmark for investigating fine-grained classification under several challenges found in real-world data.
summary.tldr: WikiChurches tests architectural style recognition with subtle visual distinctions, imbalanced classes, varied viewpoints, and partially specific labels.

title: WikiChurches: A Fine-Grained Dataset of Architectural Styles with Real-World Challenges

abstract: Predictive distributions quantify uncertainties ignored by point estimates. This paper introduces The Neural Testbed: an open source benchmark for controlled and principled evaluation of agents that generate such predictions. Crucially, the testbed assesses agents not only on the quality of their marginal predictions per input, but also on their joint predictions across many inputs. We evaluate a range of agents using a simple neural network data generating process.Our results indicate that some popular Bayesian deep learning agents do not fare well with joint predictions, even when they can produce accurate marginal predictions. We also show that the quality of joint predictions drives performance in downstream decision tasks. We find these results are robust across choice a wide range of generative models, and highlight the practical importance of joint predictions to the community.

paragraphs: A predictive distribution describes uncertainty that a single best guess cannot express. Evaluating such predictions one input at a time, however, does not establish how well a model represents uncertainty across several inputs together. The Neural Testbed is an open-source benchmark designed to examine both individual, marginal predictions and joint predictions.

The authors evaluate a range of prediction-generating agents using a simple neural-network data-generating process. This provides a controlled setting for assessing their uncertainty estimates. Some popular Bayesian deep learning agents produce accurate marginal predictions but perform poorly on joint predictions, showing that success on the first evaluation does not ensure success on the second.

The study also finds that joint-prediction quality drives performance in downstream decision tasks. The reported findings remain robust across a wide range of generative models. This gives joint evaluation a practical motivation: uncertainty relationships across inputs can affect decisions even when predictions for each input look good in isolation. The benchmark makes those relationships an explicit part of assessment.
summary.tldr: The Neural Testbed shows that accurate per-input uncertainty can coexist with poor joint predictions that matter for downstream decisions.

title: The Neural Testbed: Evaluating Joint Predictions

abstract: Linear systems occur throughout engineering and the sciences, most notably as differential equations. In many cases the forcing function for the system is unknown, and interest lies in using noisy observations of the system to infer the forcing, as well as other unknown parameters. In differential equations, the forcing function is an unknown function of the independent variables (typically time and space), and can be modelled as a Gaussian process (GP). In this paper we show how the adjoint of a linear system can be used to efficiently infer forcing functions modelled as GPs, after using a truncated basis expansion of the GP kernel. We show how exact conjugate Bayesian inference for the truncated GP can be achieved, in many cases with substantially lower computation than would be required using MCMC methods. We demonstrate the approach on systems of both ordinary and partial differential equations, and show that the basis expansion approach approximates well the true forcing with a modest number of basis vectors. Finally, we show how to infer point estimates for the non-linear model parameters, such as the kernel length-scales, using Bayesian optimisation.

paragraphs: A differential equation can describe a system whose external driving input is unknown. This paper asks how noisy measurements of the system can reveal that input, called the forcing function, together with other unknown parameters. It represents the forcing with a Gaussian process, allowing inference about an unknown function rather than only a small set of numbers.

The method combines the adjoint of a linear system with a finite basis approximation of the Gaussian-process kernel. This creates a setting where conjugate Bayesian inference can be performed exactly for the truncated representation. The qualification matters: inference is exact within that finite approximation, while the original Gaussian process has been approximated. In many cases, this requires substantially less computation than MCMC.

Demonstrations cover both ordinary and partial differential equations. The authors find that a modest number of basis vectors can approximate the true forcing well in these examples. They also use Bayesian optimization to obtain point estimates of nonlinear parameters, including kernel length-scales. Together, these steps provide an efficient route to recovering hidden inputs while handling different kinds of unknowns through distinct inference procedures.
summary.tldr: Adjoint calculations enable efficient Bayesian inference of unknown forcing functions represented by truncated Gaussian processes.

title: Adjoint-aided inference of Gaussian process driven differential equations

abstract: We provide the first complete continuous time framework for denoising diffusion models of discrete data. This is achieved by formulating the forward noising process and corresponding reverse time generative process as Continuous Time Markov Chains (CTMCs). The model can be efficiently trained using a continuous time version of the ELBO. We simulate the high dimensional CTMC using techniques developed in chemical physics and exploit our continuous time framework to derive high performance samplers that we show can outperform discrete time methods for discrete data. The continuous time treatment also enables us to derive a novel theoretical result bounding the error between the generated sample distribution and the true data distribution.

paragraphs: This paper develops a continuous-time framework for diffusion models that generate discrete data. The central idea is to describe both the process that adds noise and the reverse process that generates samples using continuous-time Markov chains. This gives the two directions a shared mathematical formulation while keeping the data itself discrete: continuous time describes when changes occur, rather than making the possible data values continuous.

The authors train the model with a continuous-time version of the evidence lower bound, or ELBO. For generation, they draw on techniques from chemical physics to simulate the resulting high-dimensional chains. The framework therefore connects a training objective with practical methods for producing samples, rather than stopping at a description of the underlying stochastic process.

The authors derive samplers that can outperform discrete-time methods for discrete data. They also establish a theoretical bound on the difference between the generated distribution and the true data distribution. Together, these contributions make continuous time useful for both sampler design and analysis of generation error.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time formulation of discrete diffusion models supports efficient training, improved samplers, and a theoretical bound on generation error.

title: A Continuous Time Framework for Discrete Denoising Models

abstract: A fundamental component of human vision is our ability to parse complex visual scenes and judge the relations between their constituent objects. AI benchmarks for visual reasoning have driven rapid progress in recent years with state-of-the-art systems now reaching human accuracy on some of these benchmarks. Yet, there remains a major gap between humans and AI systems in terms of the sample efficiency with which they learn new visual reasoning tasks. Humans' remarkable efficiency at learning has been at least partially attributed to their ability to harness compositionality -- allowing them to efficiently take advantage of previously gained knowledge when learning new tasks. Here, we introduce a novel visual reasoning benchmark, Compositional Visual Relations (CVR), to drive progress towards the development of more data-efficient learning algorithms. We take inspiration from fluidic intelligence and non-verbal reasoning tests and describe a novel method for creating compositions of abstract rules and generating image datasets corresponding to these rules at scale. Our proposed benchmark includes measures of sample efficiency, generalization, compositionality, and transfer across task rules. We systematically evaluate modern neural architectures and find that convolutional architectures surpass transformer-based architectures across all performance measures in most data regimes. However, all computational models are much less data efficient than humans, even after learning informative visual representations using self-supervision. Overall, we hope our challenge will spur interest in developing neural architectures that can learn to harness compositionality for more efficient learning.

paragraphs: Recognizing relations among objects is only part of visual reasoning. Another challenge is learning new combinations of those relations from few examples. This paper introduces Compositional Visual Relations, or CVR, to examine that challenge. Its motivation is the gap between strong benchmark accuracy and the much greater efficiency with which humans learn new reasoning tasks.

CVR generates image datasets from compositions of abstract rules, drawing inspiration from nonverbal reasoning tests. Composing rules makes it possible to evaluate whether models reuse previously learned knowledge when facing a new task. These findings make CVR a test of how effectively models combine knowledge, beyond whether they can eventually achieve strong accuracy.
summary.tldr: CVR tests compositional visual reasoning and finds that evaluated neural models remain much less data efficient than humans.

title: A Benchmark for Compositional Visual Reasoning

abstract: In recent years, robust Markov decision processes (MDPs) have emerged as a prominent modeling framework for dynamic decision problems affected by uncertainty. In contrast to classical MDPs, which only account for stochasticity by modeling the dynamics through a stochastic process with a known transition kernel, robust MDPs additionally account for ambiguity by optimizing in view of the most adverse transition kernel from a prescribed ambiguity set. In this paper, we develop a novel solution framework for robust MDPs with $s$-rectangular ambiguity sets that decomposes the problem into a sequence of robust Bellman updates and simplex projections. Exploiting the rich structure present in the simplex projections corresponding to $\phi$-divergence ambiguity sets, we show that the associated $s$-rectangular robust MDPs can be solved substantially faster than with state-of-the-art commercial solvers as well as a recent first-order solution scheme, thus rendering them attractive alternatives to classical MDPs in practical applications.

paragraphs: A classical Markov decision process models uncertain outcomes using a known transition rule. A robust version also allows uncertainty about that rule itself. It chooses actions while considering the most adverse transition rule within a specified set, making ambiguity about system dynamics part of the decision problem.

This paper develops a solution framework for robust problems with s-rectangular ambiguity sets, a particular structure for organizing transition uncertainty by state. The framework breaks the computation into repeated robust Bellman updates and projections onto a simplex, the space of probability vectors. For ambiguity sets defined through phi-divergences, the authors exploit additional structure in those projection problems.

They show that the resulting problems can be solved substantially faster than with leading commercial solvers and a recent first-order method. The practical significance is computational: accounting for ambiguity becomes more attractive when its repeated optimization steps can be handled efficiently. The reported advantage applies to the structured robust MDP class studied, connecting a specific uncertainty model with a specialized solution procedure.
summary.tldr: A structured solver accelerates robust MDPs with s-rectangular phi-divergence ambiguity sets through Bellman updates and simplex projections.

title: Robust $\phi$-Divergence MDPs

abstract: Recently, various methods have been introduced to address the OOD detection problem with training outlier exposure. These methods usually count on discriminative softmax metric or energy method to screen OOD samples. In this paper, we probe an alternative hypothesis on OOD detection by constructing a novel latent variable model based on independent component analysis (ICA) techniques. This novel method named Conditional-i builds upon the probabilistic formulation, and applies the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criteria that offers a convenient solution for optimizing variable dependencies. Conditional-i exclusively encodes the useful class condition into the probabilistic model, which provides the desired convenience in delivering theoretical support for the OOD detection task. To facilitate the implementation of the Conditional-i model, we construct unique memory bank architectures that allow for convenient end-to-end training within a tractable budget. Empirical results demonstrate an evident performance boost on benchmarks against SOTA methods. We also provide valuable theoretical justifications that our training strategy is guaranteed to bound the error in the context of OOD detection. Code is available at: https://github.com/OODHSIC/conditional-i.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the distribution a model is meant to handle. Many approaches using training outlier exposure rely on softmax-derived or energy scores. This paper investigates an alternative probabilistic formulation through a latent-variable model called Conditional-i.

Conditional-i draws on independent component analysis and uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion to optimize dependencies between variables. It specifically encodes useful class-conditioning information within the probabilistic model. That construction provides a basis for theoretical analysis of the detection task, connecting the model's dependency structure to its detection objective.

The authors introduce memory-bank architectures to make end-to-end training feasible within a tractable computational budget. Benchmark experiments show a clear performance improvement over state-of-the-art methods in the reported evaluation. The paper also supplies theoretical justification that its training strategy bounds detection error. Together, the architecture and analysis offer an alternative to commonly used detection scores, with empirical gains and an error-bound result supporting the proposed training strategy.
summary.tldr: Conditional-i uses a class-conditioned latent-variable model and kernel independence criterion for out-of-distribution detection, with benchmark gains and theoretical error bounds.

title: Out-of-Distribution Detection via Conditional Kernel Independence Model

abstract: Heterogeneous behaviours are widespread in many multi-agent tasks, which have not been paid much attention in the community of multi-agent reinforcement learning. It would be a key factor for improving the learning performance to efficiently characterize and automatically find heterogeneous behaviours. In this paper, we introduce the concept of the skill to explore the ability of heterogeneous behaviours. We propose a novel skill-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework to enable agents to master diverse skills. Specifically, our framework consists of the skill representation mechanism, the skill selector and the skill-based policy learning mechanism. We design an auto-encoder model to generate the latent variable as the skill representation by incorporating the environment information, which ensures the distinguishable of agents for skill selection and the discriminability for the skill learning. With the representation, a skill selection mechanism is invented to realize the assignment from agents to skills. Meanwhile, diverse skill-based policies are generated through a novel skill-based policy learning method. To promote efficient skill discovery, a mutual information based intrinsic reward function is constructed. Empirical results show that our framework obtains the best performance on three challenging benchmarks, i.e., StarCraft II micromanagement tasks, Google Research Football and GoBigger, over state-of-the-art MARL methods.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how agents in a shared task can learn different behaviors through skills. Heterogeneous behavior is common in multi-agent problems, yet the authors argue that automatically identifying and representing it has received insufficient attention. Their framework makes skill discovery, assignment, and policy learning explicit parts of training.

An autoencoder uses environmental information to produce latent skill representations. These representations help distinguish agents for skill assignment and distinguish skills during learning. A selector assigns skills to agents, while a separate learning mechanism produces policies associated with those skills. A mutual-information-based intrinsic reward encourages efficient discovery of diverse skills.

The framework is evaluated on StarCraft II micromanagement, Google Research Football, and GoBigger. The authors report the best performance among the compared state-of-the-art multi-agent reinforcement learning methods on these benchmarks. The results support treating behavioral diversity as something to represent and organize directly, with learned skills connecting the agents' differences to their task performance.
summary.tldr: A multi-agent framework learns, assigns, and rewards diverse skills, reporting leading performance on three evaluated benchmarks.

title: Heterogeneous Skill Learning for Multi-agent Tasks

abstract: The past few years have seen the development of many benchmarks for Neural Architecture Search (NAS), fueling rapid progress in NAS research. However, recent work, which shows that good hyperparameter settings can be more important than using the best architecture, calls for a shift in focus towards Joint Architecture and Hyperparameter Search (JAHS). Therefore, we present JAHS-Bench-201, the first collection of surrogate benchmarks for JAHS, built to also facilitate research on multi-objective, cost-aware and (multi) multi-fidelity optimization algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, JAHS-Bench-201 is based on the most extensive dataset of neural network performance data in the public domain. It is composed of approximately 161 million data points and 20 performance metrics for three deep learning tasks, while featuring a 14-dimensional search and fidelity space that extends the popular NAS-Bench-201 space. With JAHS-Bench-201, we hope to democratize research on JAHS and lower the barrier to entry of an extremely compute intensive field, e.g., by reducing the compute time to run a JAHS algorithm from 5 days to only a few seconds.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search studies how to choose a network’s structure, but training hyperparameters can be at least as consequential in some settings. This motivates joint architecture and hyperparameter search, where the two are explored together. JAHS-Bench-201 provides surrogate benchmarks intended to make research on this expensive combined search problem more accessible.

The collection extends the NAS-Bench-201 space to a 14-dimensional search and fidelity space. It is built from approximately 161 million data points covering twenty performance metrics across three deep learning tasks. Its design also supports research that considers multiple objectives, computational cost, and evaluations at different fidelity levels.

The practical aim is to let researchers evaluate search algorithms with far less computation through surrogate evaluations of network performance. The authors give an example of reducing an algorithm run from five days to a few seconds. This makes the benchmark useful as shared infrastructure for investigating how architecture choices and hyperparameters interact, including settings where accuracy must be considered alongside other objectives or evaluation costs.
summary.tldr: JAHS-Bench-201 supplies large-scale surrogate benchmarks to make joint architecture and hyperparameter search research much less computationally expensive.

title: JAHS-Bench-201: A Foundation For Research On Joint Architecture And Hyperparameter Search

abstract: Bayesian inference allows expressing the uncertainty of posterior belief under a probabilistic model given prior information and the likelihood of the evidence. Predominantly, the likelihood function is only implicitly established by a simulator posing the need for simulation-based inference (SBI). However, the existing algorithms can yield overconfident posteriors (Hermans *et al.*, 2022) defeating the whole purpose of credibility if the uncertainty quantification is inaccurate. We propose to include a calibration term directly into the training objective of the neural model in selected amortized SBI techniques. By introducing a relaxation of the classical formulation of calibration error we enable end-to-end backpropagation. The proposed method is not tied to any particular neural model and brings moderate computational overhead compared to the profits it introduces. It is directly applicable to existing computational pipelines allowing reliable black-box posterior inference. We empirically show on six benchmark problems that the proposed method achieves competitive or better results in terms of coverage and expected posterior density than the previously existing approaches.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference is useful when a simulator defines how observations arise but does not provide an explicit likelihood function. Neural methods can estimate posterior uncertainty in this setting, yet their outputs may be overconfident. An overly narrow posterior undermines the purpose of representing uncertainty, even when the inference procedure produces otherwise useful estimates.

The authors address this by adding a calibration term directly to the training objective of selected amortized inference methods. They relax the classical calibration-error formulation so that it supports end-to-end backpropagation. This lets calibration influence neural training itself, making uncertainty quality part of what the model learns to optimize.

The approach is not tied to a particular neural architecture and is designed to fit existing computational pipelines with moderate additional computation. Across six benchmark problems, it achieves competitive or better coverage and expected posterior density than previous approaches. These results provide empirical support for training with calibration objectives, while the stated applicability concerns selected amortized simulation-based inference techniques.
summary.tldr: A differentiable calibration objective improves uncertainty quality in selected neural simulation-based inference methods.

title: Calibrating Neural Simulation-Based Inference with Differentiable Coverage Probability

abstract: In this paper, we propose an accelerated quasi-Newton proximal extragradient method for solving unconstrained smooth convex optimization problems. With access only to the gradients of the objective, we prove that our method can achieve a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}\bigl(\min\\{\frac{1}{k^2}, \frac{\sqrt{d\log k}}{k^{2.5}}\\}\bigr)$, where $d$ is the problem dimension and $k$ is the number of iterations. In particular, in the regime where $k = \mathcal{O}(d)$, our method matches the _optimal rate_ of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{k^2})$ by Nesterov's accelerated gradient (NAG). Moreover, in the the regime where $k = \Omega(d \log d)$, it outperforms NAG and converges at a _faster rate_ of $\mathcal{O}\bigl(\frac{\sqrt{d\log k}}{k^{2.5}}\bigr)$. To the best of our knowledge, this result is the first to demonstrate a provable gain for a quasi-Newton-type method over NAG in the convex setting. To achieve such results, we build our method on a recent variant of the Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration framework and adopt an online learning perspective to update the Hessian approximation matrices, in which we relate the convergence rate of our method to the dynamic regret of a specific online convex optimization problem in the space of matrices.

The central question is whether such quasi-Newton information can deliver a provable improvement over Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method in this setting.

The algorithm combines a variant of the Monteiro–Svaiter acceleration framework with an online learning approach to updating its Hessian approximations. The proven rate is the smaller of 1/k² and √(d log k)/k²·⁵, up to constant factors. Here d is dimension and k is iteration count. It matches the accelerated gradient rate in the stated earlier regime and improves on it once iterations reach the order of d log d. Thus, the gain is dimension-dependent and emerges with sufficiently many iterations.
summary.tldr: A gradient-only quasi-Newton method provably improves on accelerated gradient convergence after a dimension-dependent number of iterations.

title: Accelerated Quasi-Newton Proximal Extragradient: Faster Rate for Smooth Convex Optimization

abstract: Geometric representation learning (e.g., hyperbolic and spherical geometry) has proven to be efficacious in solving many intricate machine learning tasks. The fundamental challenge of geometric representation learning lies in aligning the inherent geometric bias with the underlying structure of the data, which is a rarely explored topic in the literature. Existing methods heavily rely on heuristic assumptions on the data structure to decide the type of geometry to be adopted, which often leads to suboptimal performance. This work aims to automate the alignment process via a data-informed strategy such that we optimize model performance with minimal overhead. Specifically, a sparse gating mechanism is employed to enable each input data point $\mathit{p}$ to select $K$ geometric spaces from a given candidate geometric space pool with $N$ ($K<N$) spaces of different geometry. The selected $K$ spaces are then tightly integrated to formulate a Cartesian product space, which is leveraged to process this input data $\mathit{p}$. In doing so, each input data is processed by the spaces it selected with maximum specialization. We empirically show that this method can effectively align data and spaces without human interventions and further boost performance on real-world tasks, demonstrating its potential in eliciting the expressive power of geometric representations and practical usability.

paragraphs: Geometric representation learning uses spaces such as hyperbolic or spherical geometry to represent data. Its success depends partly on whether the chosen geometry matches the data’s underlying structure. This paper addresses that selection problem, which existing methods often handle through human heuristics that may lead to suboptimal choices.

The proposed method uses a sparse gate to select a subset of candidate spaces for each input point. From a pool of N spaces with different geometries, an input selects K, with K smaller than N. Those selected spaces are combined into a Cartesian product space, and the input is processed using that combination.

This design makes geometry selection specific to individual inputs, allowing different points to use different combinations of spaces. The authors aim to automate alignment between data and geometry with minimal overhead. Experiments on real-world tasks show that the method can make these choices without human intervention and improve performance. The findings support adaptive space selection as a practical way to make better use of geometric representations.
summary.tldr: A sparse gating mechanism lets each input select and combine geometric spaces, improving alignment between representations and data in experiments.

title: Data-Informed Geometric Space Selection

abstract: This paper focuses on addressing the practical yet challenging problem of model heterogeneity in federated learning, where clients possess models with different network structures. To track this problem, we propose a novel framework called pFedHR, which leverages heterogeneous model reassembly to achieve personalized federated learning. In particular, we approach the problem of heterogeneous model personalization as a model-matching optimization task on the server side. Moreover, pFedHR automatically and dynamically generates informative and diverse personalized candidates with minimal human intervention. Furthermore, our proposed heterogeneous model reassembly technique mitigates the adverse impact introduced by using public data with different distributions from the client data to a certain extent. Experimental results demonstrate that pFedHR outperforms baselines on three datasets under both IID and Non-IID settings. Additionally, pFedHR effectively reduces the adverse impact of using different public data and dynamically generates diverse personalized models in an automated manner.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning becomes challenging when participating clients use different network architectures. The paper addresses this model heterogeneity with pFedHR, a framework based on heterogeneous model reassembly. Its objective is to produce models suited to individual clients while accommodating differences in the structures they bring to the collaboration.

The framework formulates personalization as a model-matching optimization problem on the server. It automatically generates informative, varied candidate models and updates those candidates dynamically, requiring little human intervention. This makes the construction and selection of personalized architectures part of the learning framework rather than a choice that must remain fixed throughout the process.

Experiments on three datasets show pFedHR outperforming baselines under both IID and non-IID conditions, covering different degrees of similarity among clients' data distributions. The method also reduces, to an extent, the adverse effects of public data whose distribution differs from client data. The reported benefits therefore concern both architectural diversity and resilience to the public-data mismatch involved in the evaluated personalization process.
summary.tldr: pFedHR dynamically reassembles heterogeneous models into personalized candidates and partially reduces the effects of mismatched public data.

title: Towards Personalized Federated Learning via Heterogeneous Model Reassembly

abstract: The goal of causal representation learning is to find a representation of data that consists of causally related latent variables. We consider a setup where one has access to data from multiple domains that potentially share a causal representation. Crucially, observations in different domains are assumed to be unpaired, that is, we only observe the marginal distribution in each domain but not their joint distribution. In this paper, we give sufficient conditions for identifiability of the joint distribution and the shared causal graph in a linear setup. Identifiability holds if we can uniquely recover the joint distribution and the shared causal representation from the marginal distributions in each domain. We transform our results into a practical method to recover the shared latent causal graph.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning seeks hidden variables whose relationships describe causal structure. This paper considers data from multiple domains that may share such a representation. The central complication is that observations are unpaired: each domain supplies its own distribution, but the data do not directly show how observations across domains belong together.

In a linear setup, the authors give sufficient conditions for identifying both the joint distribution and the shared causal graph from those separate marginal distributions. Identifiability means the available distributions uniquely determine the target structure under the stated conditions. The result therefore addresses whether reconstruction is possible before addressing how to perform it.

The authors turn the theoretical results into a practical method for recovering the shared latent causal graph. The contribution shows that missing cross-domain pairings need not prevent causal recovery when the sufficient conditions hold. Its scope remains the stated linear setting, and the existence of sufficient conditions does not imply recovery from arbitrary collections of unpaired domains.
summary.tldr: The paper provides sufficient conditions and a practical method for recovering shared latent causal structure from unpaired domains in a linear setting.

title: Unpaired Multi-Domain Causal Representation Learning

abstract: First-order optimization methods tend to inherently favor certain solutions over others when minimizing a given training objective with multiple local optima. This phenomenon, known as \emph{implicit bias}, plays a critical role in understanding the generalization capabilities of optimization algorithms. Recent research has revealed that gradient-descent-based methods exhibit an implicit bias for the $\ell_2$-maximal margin classifier in the context of separable binary classification. In contrast, generic optimization methods, such as mirror descent and steepest descent, have been shown to converge to maximal margin classifiers defined by alternative geometries. However, while gradient-descent-based algorithms demonstrate fast implicit bias rates, the implicit bias rates of generic optimization methods have been relatively slow. To address this limitation, in this paper, we present a series of state-of-the-art implicit bias rates for mirror descent and steepest descent algorithms. Our primary technique involves transforming a generic optimization algorithm into an online learning dynamic that solves a regularized bilinear game, providing a unified framework for analyzing the implicit bias of various optimization methods. The accelerated rates are derived leveraging the regret bounds of online learning algorithms within this game framework.

paragraphs: An optimizer can favor particular solutions even when the training objective does not explicitly select them. This implicit bias helps explain how the choice of optimization method affects the learned classifier. In separable binary classification, gradient-descent methods favor a maximum-margin solution in Euclidean geometry, while other methods can favor margins defined by different geometries.

This paper addresses how quickly generic methods approach their preferred maximum-margin classifiers. Earlier rates for mirror descent and steepest descent were comparatively slow. The authors establish improved, state-of-the-art implicit-bias rates for these methods by changing the mathematical perspective used to analyze their behavior.

The main technique translates an optimization algorithm into an online learning process that solves a regularized bilinear game. Regret bounds for that process then yield faster margin-maximization rates. This shared framework connects several optimization methods and their geometry-dependent preferences. The result concerns the speed of approaching these preferred classifiers, providing a more unified account of implicit bias beyond gradient descent.
summary.tldr: An online-learning game framework yields faster implicit-bias rates for mirror descent and steepest descent toward their maximum-margin classifiers.

title: Faster Margin Maximization Rates for Generic Optimization Methods

abstract: Cylindrical Algebraic Decomposition (CAD) is one of the pillar algorithms of symbolic computation, and its worst-case complexity is double exponential to the number of variables. Researchers found that variable order dramatically affects efficiency and proposed various heuristics. The existing learning-based methods are all supervised learning methods that cannot cope with diverse polynomial sets.This paper proposes two Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches combined with Graph Neural Networks (GNN) for Suggesting Variable Order (SVO). One is GRL-SVO(UP), a branching heuristic integrated with CAD. The other is GRL-SVO(NUP), a fast heuristic providing a total order directly. We generate a random dataset and collect a real-world dataset from SMT-LIB. The experiments show that our approaches outperform state-of-the-art learning-based heuristics and are competitive with the best expert-based heuristics. Interestingly, our models show a strong generalization ability, working well on various datasets even if they are only trained on a 3-var random dataset. The source code and data are available at https://github.com/dongyuhang22/GRL-SVO.

The order in which variables are handled can dramatically affect efficiency. This paper uses reinforcement learning with graph neural networks to select that order, addressing the difficulty existing supervised approaches have with diverse polynomial sets.

The authors propose two methods with different ways of supplying ordering decisions. GRL-SVO(UP) acts as a branching heuristic integrated into the decomposition procedure. GRL-SVO(NUP) provides a complete order directly as a fast heuristic. The evaluation combines a generated random dataset with a real-world dataset collected from SMT-LIB, testing the approaches across these different sources of problems.

The methods outperform state-of-the-art learning-based heuristics and are competitive with the best expert-designed heuristics in the reported experiments. They also perform well across various datasets after training only on a random dataset with three variables. This provides empirical evidence of generalization beyond that training setting and supports learned variable ordering as a useful tool for improving symbolic computation.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement learning with graph neural networks learns effective variable-ordering heuristics for cylindrical algebraic decomposition and generalizes across tested datasets.

title: Suggesting Variable Order for Cylindrical Algebraic Decomposition via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Sign languages are used as a primary language by approximately 70 million D/deaf people world-wide. However, most communication technologies operate in spoken and written languages, creating inequities in access. To help tackle this problem, we release ASL Citizen, the first crowdsourced Isolated Sign Language Recognition (ISLR) dataset, collected with consent and containing 83,399 videos for 2,731 distinct signs filmed by 52 signers in a variety of environments. We propose that this dataset be used for sign language dictionary retrieval for American Sign Language (ASL), where a user demonstrates a sign to their webcam to retrieve matching signs from a dictionary. We show that training supervised machine learning classifiers with our dataset advances the state-of-the-art on metrics relevant for dictionary retrieval, achieving 63\% accuracy and a recall-at-10 of 91\%, evaluated entirely on videos of users who are not present in the training or validation sets.

paragraphs: ASL Citizen addresses a gap between communication technologies built around spoken or written language and the needs of sign-language users. The contribution is a consent-based, crowdsourced dataset for recognizing individual American Sign Language signs. It contains 83,399 videos covering 2,731 distinct signs, recorded by 52 signers across a variety of environments.

The proposed use is dictionary retrieval. A person demonstrates a sign to a webcam, and a recognition system returns matching dictionary entries. This connects isolated sign recognition to a concrete lookup task. For that application, both the accuracy of the first result and whether the correct sign appears among several suggestions are relevant measures.

Supervised classifiers trained on the dataset achieved 63% accuracy and 91% recall-at-10, advancing the reported state of the art on dictionary-retrieval metrics. Crucially, evaluation used videos from people absent from both training and validation. The results therefore test recognition across unseen signers, while the high recall-at-10 indicates that the correct sign often appears within a shortlist even when the first prediction is incorrect.
summary.tldr: ASL Citizen provides consent-based community videos that improve isolated ASL sign recognition for dictionary lookup, including evaluation on unseen signers.

title: ASL Citizen: A Community-Sourced Dataset for Advancing Isolated Sign Language Recognition

abstract: We present Meta 3D AssetGen (AssetGen), a significant advancement in text-to-3D generation which produces faithful, high-quality meshes with texture and material control. Compared to works that bake shading in the 3D object’s appearance, AssetGen outputs physically-based rendering (PBR) materials, supporting realistic relighting. AssetGen generates first several views of the object with separate shaded and albedo appearance channels, and then reconstructs colours, metalness and roughness in 3D, using a deferred shading loss for efficient supervision. It also uses a sign-distance function to represent 3D shape more reliably and introduces acorresponding loss for direct shape supervision. This is implemented using fused kernels for high memory efficiency. After mesh extraction, a texture refinement transformer operating in UV space significantly improves sharpness and details. AssetGen achieves 17% improvement in Chamfer Distance and 40% in LPIPS over the best concurrent work for few-view reconstruction, and a human preference of 72% over the best industry competitors of comparable speed, including those that support PBR. Project page with generated assets: https://assetgen.github.io

paragraphs: AssetGen turns text into textured three-dimensional meshes with controllable materials. Its output includes physically based rendering materials, allowing objects to be relit realistically. This addresses a problem with generated appearances that already contain baked-in shading: the visible lighting becomes entangled with the object's appearance.

The system first generates multiple object views with separate shaded and albedo channels. It reconstructs color, metalness, and roughness in three dimensions using a deferred shading loss. Shape is represented through a signed-distance function with direct shape supervision, and fused kernels improve memory efficiency. After extracting the mesh, a transformer refines the texture in UV space to sharpen detail.

For reconstruction from a few views, the authors report improvements of 17% in Chamfer Distance and 40% in LPIPS over the best concurrent work. They also report 72% human preference over leading industry competitors of comparable speed, including competitors supporting physically based materials. Together, these findings concern geometric quality, visual appearance, and preference for generated assets within the stated comparisons.
summary.tldr: AssetGen creates detailed text-driven 3D meshes with physically based materials that support realistic relighting.

title: Meta 3D AssetGen: Text-to-Mesh Generation with High-Quality Geometry, Texture, and PBR Materials

abstract: Solving complex Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) accurately and efficiently is an essential and challenging problem in all scientific and engineering disciplines. Mesh movement methods provide the capability to improve the accuracy of the numerical solution without increasing the overall mesh degree of freedom count. Conventional sophisticated mesh movement methods are extremely expensive and struggle to handle scenarios with complex boundary geometries. However, existing learning-based methods require re-training from scratch given a different PDE type or boundary geometry, which limits their applicability, and also often suffer from robustness issues in the form of inverted elements. In this paper, we introduce the Universal Mesh Movement Network (UM2N), which -- once trained -- can be applied in a non-intrusive, zero-shot manner to move meshes with different size distributions and structures, for solvers applicable to different PDE types and boundary geometries. UM2N consists of a Graph Transformer (GT) encoder for extracting features and a Graph Attention Network (GAT) based decoder for moving the mesh. We evaluate our method on advection and Navier-Stokes based examples, as well as a real-world tsunami simulation case. Our method out-performs existing learning-based mesh movement methods in terms of the benchmarks described above. In comparison to the conventional sophisticated Monge-Ampère PDE-solver based method, our approach not only significantly accelerates mesh movement, but also proves effective in scenarios where the conventional method fails. Our project page can be found at https://erizmr.github.io/UM2N/.

Conventional sophisticated movement methods can be expensive and struggle with complex boundaries, while existing learned methods often require retraining for different equations or geometries and can produce inverted elements.

UM2N is designed to transfer mesh movement across settings after a single training process. It combines a Graph Transformer encoder that extracts features with a Graph Attention Network decoder that moves the mesh. These results support transferable mesh adaptation as a way to improve solver workflows across varied problems.
summary.tldr: UM2N learns mesh movement that transfers without retraining across varied meshes, PDEs, and geometries, with strong reported efficiency and performance.

title: Towards Universal Mesh Movement Networks

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) demonstrate remarkable performance in image classification through visual-token interaction learning, particularly when equipped with local information via region attention or convolutions. Although such architectures improve the feature aggregation from different granularities, they often fail to contribute to the robustness of the networks. Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) enables the modeling of global visual-token representations through local interactions, with its training strategies and architecture design conferring strong generalization ability and robustness against noisy input. In this paper, we propose Adaptor Neural Cellular Automata (AdaNCA) for Vision Transformers that uses NCA as plug-and-play adaptors between ViT layers, thus enhancing ViT's performance and robustness against adversarial samples as well as out-of-distribution inputs. To overcome the large computational overhead of standard NCAs, we propose Dynamic Interaction for more efficient interaction learning. Using our analysis of AdaNCA placement and robustness improvement, we also develop an algorithm for identifying the most effective insertion points for AdaNCA. With less than a 3% increase in parameters, AdaNCA contributes to more than 10% absolute improvement in accuracy under adversarial attacks on the ImageNet1K benchmark. Moreover, we demonstrate with extensive evaluations across eight robustness benchmarks and four ViT architectures that AdaNCA, as a plug-and-play module, consistently improves the robustness of ViTs.

paragraphs: AdaNCA addresses a gap between image classification performance and robustness in Vision Transformers. Adding local information through convolutions or regional attention can improve feature aggregation without reliably improving resilience to challenging inputs. The paper instead introduces neural cellular automata as adapters placed between Transformer layers.

These automata build broader visual representations through local interactions among visual tokens. The approach uses this interaction mechanism to improve performance under adversarial perturbations and inputs outside the training distribution. Because standard neural cellular automata can be computationally expensive, the authors introduce Dynamic Interaction to make their interaction learning more efficient. They also analyze how adapter placement relates to robustness and develop an algorithm for selecting effective insertion locations.

On ImageNet1K, the paper reports more than a 10-percentage-point improvement in accuracy under adversarial attacks while adding less than 3% to the parameter count. Evaluations across eight robustness benchmarks and four Vision Transformer architectures show consistent robustness improvements. These findings support the usefulness of the adapters across the tested architectures and robustness settings.
summary.tldr: AdaNCA inserts neural cellular automata between Vision Transformer layers to improve measured robustness with a small parameter increase.

title: AdanCA: Neural Cellular Automata As Adaptors For More Robust Vision Transformer

abstract: Analytics on structured data is a mature field with many successful methods.However, most real world data exists in unstructured form, such as images and conversations.We investigate the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) to enable unstructured data analytics.In particular, we propose a new Universal Query Engine (UQE) that directly interrogates and draws insights from unstructured data collections.This engine accepts queries in a Universal Query Language (UQL), a dialect of SQL that provides full natural language flexibility in specifying conditions and operators.The new engine leverages the ability of LLMs to conduct analysis of unstructured data, while also allowing us to exploit advances in sampling and optimization techniques to achieve efficient and accurate query execution.In addition, we borrow techniques from classical compiler theory to better orchestrate the workflow between sampling methods and foundation model calls.We demonstrate the efficiency of UQE on data analytics across different modalities, including images, dialogs and reviews, across a range of useful query types, including conditional aggregation, semantic retrieval and abstraction aggregation.

paragraphs: Many useful data collections consist of images, conversations, or reviews rather than neatly structured tables. UQE investigates how language models can support analytics directly over these collections. Its goal is to combine the expressive semantic interpretation of foundation models with the organized execution of a database query engine.

Users write requests in Universal Query Language, a SQL dialect whose conditions and operators can be expressed flexibly in natural language. The engine uses language models to interpret unstructured content, while sampling and optimization techniques support efficient, accurate execution. It also applies ideas from compiler theory to coordinate sampling operations and foundation-model calls within the query workflow.

The paper demonstrates the engine across images, dialogs, and reviews, with tasks including conditional aggregation, semantic retrieval, and abstraction aggregation. These demonstrations establish the usefulness of coordinating model-based analysis through a query system. The contribution lies in connecting a flexible interface for asking questions with an execution strategy that manages how unstructured data is sampled and analyzed, rather than treating each model call as an isolated operation.
summary.tldr: UQE combines a natural-language-flexible SQL dialect with model calls, sampling, and optimization to analyze unstructured data collections.

title: UQE: A Query Engine for Unstructured Databases

abstract: Language-image pre-training is an effective technique for learning powerful representations in general domains. However, when directly turning to person representation learning, these general pre-training methods suffer from unsatisfactory performance. The reason is that they neglect critical person-related characteristics, i.e., fine-grained attributes and identities. To address this issue, we propose a novel language-image pre-training framework for person representation learning, termed PLIP. Specifically, we elaborately design three pretext tasks: 1) Text-guided Image Colorization, aims to establish the correspondence between the person-related image regions and the fine-grained color-part textual phrases. 2) Image-guided Attributes Prediction, aims to mine fine-grained attribute information of the person body in the image; and 3) Identity-based Vision-Language Contrast, aims to correlate the cross-modal representations at the identity level rather than the instance level. Moreover, to implement our pre-train framework, we construct a large-scale person dataset with image-text pairs named SYNTH-PEDES by automatically generating textual annotations. We pre-train PLIP on SYNTH-PEDES and evaluate our models by spanning downstream person-centric tasks. PLIP not only significantly improves existing methods on all these tasks, but also shows great ability in the zero-shot and domain generalization settings. The code, dataset and weight will be made publicly available.

PLIP designs its pretraining around those characteristics, aiming to produce representations better suited to matching and analyzing people across images and descriptions.

Three pretext tasks align text with image-region colors, predict attributes from images, and contrast visual and language representations at the identity level. The authors construct SYNTH-PEDES by automatically generating textual annotations for a large person-image dataset, then use it to pretrain the model.

Evaluation across person-centric downstream tasks shows improvements over existing methods and strong zero-shot and domain-generalization behavior. The abstract does not list task scores or analyze annotation error. The contribution is targeted representation learning and a paired dataset; its evidence concerns the evaluated recognition tasks rather than a general guarantee of accurate or unbiased person understanding.
summary.tldr: PLIP adds person-specific attributes and identity supervision to language-image pretraining.

title: PLIP: Language-Image Pre-training for Person Representation Learning

abstract: Clouds in satellite imagery pose a significant challenge for downstream applications.A major challenge in current cloud removal research is the absence of a comprehensive benchmark and a sufficiently large and diverse training dataset.To address this problem, we introduce the largest public dataset -- *AllClear* for cloud removal, featuring 23,742 globally distributed regions of interest (ROIs) with diverse land-use patterns, comprising 4 million images in total. Each ROI includes complete temporal captures from the year 2022, with (1) multi-spectral optical imagery from Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8/9, (2) synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery from Sentinel-1, and (3) auxiliary remote sensing products such as cloud masks and land cover maps.We validate the effectiveness of our dataset by benchmarking performance, demonstrating the scaling law - the PSNR rises from $28.47$ to $33.87$ with $30\times$ more data, and conducting ablation studies on the temporal length and the importance of individual modalities. This dataset aims to provide comprehensive coverage of the Earth's surface and promote better cloud removal results.

paragraphs: Cloud cover makes satellite images harder to use in downstream applications. Progress on removing it also depends on having enough varied training examples and a common way to evaluate methods. AllClear addresses these needs with a public dataset containing four million images across 23,742 regions distributed around the world and covering diverse land uses.

Each region includes temporal observations throughout 2022. The collection brings together multispectral optical images from Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8/9, radar images from Sentinel-1, and supporting products such as cloud masks and land cover maps. This combination makes it possible to study cloud removal using observations across time and different imaging modalities within one dataset.

The authors benchmark performance and report that increasing training data by a factor of 30 raises PSNR from 28.47 to 33.87. This provides empirical evidence that additional data improves reconstruction quality in their evaluation. They also investigate temporal coverage and the contributions of individual modalities through ablation studies, making AllClear a resource for examining which information helps cloud removal.
summary.tldr: AllClear supplies four million satellite images and a benchmark for studying how data scale, time coverage, and imaging modalities improve cloud removal.

title: AllClear: A Comprehensive Dataset and Benchmark for Cloud Removal in Satellite Imagery

abstract: Given time series data, how can we answer questions like ``what will happen in the future?'' and ``how did we get here?'' These sorts of probabilistic inference questions are challenging when observations are high-dimensional. In this paper, we show how these questions can have compact, closed form solutions in terms of learned representations. The key idea is to apply a variant of contrastive learning to time series data. Prior work already shows that the representations learned by contrastive learning encode a probability ratio. By extending prior work to show that the marginal distribution over representations is Gaussian, we can then prove that joint distribution of representations is also Gaussian. Taken together, these results show that representations learned via temporal contrastive learning follow a Gauss-Markov chain, a graphical model where inference (e.g., prediction, planning) over representations corresponds to inverting a low-dimensional matrix. In one special case, inferring intermediate representations will be equivalent to interpolating between the learned representations. We validate our theory using numerical simulations on tasks up to 46-dimensions.

paragraphs: Predicting future observations or explaining how a system reached its current state can be difficult when each observation has many dimensions. This paper shows how a variant of temporal contrastive learning can produce representations in which such probabilistic questions admit compact, closed-form answers. The focus is on the structure of the learned representation space.

The analysis builds on the result that contrastive representations encode a probability ratio. The authors extend this reasoning by establishing Gaussian marginal distributions over representations and then a Gaussian joint distribution. Together, these results give the representations a Gauss-Markov-chain structure, connecting the learning procedure to a tractable model of temporal dependence.

Within this structure, prediction and planning reduce to inverting a low-dimensional matrix. In one special case, estimating intermediate representations becomes interpolation between learned representations. The authors validate their theory with numerical simulations on tasks with up to 46 dimensions. The interpolation result is explicitly a special case; the broader contribution is a theoretical route from temporal representation learning to efficient probabilistic inference.
summary.tldr: A temporal contrastive-learning analysis yields Gaussian representations that support compact inference, with interpolation solving one special case.

title: Inference via Interpolation: Contrastive Representations Provably Enable Planning and Inference

abstract: In this paper, we question if well pre-trained vision transformer (ViT) models could be used as teachers that exhibit scalable properties to advance cross architecture knowledge distillation research, in the context of adopting mainstream large-scale visual recognition datasets for evaluation. To make this possible, our analysis underlines the importance of seeking effective strategies to align (1) feature computing paradigm differences, (2) model scale differences, and (3) knowledge density differences. By combining three closely coupled components namely *cross attention projector*, *dual-view feature mimicking* and *teacher parameter perception* tailored to address the alignment problems stated above, we present a simple and effective knowledge distillation method, called *ScaleKD*. Our method can train student backbones that span across a variety of convolutional neural network (CNN), multi-layer perceptron (MLP), and ViT architectures on image classification datasets, achieving state-of-the-art knowledge distillation performance. For instance, taking a well pre-trained Swin-L as the teacher model, our method gets 75.15\%|82.03\%|84.16\%|78.63\%|81.96\%|83.93\%|83.80\%|85.53\% top-1 accuracies for MobileNet-V1|ResNet-50|ConvNeXt-T|Mixer-S/16|Mixer-B/16|ViT-S/16|Swin-T|ViT-B/16 models trained on ImageNet-1K dataset from scratch, showing 3.05\%|3.39\%|2.02\%|4.61\%|5.52\%|4.03\%|2.62\%|3.73\% absolute gains to the individually trained counterparts. Intriguingly, when scaling up the size of teacher models or their pre-training datasets, our method showcases the desired scalable properties, bringing increasingly larger gains to student models. We also empirically show that the student backbones trained by our method transfer well on downstream MS-COCO and ADE20K datasets. More importantly, our method could be used as a more efficient alternative to the time-intensive pre-training paradigm for any target student model on large-scale datasets if a strong pre-trained ViT is available, reducing the amount of viewed training samples up to 195$\times$. The code is available at *https://github.com/deep-optimization/ScaleKD*.

title: ScaleKD: Strong Vision Transformers Could Be Excellent Teachers

abstract: The design of Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is inspired by the working patterns of the human brain. Connections in biological neural networks are sparse, as they only exist between few neurons. Meanwhile, the sparse representation in ANNs has been shown to possess significant advantages. Activation responses of ANNs are typically expected to promote sparse representations, where key signals get activated while irrelevant/redundant signals are suppressed. It can be observed that samples of each category are only correlated with sparse and specific channels in ANNs. However, existing activation mechanisms often struggle to suppress signals from other irrelevant channels entirely, and these signals have been verified to be detrimental to the network's final decision. To address the issue of channel noise interference in ANNs, a novel end-to-end trainable Dual-Perspective Activation (DPA) mechanism is proposed. DPA efficiently identifies irrelevant channels and applies channel denoising under the guidance of a joint criterion established online from both forward and backward propagation perspectives while preserving activation responses from relevant channels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DPA successfully denoises channels and facilitates sparser neural representations. Moreover, DPA is parameter-free, fast, applicable to many mainstream ANN architectures, and achieves remarkable performance compared to other existing activation counterparts across multiple tasks and domains. Code is available at https://github.com/horrible-dong/DPA.

paragraphs: The paper examines interference from neural-network channels that are irrelevant to the current input's category. Its motivation is that useful information can be concentrated in a sparse subset of channels, while existing activation mechanisms may leave distracting responses active. Those responses can affect the network's final decision even when they carry irrelevant or redundant information.

Dual-Perspective Activation, or DPA, identifies and suppresses these channels using a criterion constructed during training from both forward and backward propagation. It preserves responses in relevant channels while removing channel noise. The mechanism is trainable as part of the full network and introduces no additional parameters, making the denoising operation compatible with end-to-end learning.

The authors also describe DPA as fast and applicable to many mainstream architectures. These findings support using information from both propagation directions to decide which activations should contribute to a network's prediction.
summary.tldr: DPA uses forward and backward propagation signals to suppress irrelevant channels without adding parameters.

title: Dual-Perspective Activation: Efficient Channel Denoising via Joint Forward-Backward Criterion for Artificial Neural Networks

abstract: A popular paradigm for offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) tasks is to first fit the offline trajectories to a sequence model, and then prompt the model for actions that lead to high expected return. In addition to obtaining accurate sequence models, this paper highlights that tractability, the ability to exactly and efficiently answer various probabilistic queries, plays an important role in offline RL. Specifically, due to the fundamental stochasticity from the offline data-collection policies and the environment dynamics, highly non-trivial conditional/constrained generation is required to elicit rewarding actions. While it is still possible to approximate such queries, we observe that such crude estimates undermine the benefits brought by expressive sequence models. To overcome this problem, this paper proposes Trifle (Tractable Inference for Offline RL), which leverages modern tractable generative models to bridge the gap between good sequence models and high expected returns at evaluation time. Empirically, Trifle achieves $7$ state-of-the-art scores and the highest average scores in $9$ Gym-MuJoCo benchmarks against strong baselines. Further, Trifle significantly outperforms prior approaches in stochastic environments and safe RL tasks with minimum algorithmic modifications.

paragraphs: One approach to offline reinforcement learning trains a sequence model on previously collected trajectories, then asks it for actions associated with high returns. This paper argues that accurate trajectory modeling is only part of the problem. The model must also answer the probabilistic questions needed to select rewarding actions efficiently and accurately.

Those questions become difficult because both the behavior that collected the data and the environment can be stochastic. Choosing actions therefore requires conditional generation, sometimes with additional constraints. The authors observe that crude approximations to these queries can erode the benefits of expressive sequence models. Their method, Trifle, uses tractable generative models that support exact, efficient probabilistic inference to connect learned trajectories with action selection.

Across nine Gym-MuJoCo benchmarks, Trifle achieves seven state-of-the-art scores and the highest average score against the evaluated baselines. It also substantially improves on prior approaches in stochastic environments and safe reinforcement learning tasks with minimal algorithm changes. These findings support treating inference capability as a central design choice alongside the quality of the sequence model.
summary.tldr: Trifle improves offline reinforcement learning by making the probabilistic queries behind action selection exact and efficient.

title: A Tractable Inference Perspective of Offline RL

abstract: Despite the remarkable empirical performance of Transformers, their theoretical understanding remains elusive. Here, we consider a deep multi-head self-attention network, that is closely related to Transformers yet analytically tractable. We develop a statistical mechanics theory of Bayesian learning in this model, deriving exact equations for the network's predictor statistics under the finite-width thermodynamic limit, i.e., $N,P\rightarrow\infty$, $P/N=\mathcal{O}(1)$, where $N$ is the network width and $P$ is the number of training examples. Our theory shows that the predictor statistics are expressed as a sum of independent kernels, each one pairing different "attention paths", defined as information pathways through different attention heads across layers. The kernels are weighted according to a "task-relevant kernel combination" mechanism that aligns the total kernel with the task labels. As a consequence, this interplay between attention paths enhances generalization performance. Experiments confirm our findings on both synthetic and real-world sequence classification tasks. Finally, our theory explicitly relates the kernel combination mechanism to properties of the learned weights, allowing for a qualitative transfer of its insights to models trained via gradient descent. As an illustration, we demonstrate an efficient size reduction of the network, by pruning those attention heads that are deemed less relevant by our theory.

paragraphs: This paper studies how information pathways through attention heads contribute to prediction and generalization. The authors analyze a deep multi-head self-attention network closely related to transformers but mathematically tractable. Their statistical mechanics theory describes Bayesian learning when network width and the number of training examples both grow while their ratio remains of constant order.

Within that limit, the authors derive exact equations for predictor statistics. These statistics combine kernels associated with pairs of attention paths, where a path passes through particular heads across layers. A task-dependent weighting mechanism aligns the combined kernel with the training labels. The theory identifies this interaction between paths as a source of improved generalization.

summary.tldr: A tractable attention-network theory explains how task-dependent interactions between attention paths improve generalization and guide head pruning.

title: Dissecting the Interplay of Attention Paths in a Statistical Mechanics Theory of Transformers

abstract: Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) aims to perform geometric completion and semantic segmentation simultaneously. Despite the promising results achieved by existing studies, the inherently ill-posed nature of the task presents significant challenges in diverse driving scenarios. This paper introduces TALoS, a novel test-time adaptation approach for SSC that excavates the information available in driving environments. Specifically, we focus on that observations made at a certain moment can serve as Ground Truth (GT) for scene completion at another moment. Given the characteristics of the LiDAR sensor, an observation of an object at a certain location confirms both 1) the occupation of that location and 2) the absence of obstacles along the line of sight from the LiDAR to that point. TALoS utilizes these observations to obtain self-supervision about occupancy and emptiness, guiding the model to adapt to the scene in test time. In a similar manner, we aggregate reliable SSC predictions among multiple moments and leverage them as semantic pseudo-GT for adaptation. Further, to leverage future observations that are not accessible at the current time, we present a dual optimization scheme using the model in which the update is delayed until the future observation is available. Evaluations on the SemanticKITTI validation and test sets demonstrate that TALoS significantly improves the performance of the pre-trained SSC model.

paragraphs: Semantic scene completion predicts both the geometry of a scene and the semantic labels of its contents. Driving observations leave parts of the scene uncertain, making this task inherently difficult. TALoS adapts a pretrained model during testing by using information gathered at different moments to supervise predictions about the scene.

The method draws two kinds of geometric evidence from a LiDAR observation. A detected point indicates that its location is occupied, while the line of sight from the sensor to that point indicates empty space. TALoS converts these observations into supervision for occupancy and emptiness. It also combines reliable predictions across multiple moments to create semantic pseudo-labels for adaptation.

Some useful observations arrive only in the future. A dual optimization scheme handles this by delaying an update until the relevant observation becomes available. Evaluations on the SemanticKITTI validation and test sets show significant improvements over the pretrained scene-completion model. The approach uses observations accumulated during deployment to refine both geometric and semantic predictions.
summary.tldr: TALoS improves scene completion through test-time adaptation using LiDAR evidence of occupied and empty space plus semantic predictions across time.

title: TALoS: Enhancing Semantic Scene Completion via Test-time Adaptation on the Line of Sight

abstract: Large-vocabulary object detectors (LVDs) aim to detect objects of many categories, which learn super objectness features and can locate objects accurately while applied to various downstream data. However, LVDs often struggle in recognizing the located objects due to domain discrepancy in data distribution and object vocabulary. At the other end, recent vision-language foundation models such as CLIP demonstrate superior open-vocabulary recognition capability. This paper presents KGD, a Knowledge Graph Distillation technique that exploits the implicit knowledge graphs (KG) in CLIP for effectively adapting LVDs to various downstream domains.KGD consists of two consecutive stages: 1) KG extraction that employs CLIP to encode downstream domain data as nodes and their feature distances as edges, constructing KG that inherits the rich semantic relations in CLIP explicitly; and 2) KG encapsulation that transfers the extracted KG into LVDs to enable accurate cross-domain object classification. In addition, KGD can extract both visual and textual KG independently, providing complementary vision and language knowledge for object localization and object classification in detection tasks over various downstream domains. Experiments over multiple widely adopted detection benchmarks show that KGD outperforms the state-of-the-art consistently by large margins. Codes will be released.

However, LVDs often struggle in recognizing the located objects due to domain discrepancy in data distribution and object vocabulary. At the other end, recent vision-language foundation models such as CLIP demonstrate superior open-vocabulary recognition capability. This paper presents KGD, a Knowledge Graph Distillation technique that exploits the implicit knowledge graphs (KG) in CLIP for effectively adapting LVDs to various downstream domains.KGD consists of two consecutive stages: 1) KG extraction that employs CLIP to encode downstream domain data as nodes and their feature distances as edges, constructing KG that inherits the rich semantic relations in CLIP explicitly; and 2) KG encapsulation that transfers the extracted KG into LVDs to enable accurate cross-domain object classification. In addition, KGD can extract both visual and textual KG independently, providing complementary vision and language knowledge for object localization and object classification in detection tasks over various downstream domains. Experiments over multiple widely adopted detection benchmarks show that KGD outperforms the state-of-the-art consistently by large margins. Codes will be released.

paragraphs: Large-vocabulary object detectors can locate objects across many categories, yet recognizing those objects becomes difficult when downstream images or category vocabularies differ from training. This paper targets that gap between finding an object and assigning it the right identity. It draws on CLIP's open-vocabulary recognition knowledge to adapt an existing detector to downstream domains.

The proposed Knowledge Graph Distillation method first represents downstream data using CLIP. Data representations become graph nodes, and distances between their features define graph edges. This exposes semantic relationships carried implicitly by CLIP. A second stage transfers the extracted graph into the detector to improve classification across domains.

The method can extract visual and textual graphs separately, supplying complementary information for localization and classification. Across multiple established detection benchmarks, the authors report consistently large improvements over the compared state of the art. The contribution is a structured transfer mechanism: adaptation uses relationships among representations to bring recognition knowledge into a detector facing different data and object vocabularies.
summary.tldr: Knowledge Graph Distillation transfers CLIP's visual and textual relationships into object detectors to improve recognition in new domains.

title: Domain Adaptation for Large-Vocabulary Object Detectors

abstract: The goal of this paper is to investigate the complexity of gradient algorithms when learning sparse functions (juntas). We introduce a type of Statistical Queries ($\mathsf{SQ}$), which we call Differentiable Learning Queries ($\mathsf{DLQ}$), to model gradient queries on a specified loss with respect to an arbitrary model. We provide a tight characterization of the query complexity of $\mathsf{DLQ}$ for learning the support of a sparse function over generic product distributions. This complexity crucially depends on the loss function. For the squared loss, $\mathsf{DLQ}$ matches the complexity of Correlation Statistical Queries $(\mathsf{CSQ})$—potentially much worse than $\mathsf{SQ}$. But for other simple loss functions, including the $\ell_1$ loss, $\mathsf{DLQ}$ always achieves the same complexity as $\mathsf{SQ}$. We also provide evidence that $\mathsf{DLQ}$ can indeed capture learning with (stochastic) gradient descent by showing it correctly describes the complexity of learning with a two-layer neural network in the mean field regime and linear scaling.
