paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned model of environment dynamics to reason about possible futures. Errors in that model can accumulate during imagined rollouts and affect the resulting policy. This paper studies whether the shape of the model's training loss helps explain and improve downstream control performance.

The method adds Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, to world-model training while leaving the planner, policy components, and architecture unchanged. SAM encourages flatter minima, where the loss is less sensitive to nearby parameter changes. The authors derive PAC-Bayesian bounds connecting first-order sharpness with errors in value estimation and the performance gap between model-optimal and true-optimal policies; reduced sharpness tightens these bounds.

Experiments on HumanoidBench, Atari-100k, and high-dimensional DeepMind Control tasks show reduced measured sharpness, lower value-prediction error, and improved returns. Gains are especially large in settings with high-dimensional state-action spaces. Positive transfer across algorithms and input modalities, including a transformer world model, supports flatness-aware training as a broadly useful modification within the tested systems.
summary.tldr: Applying SAM to world-model training tightens sharpness-based theoretical bounds and improves control returns across the evaluated reinforcement-learning systems.

title: Improving Model-Based Reinforcement Learning by Converging to Flatter Minima

abstract: Deep neural networks using state space models as layers are well suited for long-range sequence tasks but can be challenging to compress after training. We use that regularizing the sum of Hankel singular values of state space models leads to a fast decay of these singular values and thus to compressible models. To make the proposed Hankel singular value regularization scalable, we develop an algorithm to efficiently compute the Hankel singular values during training iterations by exploiting the specific block-diagonal structure of the system matrices that is we use in our state space model parametrization. Experiments on Long Range Arena benchmarks demonstrate that the regularized state space layers are up to 10$\times$ more compressible than standard state space layers while maintaining high accuracy.

paragraphs: State space layers can handle long-range sequence tasks, but reducing their size after training can be difficult. This paper tackles that problem during training by encouraging a structure that is easier to compress later. Its regularization target is the sum of the layer’s Hankel singular values.

The approach uses the relationship between rapidly decaying Hankel singular values and compressibility. Penalizing their sum encourages that decay, preparing the trained state space model for compression. To make this practical during repeated training updates, the authors develop an efficient computation algorithm that exploits the block-diagonal system matrices used in their chosen parameterization.

Experiments on Long Range Arena show that the regularized state space layers can be up to ten times more compressible than standard state space layers while retaining high accuracy. The result concerns compressibility rather than a reported tenfold acceleration of the entire network. The broader idea is to make eventual compression part of the training objective, supported by a computation strategy tailored to the model’s matrix structure.
summary.tldr: Regularizing Hankel singular values during training makes state space layers up to ten times more compressible while maintaining high accuracy.

title: Hankel Singular Value Regularization for Highly Compressible State Space Models

abstract: The rapid emergence of diverse large language models (LLMs) has spurred the development of LLM routers that assign user queries to the most suitable model. However, existing LLM routers typically perform a single-round, one-to-one mapping (\textit{i.e.}, assigning each query to a single model in isolation), which limits their capability to tackle complex tasks that demand the complementary strengths of multiple LLMs. In this paper, we present \textbf{Router-R1}, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that formulates multi-LLM routing and aggregation as a sequential decision process. Router-R1 instantiates the router itself as a capable LLM, leveraging its reasoning ability to interleave "think" actions (internal deliberation) with "route" actions (dynamic model invocation), and integrates each response into its evolving context. To facilitate learning, we employ a lightweight rule-based reward comprising format rewards, final outcome rewards, and a novel cost reward for optimizing the balance between performance and cost, opening a pathway toward enhancing performance-cost trade-offs via RL. Router-R1 also conditions only on simple model descriptors such as pricing, latency, and example performance, enabling strong generalization to unseen model selection. Experiments on seven general and multi-hop QA benchmarks show that Router-R1 outperforms several strong baselines, achieving superior performance while maintaining robust generalization and cost management.

paragraphs: A language-model router usually sends each query to one model. That can limit performance on questions that benefit from several models’ complementary strengths. Router-R1 treats routing and answer aggregation as a sequence of decisions, allowing the system to use information gained from one model when deciding what to do next.

The router is itself a language model. It alternates between internal deliberation and calls to other models, adding each response to its evolving context. Reinforcement learning trains this behavior using a lightweight reward that combines formatting, final-answer quality, and cost. Including cost makes the expense of model calls part of the learned decision process rather than leaving performance as the only objective.

Routing decisions use simple model descriptions, including pricing, latency, and example performance. The authors report strong generalization to selecting previously unseen models. Across seven general and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, Router-R1 outperforms several strong baselines while maintaining cost management. The results support learning when to consult additional models and how to combine their contributions.
summary.tldr: Router-R1 learns to alternate reasoning with multiple model calls, combining responses while balancing answer quality and cost.

title: Router-R1: Teaching LLMs Multi-Round Routing and Aggregation via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We revisit scene-level 3D object detection as the output of an object-centric framework capable of both localization and mapping using 3D oriented boxes as the underlying geometric primitive. While existing 3D object detection approaches operate globally and implicitly rely on the a priori existence of metric camera poses, our method, Rooms from Motion (RfM) operates on a collection of un-posed images. By replacing the standard 2D keypoint-based matcher of structure-from-motion with an object-centric matcher based on image-derived 3D boxes, we estimate metric camera poses, object tracks, and finally produce a global, semantic 3D object map. When a priori pose is available, we can significantly improve map quality through optimization of global 3D boxes against individual observations. RfM shows strong localization performance and subsequently produces maps of higher quality than leading point-based and multi-view 3D object detection methods on CA-1M and ScanNet++, despite these global methods relying on overparameterization through point clouds or dense volumes. Rooms from Motion achieves a general, object-centric representation which not only extends the work of Cubify Anything to full scenes but also allows for inherently sparse localization and parametric mapping proportional to the number of objects in a scene.

paragraphs: Rooms from Motion treats indoor object detection as a combined camera-localization and mapping problem. It starts from images without known camera poses and represents scene geometry through oriented 3D object boxes. This lets the method build a semantic scene map while also estimating where the cameras were when the images were captured.

The key change is replacing a conventional structure-from-motion matcher based on 2D keypoints with an object-based matcher using 3D boxes derived from images. Matching these boxes yields metric camera poses and object tracks, which support construction of a global map. When camera poses are already available, optimizing global boxes against individual observations further improves map quality.

On CA-1M and ScanNet++, the method reports strong localization and higher-quality maps than leading point-based and multi-view object-detection methods. Its representation remains sparse because mapping complexity is proportional to the number of objects. The result extends object-level box representations to complete scenes while bringing localization and semantic mapping into a shared geometric framework.
summary.tldr: Rooms from Motion matches image-derived 3D object boxes to jointly estimate camera poses and build sparse semantic scene maps.

title: Rooms from Motion: Un-posed Indoor 3D Object Detection as Localization and Mapping

abstract: Many machine learning tasks can benefit from external knowledge. Large knowledge graphs store such knowledge, and embedding methods can be used to distill it into ready-to-use vector representations for downstream applications. For this purpose, current models have however two limitations: they are primarily optimized for link prediction, via local contrastive learning, and their application to the largest graphs requires significant engineering effort due to GPU memory limits. To address these, we introduce SEPAL: a Scalable Embedding Propagation ALgorithm for large knowledge graphs designed to produce high-quality embeddings for downstream tasks at scale. The key idea of SEPAL is to ensure global embedding consistency by optimizing embeddings only on a small core of entities, and then propagating them to the rest of the graph with message passing. We evaluate SEPAL on 7 large-scale knowledge graphs and 46 downstream machine learning tasks. Our results show that SEPAL significantly outperforms previous methods on downstream tasks. In addition, SEPAL scales up its base embedding model, enabling fitting huge knowledge graphs on commodity hardware. Our code is available at: .

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs can supply external information to machine-learning systems through vector representations of their entities. Existing embedding methods, however, often focus on predicting missing links rather than producing features for other tasks. Their memory requirements also make applying them to very large graphs an engineering challenge.

SEPAL addresses both issues by optimizing embeddings for only a small core of entities, then spreading those representations through the remaining graph with message passing. The design aims to maintain global consistency across embeddings while limiting the portion of the graph requiring direct optimization. This makes propagation central to both representation quality and scalability.

The authors evaluate the method on seven large knowledge graphs and 46 downstream machine-learning tasks. They report significant improvements over previous methods on those tasks, alongside the ability to scale the underlying embedding model to huge graphs on commodity hardware. These findings support judging graph embeddings by their usefulness as external features, and show how a core-and-propagation strategy can make that objective practical at larger scales.
summary.tldr: SEPAL learns embeddings on a small graph core and propagates them outward, improving downstream features while scaling to huge knowledge graphs.

title: Scalable Feature Learning on Huge Knowledge Graphs for Downstream Machine Learning

abstract: Preventing feature co-adaptation by encouraging independent contributions from different features often improves classification and regression performance. Dropout training (Hinton et al., 2012) does this by randomly dropping out (zeroing) hidden units and input features during training of neural networks. However, repeatedly sampling a random subset of input features makes training much slower. Based on an examination of the implied objective function of dropout training, we show how to do fast dropout training by sampling from or integrating a Gaussian approximation, instead of doing Monte Carlo optimization of this objective. This approximation, justified by the central limit theorem and empirical evidence, gives an order of magnitude speedup and more stability. We show how to do fast dropout training for classification, regression, and multilayer neural networks. Beyond dropout, our technique is extended to integrate out other types of noise and small image transformations.

paragraphs: Dropout trains neural networks while randomly setting some inputs and hidden units to zero. This encourages features to contribute independently instead of depending too strongly on particular companions. Such reduced co-adaptation often improves classification and regression, but repeatedly drawing random subsets makes the training procedure slower.

The paper examines the objective implied by dropout and replaces its repeated Monte Carlo optimization with a Gaussian approximation. Training can then sample from that approximation or integrate over it. The authors support this approximation through the central limit theorem and empirical evidence, connecting the computational shortcut to the behavior of the noise introduced by dropout.

The reported result is an order-of-magnitude speedup together with greater stability. The paper develops the approach for classification, regression, and multilayer neural networks. It also extends the technique to integrate out other noise sources and small image transformations. The broader contribution is a way to account for training-time variability through approximation, reducing the work required to repeatedly realize that variability through explicit random choices.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian approximation to dropout delivers a reported order-of-magnitude training speedup and greater stability.

title: Fast dropout training

abstract: We introduce Deep Canonical Correlation Analysis (DCCA), a method to learn complex nonlinear transformations of two views of data such that the resulting representations are highly linearly correlated. Parameters of both transformations are jointly learned to maximize the (regularized) total correlation. It can be viewed as a nonlinear extension of the linear method \emphcanonical correlation analysis (CCA). It is an alternative to the nonparametric method \emphkernel canonical correlation analysis (KCCA) for learning correlated nonlinear transformations. Unlike KCCA, DCCA does not require an inner product, and has the advantages of a parametric method: training time scales well with data size and the training data need not be referenced when computing the representations of unseen instances. In experiments on two real-world datasets, we find that DCCA learns representations with significantly higher correlation than those learned by CCA and KCCA. We also introduce a novel non-saturating sigmoid function based on the cube root that may be useful more generally in feedforward neural networks.

paragraphs: Deep Canonical Correlation Analysis learns representations of two views of data so that the transformed views have strong linear correlation. Each transformation can be complex and nonlinear. Their parameters are learned jointly to maximize regularized total correlation, extending the aim of linear canonical correlation analysis to a more flexible representation family.

The paper positions DCCA as a parametric alternative to kernel canonical correlation analysis. It does not require an inner product, and the learned transformations can represent unseen instances without referring back to the training data. The authors also identify favorable scaling of training time with data size as an advantage of the parametric approach.

On two real-world datasets, DCCA learns representations with significantly higher correlation than those produced by CCA and KCCA. This finding directly supports its ability to capture shared variation between views. The paper additionally introduces a cube-root-based, non-saturating sigmoid function and suggests that it may have broader use in feedforward neural networks.
summary.tldr: DCCA jointly learns nonlinear transformations of two data views, achieving higher representation correlation than CCA and KCCA on two datasets.

title: Deep Canonical Correlation Analysis

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating distributional parameters that are expected values of given feature functions. We are interested in recovery under high-dimensional regimes, where the number of variables p is potentially larger than the number of samples n, and where we need to impose structural constraints upon the parameters. In a natural distributional setting for this problem, the feature functions comprise the sufficient statistics of an exponential family, so that the problem would entail estimating structured moments of exponential family distributions. A special case of the above involves estimating the covariance matrix of a random vector, and where the natural distributional setting would correspond to the multivariate Gaussian distribution. Unlike the inverse covariance estimation case, we show that the regularized MLEs for covariance estimation, as well as natural Dantzig variants, are \emphnon-convex, even when the regularization functions themselves are convex; with the same holding for the general structured moment case. We propose a class of elementary convex estimators, that in many cases are available in \emphclosed-form, for estimating general structured moments. We then provide a unified statistical analysis of our class of estimators. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our class of estimators on real-world climatology and biology datasets.

paragraphs: The paper considers estimating parameters defined as averages of feature functions, including covariance matrices. It focuses on high-dimensional settings where the number of variables may exceed the number of samples. Structural constraints then become part of the estimation problem, such as the sparsity highlighted in covariance estimation.

A key finding is that familiar regularization does not automatically produce a convex optimization problem here. The authors show that regularized maximum likelihood formulations and natural Dantzig variants for covariance estimation are non-convex even when their regularizers are convex. The same issue extends to the broader structured-moment setting, including moments associated with exponential families.

The proposed alternative is a family of elementary convex estimators, many of which have closed-form solutions. A unified statistical analysis treats these estimators within one framework. Applications to climatology and biology data demonstrate their use in real problems. The contribution combines a diagnosis of why standard formulations can be difficult with an alternative that makes computation simpler while retaining a basis for statistical analysis.
summary.tldr: Elementary convex estimators provide an alternative to non-convex regularized formulations for covariance matrices and other structured moments.

title: Elementary Estimators for Sparse Covariance Matrices and other Structured Moments

abstract: In this paper we present a new way of predicting the performance of a reinforcement learning policy given historical data that may have been generated by a different policy. The ability to evaluate a policy from historical data is important for applications where the deployment of a bad policy can be dangerous or costly. We show empirically that our algorithm produces estimates that often have orders of magnitude lower mean squared error than existing methods—it makes more efficient use of the available data. Our new estimator is based on two advances: an extension of the doubly robust estimator (Jiang & Li, 2015), and a new way to mix between model based and importance sampling based estimates.
originalAbstract: In this paper we present a new way of predicting the performance of a reinforcement learning policy given historical data that may have been generated by a different policy. The ability to evaluate a policy from historical data is important for applications where the deployment of a bad policy can be dangerous or costly. We show empirically that our algorithm produces estimates that often have orders of magnitude lower mean squared error than existing methods—it makes more efficient use of the available data. Our new estimator is based on two advances: an extension of the doubly robust estimator (Jiang & Li, 2015), and a new way to mix between model based and importance sampling based estimates.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to estimate a reinforcement learning policy's performance using historical data, even when another policy generated those records. This is off-policy evaluation: the decision rule being assessed need not be the rule that produced the observations. It matters when deploying a poor policy could be expensive or dangerous.

The proposed estimator combines two advances. First, it extends a doubly robust estimator. Second, it introduces a new way to mix model-based estimates with estimates based on importance sampling. These provide different routes from historical observations to an assessment of the target policy, and the paper develops a way to combine them more effectively.

The empirical finding is that the resulting estimates often have mean squared error orders of magnitude below existing methods. This means substantially better estimation accuracy from the available data in many of the reported comparisons. The word 'often' is central: the evidence supports improved data efficiency in the experiments, rather than an unconditional guarantee for every policy or dataset.
summary.tldr: An estimator combining an extended doubly robust approach with a new mixing strategy often greatly reduces off-policy evaluation error in experiments.

title: Data-Efficient Off-Policy Policy Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Cross-graph Relational Learning (CGRL) refers to the problem of predicting the strengths or labels of multi-relational tuples of heterogeneous object types, through the joint inference over multiple graphs which specify the internal connections among each type of objects. CGRL is an open challenge in machine learning due to the daunting number of all possible tuples to deal with when the numbers of nodes in multiple graphs are large, and because the labeled training instances are extremely sparse as typical. Existing methods such as tensor factorization or tensor-kernel machines do not work well because of the lack of convex formulation for the optimization of CGRL models, the poor scalability of the algorithms in handling combinatorial numbers of tuples, and/or the non-transductive nature of the learning methods which limits their ability to leverage unlabeled data in training. This paper proposes a novel framework which formulates CGRL as a convex optimization problem, enables transductive learning using both labeled and unlabeled tuples, and offers a scalable algorithm that guarantees the optimal solution and enjoys a constant time complexity with respect to the sizes of input graphs. In our experiments with a subset of DBLP publication records and an Enzyme multi-source dataset, the proposed method successfully scaled to the large cross-graph inference problem, and outperformed other representative approaches significantly.

paragraphs: Cross-graph relational learning predicts relationships involving several kinds of objects, while using a separate graph to describe connections within each kind. A prediction concerns a tuple of objects drawn across these graphs. The difficulty is that possible tuples grow combinatorially, while labeled examples are typically extremely sparse.

The paper proposes a convex formulation that learns jointly from labeled and unlabeled tuples. This transductive design allows the unlabeled tuples to participate in training, rather than leaving their information unused. The authors also provide an algorithm guaranteed to reach the optimal solution of their formulation and report constant time complexity with respect to input graph sizes.

Experiments use a subset of DBLP publication records and an Enzyme dataset combining multiple sources. The method scales to the large cross-graph inference problem and significantly outperforms representative alternatives in those evaluations. Together, the formulation and results address three linked obstacles: difficult optimization, the huge collection of possible associations, and the limited supply of labeled relationships.
summary.tldr: A convex, transductive framework learns cross-graph relationships from sparse labels and unlabeled tuples, with strong reported scalability and empirical results.

title: Cross-Graph Learning of Multi-Relational Associations

abstract: We develop continuous-time probabilistic models to study trajectory data consisting of times and locations of user “check-ins”. We model the data as realizations of a marked point process, with intensity and mark-distribution modulated by a latent Markov jump process (MJP). We also include user-heterogeneity in our model by assigning each user a vector of “preferred locations”. Our model extends latent Dirichlet allocation by dropping the bag-of-words assumption and operating in continuous time. We show how an appropriate choice of priors allows efficient posterior inference. Our experiments demonstrate the usefulness of our approach by comparing with various baselines on a variety of tasks.

paragraphs: The paper models trajectories recorded as the times and locations of users' check-ins. It treats these observations as a marked point process in continuous time. This representation combines when an event occurs with its associated location, allowing both parts of a check-in record to enter a single probabilistic model.

A hidden Markov jump process modulates both the event intensity and the distribution of locations. The model also assigns each user a vector of preferred locations to capture differences between users. Thus, changing latent behavior and persistent personal preferences both contribute to how the observed trajectories are represented.

The authors describe the model as extending latent Dirichlet allocation by dropping its bag-of-words assumption and working in continuous time. They show that suitable priors permit efficient posterior inference. Experiments compare the approach with multiple baselines across several tasks and demonstrate its usefulness. The contribution connects a temporal probabilistic representation of check-ins with an inference strategy that makes the model practical to evaluate.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time check-in model combines latent behavioral changes with user location preferences and supports efficient posterior inference.

title: Markov-modulated Marked Poisson Processes for Check-in Data

abstract: Due to its numerous applications, rank aggregation has become a problem of major interest across many fields of the computer science literature. In the vast majority of situations, Kemeny consensus(es) are considered as the ideal solutions. It is however well known that their computation is NP-hard. Many contributions have thus established various results to apprehend this complexity. In this paper we introduce a practical method to predict, for a ranking and a dataset, how close the Kemeny consensus(es) are to this ranking. A major strength of this method is its generality: it does not require any assumption on the dataset nor the ranking. Furthermore, it relies on a new geometric interpretation of Kemeny aggregation that, we believe, could lead to many other results.

paragraphs: Rank aggregation combines a collection of rankings into a consensus ranking. Kemeny consensuses are widely regarded as ideal answers to this problem, but computing them is NP-hard. This creates a practical obstacle: even when a candidate ranking is already available, determining how close it is to an ideal consensus can seem to require solving the difficult aggregation problem first.

The paper introduces a practical method for predicting the proximity of Kemeny consensuses to a supplied ranking, using that ranking and the dataset as inputs. Its central move is to assess the relationship to the consensus without first computing the consensus itself. The method rests on a new geometric interpretation of Kemeny aggregation.

A stated strength is that the approach requires no assumptions about either the dataset or the candidate ranking. Its usefulness therefore does not depend on restricting attention to specially structured inputs. The geometric interpretation also offers a potential foundation for further results, although the abstract presents that broader prospect as the authors' expectation.
summary.tldr: A geometric approach predicts how close a ranking is to Kemeny consensuses without computing those consensuses.

title: Controlling the distance to a Kemeny consensus without computing it

abstract: Symmetric distribution properties such as support size, support coverage, entropy, and proximity to uniformity, arise in many applications. Recently, researchers applied different estimators and analysis tools to derive asymptotically sample-optimal approximations for each of these properties. We show that a single, simple, plug-in estimator— profile maximum likelihood (PML) —is sample competitive for all symmetric properties, and in particular is asymptotically sample-optimal for all the above properties.
originalAbstract: Symmetric distribution properties such as support size, support coverage, entropy, and proximity to uniformity, arise in many applications. Recently, researchers applied different estimators and analysis tools to derive asymptotically sample-optimal approximations for each of these properties. We show that a single, simple, plug-in estimator— profile maximum likelihood (PML) —is sample competitive for all symmetric properties, and in particular is asymptotically sample-optimal for all the above properties.

paragraphs: Many questions about a discrete distribution concern its overall structure rather than the names assigned to its outcomes. Examples include its support size, support coverage, entropy, and proximity to uniformity. These are symmetric properties. Earlier work had developed separate estimators and analytical tools to estimate each of these quantities with asymptotically optimal sample requirements.

The paper shows that one estimator, profile maximum likelihood, can provide a common approach. It is a plug-in estimator: a distribution estimate serves as the basis for estimating the desired property. The key contribution is that the same estimation principle comes with sample-competitiveness guarantees across all symmetric properties, rather than requiring a different principle for each one.

For the four properties explicitly listed, the result is stronger: profile maximum likelihood achieves asymptotically optimal sample efficiency. This concerns how much sampled data estimation requires in the asymptotic regime. The significance is a unified statistical foundation for problems that previously had separate sample-optimal treatments, with the broader competitiveness claim distinguished from optimality for the named properties.
summary.tldr: Profile maximum likelihood provides one sample-competitive estimator for symmetric distribution properties and asymptotically optimal estimates for several prominent examples.

title: A Unified Maximum Likelihood Approach for Estimating Symmetric Properties of Discrete Distributions

abstract: Topic models have been widely explored as probabilistic generative models of documents. Traditional inference methods have sought closed-form derivations for updating the models, however as the expressiveness of these models grows, so does the difficulty of performing fast and accurate inference over their parameters. This paper presents alternative neural approaches to topic modelling by providing parameterisable distributions over topics which permit training by backpropagation in the framework of neural variational inference. In addition, with the help of a stick-breaking construction, we propose a recurrent network that is able to discover a notionally unbounded number of topics, analogous to Bayesian non-parametric topic models. Experimental results on the MXM Song Lyrics, 20NewsGroups and Reuters News datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of these neural topic models.

paragraphs: Topic models explain documents through underlying topics, but inference becomes harder as the models become more expressive. Traditional approaches seek closed-form update rules, which can make that growing complexity difficult to manage. This paper develops neural approaches that make topic-model training compatible with backpropagation through neural variational inference.

The method supplies parameterizable distributions over topics, allowing neural training machinery to carry out the inference process. It also introduces a recurrent network using a stick-breaking construction. That construction lets the model discover a notionally unbounded number of topics, giving it an analogy to Bayesian nonparametric topic models rather than requiring its conceptual topic capacity to stop at a fixed count.

Experiments on MXM Song Lyrics, 20NewsGroups, and Reuters News demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed neural topic models. The results support the combination of flexible topic representations and trainable inference on these document collections. The contribution brings both backpropagation-based training and an expandable topic construction into the same modeling direction.
summary.tldr: Neural variational inference trains topic models by backpropagation, including a recurrent model with notionally unbounded topic capacity.

title: Discovering Discrete Latent Topics with Neural Variational Inference

abstract: In many real-world scenarios, rewards extrinsic to the agent are extremely sparse, or absent altogether. In such cases, curiosity can serve as an intrinsic reward signal to enable the agent to explore its environment and learn skills that might be useful later in its life. We formulate curiosity as the error in an agent’s ability to predict the consequence of its own actions in a visual feature space learned by a self-supervised inverse dynamics model. Our formulation scales to high-dimensional continuous state spaces like images, bypasses the difficulties of directly predicting pixels, and, critically, ignores the aspects of the environment that cannot affect the agent. The proposed approach is evaluated in two environments: VizDoom and Super Mario Bros. Three broad settings are investigated: 1) sparse extrinsic reward, where curiosity allows for far fewer interactions with the environment to reach the goal; 2) exploration with no extrinsic reward, where curiosity pushes the agent to explore more efficiently; and 3) generalization to unseen scenarios (e.g. new levels of the same game) where the knowledge gained from earlier experience helps the agent explore new places much faster than starting from scratch.

paragraphs: This paper gives an agent a reason to explore when external rewards are rare or unavailable. It defines curiosity through prediction error: an action is interesting when the agent struggles to predict its consequences. The prediction takes place in a learned visual representation rather than directly over image pixels.

A self-supervised inverse dynamics model learns that representation. The resulting formulation handles high-dimensional continuous observations such as images while avoiding the difficulties of predicting every pixel. The authors also emphasize that it ignores environmental aspects that cannot affect the agent, making the chosen representation central to what counts as a useful source of curiosity.

Without external rewards, it improves exploration efficiency. When the agent encounters unseen scenarios, knowledge acquired earlier helps it explore faster than starting over. Together, these findings support curiosity as both an immediate exploration signal and a way to build experience useful in later settings.
summary.tldr: Prediction errors in a learned visual feature space provide curiosity rewards that improve exploration and transfer in two game environments.

title: Curiosity-driven Exploration by Self-supervised Prediction

abstract: In this paper, we present a stochastic version of DCA (Difference of Convex functions Algorithm) to solve a class of optimization problems whose objective function is a large sum of non-convex functions and a regularization term. We consider the $\ell_{2,0}$ regularization to deal with the group variables selection. By exploiting the special structure of the problem, we propose an efficient DC decomposition for which the corresponding stochastic DCA scheme is very inexpensive: it only requires the projection of points onto balls that is explicitly computed. As an application, we applied our algorithm for the group variables selection in multiclass logistic regression. Numerical experiments on several benchmark datasets and synthetic datasets illustrate the efficiency of our algorithm and its superiority over well-known methods, with respect to classification accuracy, sparsity of solution as well as running time.

paragraphs: The paper addresses optimization objectives made from a large sum of nonconvex functions plus a regularization term. It develops a stochastic version of the Difference of Convex functions Algorithm, or DCA. The application of interest is selecting groups of variables while training a classifier.

For group selection, the authors use ℓ₂,₀ regularization. They exploit the structure of the objective to construct an efficient difference-of-convex decomposition. The resulting stochastic procedure has inexpensive subproblems: it only requires projections of points onto balls, and those projections can be calculated explicitly. This makes the mathematical decomposition directly relevant to the cost of carrying out the algorithm.

The method is applied to group-variable selection in multiclass logistic regression. Experiments on benchmark and synthetic datasets report advantages over well-known methods in classification accuracy, solution sparsity, and running time. These findings support the approach as a practical way to combine predictive learning and group selection in the evaluated settings. The contribution links a structured nonconvex formulation to simple computations and favorable empirical results.
summary.tldr: A stochastic difference-of-convex algorithm uses inexpensive explicit projections for group-variable selection and performs favorably in multiclass classification experiments.

title: Stochastic DCA for the Large-sum of Non-convex Functions Problem and its Application to Group Variable Selection in Classification

abstract: We consider the problem of how best to use prior experience to bootstrap lifelong learning, where an agent faces a series of task instances drawn from some task distribution. First, we identify the initial policy that optimizes expected performance over the distribution of tasks for increasingly complex classes of policy and task distributions. We empirically demonstrate the relative performance of each policy class’ optimal element in a variety of simple task distributions. We then consider value-function initialization methods that preserve PAC guarantees while simultaneously minimizing the learning required in two learning algorithms, yielding MaxQInit, a practical new method for value-function-based transfer. We show that MaxQInit performs well in simple lifelong RL experiments.

We then consider value-function initialization methods that preserve PAC guarantees while simultaneously minimizing the learning required in two learning algorithms, yielding MaxQInit, a practical new method for value-function-based transfer. paragraphs: In lifelong reinforcement learning, an agent encounters a sequence of tasks drawn from a task distribution. Previous experience can provide a useful starting point, but choosing what to transfer is itself a learning problem. This paper studies two forms of initialization: the policy the agent starts with and the values it assigns before learning a new task.

For policy transfer, the authors identify initial policies that optimize expected performance over the task distribution. They consider increasingly complex classes of policies and task distributions, then compare the best policies from these classes empirically on simple task distributions. This makes the starting policy a deliberate choice based on expected performance across tasks.

For value transfer, they investigate initializations that preserve PAC learning guarantees while minimizing the learning required by two algorithms. This produces MaxQInit, a practical method for transferring value-function information. Experiments show good performance in simple lifelong reinforcement learning settings, demonstrating how prior experience can initialize learning while retaining the guarantees considered in the analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper studies effective initial policies and introduces MaxQInit for value transfer that preserves PAC guarantees in lifelong reinforcement learning.

title: Policy and Value Transfer in Lifelong Reinforcement Learning

abstract: It is increasingly common in many types of natural and physical systems (especially biological systems) to have different types of measurements performed on the same underlying system. In such settings, it is important to align the manifolds arising from each measurement in order to integrate such data and gain an improved picture of the system; we tackle this problem using generative adversarial networks (GANs). Recent attempts to use GANs to find correspondences between sets of samples do not explicitly perform proper alignment of manifolds. We present the new Manifold Aligning GAN (MAGAN) that aligns two manifolds such that related points in each measurement space are aligned. We demonstrate applications of MAGAN in single-cell biology in integrating two different measurement types together: cells from the same tissue are measured with both genomic (single-cell RNA-sequencing) and proteomic (mass cytometry) technologies. We show that MAGAN successfully aligns manifolds such that known correlations between measured markers are improved compared to other recently proposed models.

paragraphs: Different measurement technologies can describe the same biological system in different spaces. Integrating those measurements requires aligning their manifolds, the structures formed by the observations, so that corresponding biological information can be brought together. The paper argues that recent GAN-based correspondence methods do not explicitly achieve the required manifold alignment.

MAGAN, the Manifold Aligning GAN, is designed to align two manifolds so that related points in their respective measurement spaces line up. This makes the relationship between observations central to the integration task. The intended result is a combined view of the underlying system that respects which observations are related across measurement types.

The authors demonstrate the approach in single-cell biology using genomic measurements from single-cell RNA sequencing and proteomic measurements from mass cytometry on cells from the same tissue. MAGAN improves known correlations between measured markers compared with other recently proposed models. Those correlations provide evidence that the learned alignment preserves meaningful biological relationships across the two forms of measurement.
summary.tldr: MAGAN aligns biological measurement spaces so related points correspond, improving known marker correlations in single-cell data integration.

title: MAGAN: Aligning Biological Manifolds

abstract: Techniques for reducing the variance of gradient estimates used in stochastic programming algorithms for convex finite-sum problems have received a great deal of attention in recent years. By leveraging dissipativity theory from control, we provide a new perspective on two important variance-reduction algorithms: SVRG and its direct accelerated variant Katyusha. Our perspective provides a physically intuitive understanding of the behavior of SVRG-like methods via a principle of energy conservation. The tools discussed here allow us to automate the convergence analysis of SVRG-like methods by capturing their essential properties in small semidefinite programs amenable to standard analysis and computational techniques. Our approach recovers existing convergence results for SVRG and Katyusha and generalizes the theory to alternative parameter choices. We also discuss how our approach complements the linear coupling technique. Our combination of perspectives leads to a better understanding of accelerated variance-reduced stochastic methods for finite-sum problems.

Our combination of perspectives leads to a better understanding of accelerated variance-reduced stochastic methods for finite-sum problems.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization uses gradient estimates, and reducing their variability can improve the behavior of optimization algorithms. This paper studies that idea for convex objectives made from finite sums, focusing on SVRG and its accelerated variant Katyusha. Its contribution is a shared analytical viewpoint for understanding their convergence and the role of acceleration.

The authors bring dissipativity theory from control into the analysis. Through an energy-conservation perspective, they express essential properties of these optimization methods using small semidefinite programs. This provides a route to automating convergence analysis with standard mathematical and computational tools, while also giving a physically motivated interpretation of algorithm behavior.

The framework recovers established convergence results for both SVRG and Katyusha and extends the analysis to alternative parameter choices. The authors also explain how it complements linear coupling, another technique for understanding acceleration. Together, these perspectives clarify accelerated variance reduction and offer a more systematic way to analyze related algorithms within the convex finite-sum setting.
summary.tldr: Control-theoretic dissipativity yields a unified, partly automatable convergence analysis of SVRG and Katyusha through small semidefinite programs.

title: Dissipativity Theory for Accelerating Stochastic Variance Reduction: A Unified Analysis of SVRG and Katyusha Using Semidefinite Programs

abstract: Sequential models achieve state-of-the-art results in audio, visual and textual domains with respect to both estimating the data distribution and generating desired samples. Efficient sampling for this class of models at the cost of little to no loss in quality has however remained an elusive problem. With a focus on text-to-speech synthesis, we describe a set of general techniques for reducing sampling time while maintaining high output quality. We first describe a single-layer recurrent neural network, the WaveRNN, with a dual softmax layer that matches the quality of the state-of-the-art WaveNet model. The compact form of the network makes it possible to generate 24 kHz 16-bit audio 4 times faster than real time on a GPU. Secondly, we apply a weight pruning technique to reduce the number of weights in the WaveRNN. We find that, for a constant number of parameters, large sparse networks perform better than small dense networks and this relationship holds past sparsity levels of more than 96%. The small number of weights in a Sparse WaveRNN makes it possible to sample high-fidelity audio on a mobile phone CPU in real time. Finally, we describe a new dependency scheme for sampling that lets us trade a constant number of non-local, distant dependencies for the ability to generate samples in batches. The Batch WaveRNN produces 8 samples per step without loss of quality and offers orthogonal ways of further increasing sampling efficiency.

Its first contribution, WaveRNN, uses a single recurrent layer and a dual softmax output layer. summary.tldr: WaveRNN combines a compact recurrent architecture, pruning, and batched sampling to accelerate high-quality audio generation, including real-time synthesis on a mobile CPU.

title: Efficient Neural Audio Synthesis

abstract: Weighted correlation clustering is hard to solve and hard to approximate for general graphs. Its applications in network analysis and computer vision call for efficient algorithms. To this end, we make three contributions: We establish partial optimality conditions that can be checked efficiently, and doing so recursively solves the problem for series-parallel graphs to optimality, in linear time. We exploit the packing dual of the problem to compute a heuristic, but non-trivial lower bound faster than that of a canonical linear program relaxation. We introduce a re-weighting with the dual solution by which efficient local search algorithms converge to better feasible solutions. The effectiveness of our methods is demonstrated empirically on a number of benchmark instances.

To this end, we make three contributions: We establish partial optimality conditions that can be checked efficiently, and doing so recursively solves the problem for series-parallel graphs to optimality, in linear time. We exploit the packing dual of the problem to compute a heuristic, but non-trivial lower bound faster than that of a canonical linear program relaxation. We introduce a re-weighting with the dual solution by which efficient local search algorithms converge to better feasible solutions. The effectiveness of our methods is demonstrated empirically on a number of benchmark instances.

paragraphs: Weighted correlation clustering poses difficult optimization and approximation problems on general graphs, despite its usefulness in network analysis and computer vision. This paper develops three complementary tools: conditions for establishing parts of an optimal solution, fast lower bounds, and a way to improve solutions found through local search.

The partial optimality conditions can be checked efficiently. Applying them recursively solves series-parallel graphs exactly in linear time, giving a strong result for that graph class. For more general instances, the authors use a packing dual formulation to obtain a nontrivial lower bound through a heuristic procedure that runs faster than a canonical linear programming relaxation.

A third contribution uses the dual solution to reweight the problem so that efficient local search algorithms converge to better feasible solutions. Benchmark experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods. The contributions serve different purposes: partial optimality certifies structure, lower bounds help assess achievable cost, and reweighting improves search, without claiming an efficient exact solution for arbitrary graphs.
summary.tldr: Partial optimality tests, fast lower bounds, and dual-based reweighting improve weighted correlation clustering, with exact linear-time solutions for series-parallel graphs.

title: Partial Optimality and Fast Lower Bounds for Weighted Correlation Clustering

abstract: Inference models are a key component in scaling variational inference to deep latent variable models, most notably as encoder networks in variational auto-encoders (VAEs). By replacing conventional optimization-based inference with a learned model, inference is amortized over data examples and therefore more computationally efficient. However, standard inference models are restricted to direct mappings from data to approximate posterior estimates. The failure of these models to reach fully optimized approximate posterior estimates results in an amortization gap. We aim toward closing this gap by proposing iterative inference models, which learn to perform inference optimization through repeatedly encoding gradients. Our approach generalizes standard inference models in VAEs and provides insight into several empirical findings, including top-down inference techniques. We demonstrate the inference optimization capabilities of iterative inference models and show that they outperform standard inference models on several benchmark data sets of images and text.

However, standard inference models are restricted to direct mappings from data to approximate posterior estimates. The failure of these models to reach fully optimized approximate posterior estimates results in an amortization gap. We aim toward closing this gap by proposing iterative inference models, which learn to perform inference optimization through repeatedly encoding gradients. Our approach generalizes standard inference models in VAEs and provides insight into several empirical findings, including top-down inference techniques. We demonstrate the inference optimization capabilities of iterative inference models and show that they outperform standard inference models on several benchmark data sets of images and text.

paragraphs: Variational auto-encoders use inference networks to estimate distributions over hidden variables from observations. Learning this mapping shares inference effort across examples, making inference computationally efficient. However, a direct prediction can fall short of the approximate posterior obtainable through fuller optimization. The difference is known as the amortization gap.

This paper proposes iterative inference models that learn how to refine their estimates through repeated encoding of gradients. Instead of producing an approximate posterior in a single direct mapping, the model learns an optimization process that updates the estimate. The approach generalizes standard VAE inference networks and aims to reduce the gap between fast learned inference and more fully optimized approximate posteriors.

The authors demonstrate that these models can perform inference optimization and outperform standard inference networks on several image and text benchmarks. The framework also offers insight into empirical findings involving top-down inference techniques. Its main contribution is to make iterative improvement part of learned inference itself, retaining the idea of sharing computation across examples while allowing each posterior estimate to be progressively refined.
summary.tldr: Iterative inference networks repeatedly encode gradients to refine approximate posteriors and outperform standard direct inference models on image and text benchmarks.

title: Iterative Amortized Inference

abstract: Existing algorithms for dictionary learning assume that the entries of the (high-dimensional) input data are fully observed. However, in several practical applications, only an incomplete fraction of the data entries may be available. For incomplete settings, no provably correct and polynomial-time algorithm has been reported in the dictionary learning literature. In this paper, we provide provable approaches for learning – from incomplete samples – a family of dictionaries whose atoms have sufficiently “spread-out” mass. First, we propose a descent-style iterative algorithm that linearly converges to the true dictionary when provided a sufficiently coarse initial estimate. Second, we propose an initialization algorithm that utilizes a small number of extra fully observed samples to produce such a coarse initial estimate. Finally, we theoretically analyze their performance and provide asymptotic statistical and computational guarantees.

The authors consider a family of dictionaries whose atoms distribute their mass sufficiently broadly across coordinates. They propose an iterative descent-style algorithm that converges linearly to the true dictionary when started from a sufficiently coarse initial estimate. The result therefore links successful recovery to both the structure of the dictionary and the quality of the starting point.

A second algorithm supplies that initialization using a small additional collection of fully observed samples. The overall approach thus combines learning from incomplete data with limited access to complete examples for initialization. The paper provides asymptotic statistical and computational guarantees for these procedures, establishing a theoretical route to recovery under the stated conditions rather than assuming every training example is fully available.
summary.tldr: The paper gives provable dictionary-learning algorithms for incomplete data, using spread-out atoms and a small fully observed sample set for initialization.

title: On Learning Sparsely Used Dictionaries from Incomplete Samples

abstract: We propose a fast stochastic Hamilton Monte Carlo (HMC) method, for sampling from a smooth and strongly log-concave distribution. At the core of our proposed method is a variance reduction technique inspired by the recent advance in stochastic optimization. We show that, to achieve $\epsilon$ accuracy in 2-Wasserstein distance, our algorithm achieves $\tilde O\big(n+\kappa^{2}d^{1/2}/\epsilon+\kappa^{4/3}d^{1/3}n^{2/3}/\epsilon^{2/3}\big)$ gradient complexity (i.e., number of component gradient evaluations), which outperforms the state-of-the-art HMC and stochastic gradient HMC methods in a wide regime. We also extend our algorithm for sampling from smooth and general log-concave distributions, and prove the corresponding gradient complexity as well. Experiments on both synthetic and real data demonstrate the superior performance of our algorithm.

It proposes a stochastic Hamilton Monte Carlo method that incorporates variance reduction inspired by stochastic optimization. The objective is to reduce the number of component-gradient evaluations needed to reach a specified level of sampling accuracy.

For an error target epsilon, the authors derive a gradient-complexity bound with terms n, kappa² times the square root of d divided by epsilon, and kappa^(4/3)d^(1/3)n^(2/3)/epsilon^(2/3), up to logarithmic factors. They show that the resulting complexity improves on existing HMC and stochastic-gradient HMC methods across a wide regime.

The authors also extend the algorithm to smooth log-concave distributions without the strong log-concavity requirement and prove a corresponding complexity result. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate superior performance in the reported evaluations. The contribution connects an optimization technique for controlling stochastic variability to sampling, with both explicit accuracy guarantees and evidence of practical gains.
summary.tldr: Variance reduction improves stochastic Hamilton Monte Carlo’s gradient complexity across a wide regime, with guarantees for smooth log-concave sampling.

title: Stochastic Variance-Reduced Hamilton Monte Carlo Methods

abstract: The principle of equivariance to symmetry transformations enables a theoretically grounded approach to neural network architecture design. Equivariant networks have shown excellent performance and data efficiency on vision and medical imaging problems that exhibit symmetries. Here we show how this principle can be extended beyond global symmetries to local gauge transformations. This enables the development of a very general class of convolutional neural networks on manifolds that depend only on the intrinsic geometry, and which includes many popular methods from equivariant and geometric deep learning. We implement gauge equivariant CNNs for signals defined on the surface of the icosahedron, which provides a reasonable approximation of the sphere. By choosing to work with this very regular manifold, we are able to implement the gauge equivariant convolution using a single conv2d call, making it a highly scalable and practical alternative to Spherical CNNs. Using this method, we demonstrate substantial improvements over previous methods on the task of segmenting omnidirectional images and global climate patterns.

This connects a general geometric construction to a standard computational operation, making the architecture scalable and practical.

These tasks demonstrate the usefulness of the construction for signals distributed over approximately spherical surfaces. The paper's contribution combines a broad architectural framework with a concrete implementation that makes its geometric principles computationally accessible.
summary.tldr: Gauge equivariance provides a general framework for geometric CNNs and an efficient icosahedral implementation with improved segmentation results.

title: Gauge Equivariant Convolutional Networks and the Icosahedral CNN

abstract: Bayesian inference via standard Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods such as Metropolis-Hastings is too computationally intensive to handle large datasets, since the cost per step usually scales like $O(n)$ in the number of data points $n$. We propose the Scalable Metropolis-Hastings (SMH) kernel that only requires processing on average $O(1)$ or even $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ data points per step. This scheme is based on a combination of factorized acceptance probabilities, procedures for fast simulation of Bernoulli processes, and control variate ideas. Contrary to many MCMC subsampling schemes such as fixed step-size Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics, our approach is exact insofar as the invariant distribution is the true posterior and not an approximation to it. We characterise the performance of our algorithm theoretically, and give realistic and verifiable conditions under which it is geometrically ergodic. This theory is borne out by empirical results that demonstrate overall performance benefits over standard Metropolis-Hastings and various subsampling algorithms.

paragraphs: Standard Metropolis-Hastings sampling commonly requires work proportional to the dataset size at every step, making large-scale Bayesian inference expensive. Scalable Metropolis-Hastings addresses that cost while keeping the true posterior as its invariant distribution. Here, exactness refers to the distribution preserved by the sampling process.

The method combines factorized acceptance probabilities, fast simulation of Bernoulli processes, and control-variate ideas. The authors report that it needs to process only a constant number of data points per step on average, or even a quantity scaling as the inverse square root of dataset size. These are average data-processing claims, allowing some steps to require no data-point processing.

The paper analyzes performance theoretically and gives realistic, verifiable conditions for geometric ergodicity, a property governing convergence toward the invariant distribution. Experiments support overall performance benefits relative to standard Metropolis-Hastings and several subsampling approaches. The contribution shows how substantial reductions in per-step data access can coexist with preserving the exact posterior, with convergence properties established under stated conditions.
summary.tldr: Scalable Metropolis-Hastings sharply reduces average per-step data processing while preserving the true posterior as its invariant distribution.

title: Scalable Metropolis-Hastings for Exact Bayesian Inference with Large Datasets

abstract: Many machine learning problems come in the form of networks with relational data between entities, and one of the key unsupervised learning tasks is to detect communities in such a network. We adopt the mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel as the underlying probabilistic model, and give conditions under which the memberships of a subset of nodes can be uniquely identified. Our method starts by constructing a second-order graph moment, which can be shown to converge to a specific product of the true parameters as the size of the network increases. To correctly recover the true membership parameters, we formulate an optimization problem using insights from convex geometry. We show that if the true memberships satisfy a so-called sufficiently scattered condition, then solving the proposed problem correctly identifies the ground truth. We also propose an efficient algorithm for detecting communities, which is significantly faster than prior work and with better convergence properties. Experiments on synthetic and real data justify the validity of the proposed learning framework for network data.

This paper uses a mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel to represent such networks and studies when memberships of a subset of nodes can be uniquely recovered. Its focus includes settings without pure nodes that belong exclusively to one community.

The method first constructs a second-order graph moment, a summary of network relationships. As network size increases, this summary converges to a particular product of the underlying model parameters. The authors also introduce an efficient community-detection algorithm, reporting faster operation and better convergence properties than prior work. Experiments on synthetic and real networks support the learning framework and complement its conditional identification result.
summary.tldr: A graph-moment and geometric optimization approach identifies overlapping community memberships under a sufficiently scattered condition.

title: Detecting Overlapping and Correlated Communities without Pure Nodes: Identifiability and Algorithm

abstract: The expressivity of neural networks as a function of their depth, width and type of activation units has been an important question in deep learning theory. Recently, depth separation results for ReLU networks were obtained via a new connection with dynamical systems, using a generalized notion of fixed points of a continuous map $f$, called periodic points. In this work, we strengthen the connection with dynamical systems and we improve the existing width lower bounds along several aspects. Our first main result is period-specific width lower bounds that hold under the stronger notion of $L^1$-approximation error, instead of the weaker classification error. Our second contribution is that we provide sharper width lower bounds, still yielding meaningful exponential depth-width separations, in regimes where previous results wouldn’t apply. A byproduct of our results is that there exists a universal constant characterizing the depth-width trade-offs, as long as $f$ has odd periods. Technically, our results follow by unveiling a tighter connection between the following three quantities of a given function: its period, its Lipschitz constant and the growth rate of the number of oscillations arising under compositions of the function $f$ with itself.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a neural network’s depth and width affect the functions it can represent. Its focus is depth separation: situations where reducing the number of layers requires a large increase in width. The authors investigate these trade-offs through dynamical systems, connecting neural network approximation to what happens when a continuous function is repeatedly applied to its own output.

The key mathematical objects are periodic points, which return to their starting value after repeated applications of the function. The authors derive width requirements that depend on the period and hold for L1 approximation error, strengthening earlier results based on classification error. They also sharpen width lower bounds enough to establish exponential depth-width separations in regimes where earlier results did not apply.

The analysis connects a function’s periods, its Lipschitz constant, and the growth of oscillations under repeated composition. A further result identifies a universal constant governing the trade-offs when the function has odd periods. These are theoretical statements about representational requirements: they clarify when extra depth can substantially reduce the width needed for approximation.
summary.tldr: Dynamical-systems analysis strengthens theoretical bounds on how much wider certain neural networks must become when their depth is reduced.

title: Better depth-width trade-offs for neural networks through the lens of dynamical systems

abstract: We study the problem of learning from multiple untrusted data sources, a scenario of increasing practical relevance given the recent emergence of crowdsourcing and collaborative learning paradigms. Specifically, we analyze the situation in which a learning system obtains datasets from multiple sources, some of which might be biased or even adversarially perturbed. It is known that in the single-source case, an adversary with the power to corrupt a fixed fraction of the training data can prevent PAC-learnability, that is, even in the limit of infinitely much training data, no learning system can approach the optimal test error. In this work we show that, surprisingly, the same is not true in the multi-source setting, where the adversary can arbitrarily corrupt a fixed fraction of the data sources. Our main results are a generalization bound that provides finite-sample guarantees for this learning setting, as well as corresponding lower bounds. Besides establishing PAC-learnability our results also show that in a cooperative learning setting sharing data with other parties has provable benefits, even if some participants are malicious.

paragraphs: Learning from several contributors raises a basic question: can their data still be useful when some contributors are malicious? This paper studies datasets supplied by multiple untrusted sources, allowing an adversary to corrupt a fixed fraction of those sources arbitrarily. The source structure is central to the learning setting.

The authors contrast this with a known single-source obstruction. There, corruption of a fixed fraction of training examples can prevent learning from approaching optimal test error even with unlimited data. They show that the corresponding impossibility does not hold in their multi-source setting, where corruption is specified at the level of sources.

The main results provide a generalization bound with finite-sample guarantees and corresponding lower bounds. Together, these establish PAC-learnability for the studied setting and characterize its data requirements. They also show that cooperative data sharing can have provable benefits despite malicious participants. The result depends on the analyzed multi-source corruption model, making the distinction between corrupted sources and corrupted individual examples consequential.
summary.tldr: Finite-sample guarantees show that learning from multiple sources can remain viable and beneficial despite adversarial corruption of some sources.

title: On the Sample Complexity of Adversarial Multi-Source PAC Learning

abstract: This paper studies the problem of post-hoc calibration of machine learning classifiers. We introduce the following desiderata for uncertainty calibration: (a) accuracy-preserving, (b) data-efficient, and (c) high expressive power. We show that none of the existing methods satisfy all three requirements, and demonstrate how Mix-n-Match calibration strategies (i.e., ensemble and composition) can help achieve remarkably better data-efficiency and expressive power while provably maintaining the classification accuracy of the original classifier. Mix-n-Match strategies are generic in the sense that they can be used to improve the performance of any off-the-shelf calibrator. We also reveal potential issues in standard evaluation practices. Popular approaches (e.g., histogram-based expected calibration error (ECE)) may provide misleading results especially in small-data regime. Therefore, we propose an alternative data-efficient kernel density-based estimator for a reliable evaluation of the calibration performance and prove its asymptotically unbiasedness and consistency. Our approaches outperform state-of-the-art solutions on both the calibration as well as the evaluation tasks in most of the experimental settings. Our codes are available at https://github.com/zhang64- llnl/Mix-n-Match-Calibration.

This paper argues that a useful calibrator should preserve classification accuracy, work efficiently with limited data, and express a wide range of corrections. It finds that existing methods do not meet all three requirements together and proposes combining calibrators through ensembles and composition.

These Mix-n-Match strategies can improve off-the-shelf calibrators while provably maintaining the original classifier’s accuracy. Their purpose is to improve the uncertainty estimates without sacrificing the classifier’s predictive success. The authors report substantial gains in data efficiency and expressive power from these combinations.

The paper also examines how calibration is measured. Histogram-based expected calibration error can be misleading, especially with little evaluation data. The authors propose a kernel density estimator and prove asymptotic unbiasedness and consistency, properties describing its behavior as data increase. Across most experimental settings, their approaches outperform leading alternatives in both calibration and its evaluation, addressing two connected sources of uncertainty-estimation error.
summary.tldr: Mix-n-Match combines calibrators to improve uncertainty estimates while preserving accuracy, and introduces a better-supported calibration evaluation estimator.

title: Mix-n-Match : Ensemble and Compositional Methods for Uncertainty Calibration in Deep Learning

abstract: We present the Open Predicate Query Language (OPQL); a method for constructing a virtual KB (VKB) trained entirely from text. Large Knowledge Bases (KBs) are indispensable for a wide-range of industry applications such as question answering and recommendation. Typically, KBs encode world knowledge in a structured, readily accessible form derived from laborious human annotation efforts. Unfortunately, while they are extremely high precision, KBs are inevitably highly incomplete and automated methods for enriching them are far too inaccurate. Instead, OPQL constructs a VKB by encoding and indexing a set of relation mentions in a way that naturally enables reasoning and can be trained without any structured supervision. We demonstrate that OPQL outperforms prior VKB methods on two different KB reasoning tasks and, additionally, can be used as an external memory integrated into a language model (OPQL-LM) leading to improvements on two open-domain question answering tasks.

paragraphs: Structured knowledge bases make facts accessible for applications such as question answering and recommendation. Building them requires substantial human annotation, and even highly precise collections remain incomplete. This paper presents Open Predicate Query Language, or OPQL, as a way to construct a virtual knowledge base directly from text without structured supervision.

OPQL encodes and indexes mentions of relations found in text. The representations are designed to support reasoning, allowing the resulting collection to function as a virtual knowledge resource. This approach places the learning and indexing of textual relations at the center of knowledge-base construction, avoiding a requirement for structured training annotations.

On two knowledge-base reasoning tasks, OPQL outperforms previous virtual knowledge-base methods. The authors also integrate it into a language model as an external memory, producing OPQL-LM, and report improvements on two open-domain question-answering tasks. These results demonstrate two uses for the same resource: reasoning over encoded relations directly and supplying knowledge to a language model. The empirical findings support the value of text-trained relational memory across those evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: OPQL builds a text-trained virtual knowledge base whose indexed relation representations improve reasoning and language-model question answering.

title: Reasoning Over Virtual Knowledge Bases With Open Predicate Relations

abstract: Interior point methods (IPMs) are a common approach for solving linear programs (LPs) with strong theoretical guarantees and solid empirical performance. The time complexity of these methods is dominated by the cost of solving a linear system of equations at each iteration. In common applications of linear programming, particularly in machine learning and scientific computing, the size of this linear system can become prohibitively large, requiring the use of iterative solvers, which provide an approximate solution to the linear system. However, approximately solving the linear system at each iteration of an IPM invalidates the theoretical guarantees of common IPM analyses. To remedy this, we theoretically and empirically analyze (slightly modified) predictor-corrector IPMs when using approximate linear solvers: our approach guarantees that, when certain conditions are satisfied, the number of IPM iterations does not increase and that the final solution remains feasible. We also provide practical instantiations of approximate linear solvers that satisfy these conditions for special classes of constraint matrices using randomized linear algebra.
