paragraphs: Interior-point methods solve linear programs through iterations that each require solving a linear system. For large applications, that system can dominate the computational cost and make iterative approximate solvers necessary. However, substituting approximate solutions invalidates the guarantees supplied by common analyses of interior-point methods.

This paper studies slightly modified predictor-corrector methods that explicitly accommodate approximate linear solves. Under stated conditions, the authors guarantee that the number of interior-point iterations does not increase and that the final solution remains feasible. Feasibility matters because the returned answer must still satisfy the constraints of the original linear program.

The authors analyze the approach theoretically and empirically, and provide practical approximate solvers based on randomized linear algebra. Those constructions satisfy the required conditions for special classes of constraint matrices. The contribution is a bridge between computationally necessary approximation and convergence theory: approximate inner solves can preserve the stated outer-method guarantees when their conditions are met.
summary.tldr: Modified predictor-corrector methods preserve iteration counts and feasibility with approximate linear solves under specified conditions.

title: On the Convergence of Inexact Predictor-Corrector Methods for Linear Programming

abstract: Generating programs to describe visual observations has gained much research attention recently. However, most of the existing approaches are based on non-parametric primitive functions, making them unable to handle complex visual scenes involving many attributes and details. In this paper, we propose the concept of parametric visual program induction. Learning to generate parametric programs for visual scenes is challenging due to the huge number of function variants and the complex function correlations. To solve these challenges, we propose the method of function modularization, capable of dealing with numerous function variants and complex correlations. Specifically, we model each parametric function as a multi-head self-contained neural module to cover different function variants. Moreover, to eliminate the complex correlations between functions, we propose the hierarchical heterogeneous Monto-Carlo tree search (H2MCTS) algorithm which can provide high-quality uncorrelated supervision during training, and serve as an efficient searching technique during testing. We demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method on three visual program induction datasets involving parametric primitive functions. Experimental results show that our proposed model is able to significantly outperform the state-of-the-art baseline methods in terms of generating accurate programs.

Parametric functions offer more flexibility, but introduce many possible function variants and complicated dependencies among functions, making program generation harder.

The proposed solution modularizes functions. Each parametric function receives a self-contained neural module with multiple heads to cover its variants. The method also introduces a hierarchical heterogeneous Monte Carlo tree search algorithm, H2MCTS. During training, this search supplies high-quality uncorrelated supervision to address complex function correlations; during testing, it serves as an efficient way to search for programs.

The authors evaluate the method on three visual program induction datasets involving parametric primitives. It substantially outperforms the compared leading baselines in program accuracy. The findings support handling richer visual descriptions through a combination of modular neural representations and structured search, with the same search machinery contributing both training guidance and test-time program discovery.
summary.tldr: Modular neural functions and hierarchical tree search improve generation of parametric programs that describe detailed visual scenes.

title: Parametric Visual Program Induction with Function Modularization

abstract: Implicit Processes (IPs) represent a flexible framework that can be used to describe a wide variety of models, from Bayesian neural networks, neural samplers and data generators to many others. IPs also allow for approximate inference in function-space. This change of formulation solves intrinsic degenerate problems of parameter-space approximate inference concerning the high number of parameters and their strong dependencies in large models. For this, previous works in the literature have attempted to employ IPs both to set up the prior and to approximate the resulting posterior. However, this has proven to be a challenging task. Existing methods that can tune the prior IP result in a Gaussian predictive distribution, which fails to capture important data patterns. By contrast, methods producing flexible predictive distributions by using another IP to approximate the posterior process cannot tune the prior IP to the observed data. We propose here the first method that can accomplish both goals. For this, we rely on an inducing-point representation of the prior IP, as often done in the context of sparse Gaussian processes. The result is a scalable method for approximate inference with IPs that can tune the prior IP parameters to the data, and that provides accurate non-Gaussian predictive distributions.

Working with functions addresses difficulties caused by the large number of parameters and strong parameter dependencies in large models. However, obtaining a suitably flexible inference method remains challenging.

The paper identifies a split in existing approaches. Methods that can adjust the prior implicit process to the data produce Gaussian predictive distributions, which can miss important patterns. Methods that use an implicit process for a more flexible posterior distribution cannot tune the prior to the observations. Each approach therefore achieves only one of these two objectives.

The proposed method combines both capabilities through an inducing-point representation of the prior, drawing on an approach used in sparse Gaussian processes. The resulting approximate inference procedure is scalable, learns prior parameters from the data, and produces accurate non-Gaussian predictive distributions. Its contribution is to make prior adaptation and predictive flexibility available within the same implicit-process framework.
summary.tldr: Sparse implicit processes combine data-adapted priors with flexible non-Gaussian predictions in a scalable function-space inference method.

title: Function-space Inference with Sparse Implicit Processes

abstract: Existing methods of combinatorial pure exploration mainly focus on the UCB approach. To make the algorithm efficient, they usually use the sum of upper confidence bounds within arm set $S$ to represent the upper confidence bound of $S$, which can be much larger than the tight upper confidence bound of $S$ and leads to a much higher complexity than necessary, since the empirical means of different arms in $S$ are independent. To deal with this challenge, we explore the idea of Thompson Sampling (TS) that uses independent random samples instead of the upper confidence bounds, and design the first TS-based algorithm TS-Explore for (combinatorial) pure exploration. In TS-Explore, the sum of independent random samples within arm set $S$ will not exceed the tight upper confidence bound of $S$ with high probability. Hence it solves the above challenge, and achieves a lower complexity upper bound than existing efficient UCB-based algorithms in general combinatorial pure exploration. As for pure exploration of classic multi-armed bandit, we show that TS-Explore achieves an asymptotically optimal complexity upper bound.

paragraphs: Combinatorial pure exploration concerns learning enough about individual arms to identify a good arm set. Efficient upper-confidence-bound methods often estimate uncertainty for a set by adding the bounds for its members. The paper identifies a problem with this shortcut: the resulting set bound can be much looser than necessary because different arms' empirical means are independent.

TS-Explore uses Thompson-sampling-style independent random samples in place of those individual upper bounds. The sum of samples for an arm set stays below the tight set-level upper confidence bound with high probability. This probabilistic control addresses the excess uncertainty introduced by summing separate optimistic bounds, allowing the analysis to obtain a better exploration-complexity guarantee.

In the classic multi-armed-bandit pure-exploration setting, its complexity upper bound is asymptotically optimal. These are theoretical comparisons about the amount of exploration required, with asymptotic optimality stated for the classic setting. The contribution shows how independent randomization can exploit structure that a convenient confidence-bound construction loses.
summary.tldr: TS-Explore uses independent random samples to improve exploration-complexity bounds for combinatorial bandits.

title: Thompson Sampling for (Combinatorial) Pure Exploration

abstract: Algorithms for online learning typically require one or more boundedness assumptions: that the domain is bounded, that the losses are Lipschitz, or both. In this paper, we develop a new setting for online learning with unbounded domains and non-Lipschitz losses. For this setting we provide an algorithm which guarantees $R_{T}(u)\le \tilde O(G\|u\|\sqrt{T}+L\|u\|^{2}\sqrt{T})$ regret on any problem where the subgradients satisfy $\|g_{t}\|\le G+L\|w_{t}\|$, and show that this bound is unimprovable without further assumptions. We leverage this algorithm to develop new saddle-point optimization algorithms that converge in duality gap in unbounded domains, even in the absence of meaningful curvature. Finally, we provide the first algorithm achieving non-trivial dynamic regret in an unbounded domain for non-Lipschitz losses, as well as a matching lower bound. The regret of our dynamic regret algorithm automatically improves to a novel $L^{*}$ bound when the losses are smooth.

paragraphs: Online-learning guarantees often assume decisions lie in a bounded region or that losses have uniformly bounded slopes. This paper removes both restrictions while imposing a different control on the problem: subgradient size may grow at most linearly with the size of the learner’s current decision. That permits unbounded domains and non-Lipschitz losses within a specified growth condition.

The proposed algorithm bounds regret against a fixed comparator u by terms proportional to G‖u‖√T and L‖u‖²√T, up to logarithmic factors. G and L describe the allowed subgradient growth. The authors show this bound cannot be improved without further assumptions. They then use the algorithm to construct saddle-point methods that converge in duality gap on unbounded domains, even without meaningful curvature.

The paper also provides a nontrivial dynamic-regret guarantee, which evaluates performance against changing comparators, for unbounded domains with non-Lipschitz losses. A matching lower bound accompanies that result. When losses are smooth, the algorithm automatically obtains an improved L* bound, demonstrating additional adaptation within this broader online-learning setting.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal online-learning guarantees on unbounded domains under linear subgradient growth, with extensions to saddle points and dynamic regret.

title: Unconstrained Online Learning with Unbounded Losses

abstract: Numerous deep learning algorithms have been inspired by and understood via the notion of information bottleneck, where unnecessary information is (often implicitly) minimized while task-relevant information is maximized. However, a rigorous argument for justifying why it is desirable to control information bottlenecks has been elusive. In this paper, we provide the first rigorous learning theory for justifying the benefit of information bottleneck in deep learning by mathematically relating information bottleneck to generalization errors. Our theory proves that controlling information bottleneck is one way to control generalization errors in deep learning, although it is not the only or necessary way. We investigate the merit of our new mathematical findings with experiments across a range of architectures and learning settings. In many cases, generalization errors are shown to correlate with the degree of information bottleneck: i.e., the amount of the unnecessary information at hidden layers. This paper provides a theoretical foundation for current and future methods through the lens of information bottleneck. Our new generalization bounds scale with the degree of information bottleneck, unlike the previous bounds that scale with the number of parameters, VC dimension, Rademacher complexity, stability or robustness. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/xu-ji/information-bottleneck

paragraphs: The information bottleneck perspective encourages a network to retain information useful for its task while reducing unnecessary information. Many deep learning methods draw motivation from this idea. The paper addresses the theoretical question behind that motivation: why controlling information in hidden representations can help a model generalize beyond its training data.

The authors derive learning-theoretic bounds that relate information bottlenecks to generalization error. These bounds scale with the degree of the bottleneck, offering a different basis for analysis from bounds expressed through parameter counts or other established complexity measures. Crucially, the theory establishes bottleneck control as one sufficient route to controlling generalization error, without making it necessary.

Experiments across architectures and learning settings examine the relevance of the mathematical results. In many cases, generalization error correlates with the amount of unnecessary information retained in hidden layers. These observations support the theory's practical relevance without asserting a universal empirical relationship. The work gives information-bottleneck methods a formal justification while preserving room for other explanations and mechanisms of generalization.
summary.tldr: New generalization bounds establish information-bottleneck control as a sufficient, but unnecessary, way to control generalization error.

title: How Does Information Bottleneck Help Deep Learning?

abstract: Probabilistic Circuits (PCs) are a general and unified computational framework for tractable probabilistic models that support efficient computation of various inference tasks (e.g., computing marginal probabilities). Towards enabling such reasoning capabilities in complex real-world tasks, Liu et al. (2022) propose to distill knowledge (through latent variable assignments) from less tractable but more expressive deep generative models. However, it is still unclear what factors make this distillation work well. In this paper, we theoretically and empirically discover that the performance of a PC can exceed that of its teacher model. Therefore, instead of performing distillation from the most expressive deep generative model, we study what properties the teacher model and the PC should have in order to achieve good distillation performance. This leads to a generic algorithmic improvement as well as other data-type-specific ones over the existing latent variable distillation pipeline. Empirically, we outperform SoTA TPMs by a large margin on challenging image modeling benchmarks. In particular, on ImageNet32, PCs achieve 4.06 bits-per-dimension, which is only 0.34 behind variational diffusion models (Kingma et al., 2021).

The findings show that effective distillation depends on the transfer setup and model properties, while preserving the circuit framework’s efficient inference capabilities.
summary.tldr: The paper explains and improves distillation into probabilistic circuits, showing that a circuit can outperform its generative teacher.

title: Understanding the Distillation Process from Deep Generative Models to Tractable Probabilistic Circuits

abstract: We study multi-agent reinforcement learning in the setting of episodic Markov decision processes, where many agents cooperate via communication through a central server. We propose a provably efficient algorithm based on value iteration that can simultaneously allow asynchronous communication and guarantee the benefit of cooperation with low communication complexity. Under linear function approximation, we prove that our algorithm enjoys a $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{3/2}H^2\sqrt{K})$ regret upper bound with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(dHM^2)$ communication complexity, where $d$ is the feature dimension, $H$ is the horizon length, $M$ is the total number of agents, and $K$ is the total number of episodes. We also provide a lower bound showing that an $\Omega(dM)$ communication complexity is necessary to improve the performance through collaboration.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning in episodes where multiple agents cooperate by communicating through a central server. The challenge is to obtain a genuine learning benefit from cooperation while allowing agents to communicate asynchronously and keeping the overall communication requirement low.

The proposed algorithm builds on value iteration. Under linear function approximation, its regret grows at most on the order of d^(3/2) H² √K, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here d measures feature dimension, H is the episode horizon, and K counts total episodes. Its communication bound is on the order of d H M², again suppressing logarithmic factors, where M is the number of agents.

These guarantees establish that asynchronous communication can coexist with provably efficient cooperative learning in the studied setting. The authors also prove that communication on the order of at least dM is necessary to improve performance through collaboration. Together, the results describe an achievable communication cost and a fundamental minimum, without claiming that these two bounds coincide.
summary.tldr: A value-iteration algorithm enables provably efficient cooperative learning with asynchronous server communication under linear function approximation.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Asynchronous Communication and Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models have shown an impressive generation quality although their long sampling chain leads to high computational costs. In this paper, we observe that a long sampling chain also leads to an error accumulation phenomenon, which is similar to the exposure bias problem in autoregressive text generation. Specifically, we note that there is a discrepancy between training and testing, since the former is conditioned on the ground truth samples, while the latter is conditioned on the previously generated results. To alleviate this problem, we propose a very simple but effective training regularization, consisting in perturbing the ground truth samples to simulate the inference time prediction errors. We empirically show that, without affecting the recall and precision, the proposed input perturbation leads to a significant improvement in the sample quality while reducing both the training and the inference times. For instance, on CelebA 64x64, we achieve a new state-of-the-art FID score of 1.27, while saving 37.5% of the training time. The code is available at https://github.com/forever208/DDPM-IP

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples through a long sequence of denoising steps. Beyond making generation costly, this sequence can allow prediction errors to accumulate. The paper connects that behavior to exposure bias: training conditions on ground-truth samples, while generation must proceed using the model's own earlier results, which may already contain errors.

The proposed remedy is a simple training regularizer that perturbs the ground-truth samples used as inputs. These perturbations simulate the kinds of prediction errors encountered during generation. Training therefore exposes the model to imperfect inputs resembling those it will need to handle when its own outputs feed subsequent steps.

In the reported experiments, input perturbation improves sample quality while reducing both training and inference time, without affecting precision or recall. On CelebA at 64×64 resolution, the authors report an FID score of 1.27 and a 37.5% saving in training time. These results suggest that addressing the mismatch between training inputs and generated intermediate results can improve both quality and efficiency in the evaluated diffusion models.
summary.tldr: Perturbing diffusion training inputs simulates generation errors, improving reported sample quality while reducing training and inference time.

title: Input Perturbation Reduces Exposure Bias in Diffusion Models

abstract: Contrastive Learning has recently achieved state-of-the-art performance in a wide range of unimodal and multimodal tasks. Many contrastive learning approaches use mined hard negatives to make batches more informative during training but these approaches are inefficient as they increase epoch length proportional to the number of mined negatives and require frequent updates of nearest neighbor indices or mining from recent batches. In this work, we provide an alternative to hard negative mining, Global Contrastive Batch Sampling (GCBS), an efficient approximation to the batch assignment problem that upper bounds the gap between the global and training losses, $\mathcal{L}^{Global} - \mathcal{L}^{Train}$, in contrastive learning settings. Through experimentation we find GCBS improves state-of-the-art performance in sentence embedding and code-search tasks. Additionally, GCBS is easy to implement as it requires only a few additional lines of code, does not maintain external data structures such as nearest neighbor indices, is more computationally efficient than the most minimal hard negative mining approaches, and makes no changes to the model being trained. Code is available at https://github.com/vinayak1/GCBS.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning depends on informative comparisons among examples. One common strategy mines difficult negative examples, but this can lengthen training epochs and require maintaining nearest-neighbor indexes or repeatedly searching recent batches. The paper approaches the problem through batch composition, asking how existing samples should be grouped to make training comparisons more useful.

The proposed Global Contrastive Batch Sampling method, or GCBS, efficiently approximates a batch-assignment problem tied to an upper bound on the gap between global and training losses. Its focus on sample arrangement offers an alternative to adding mined negatives. It leaves the model itself unchanged and does not maintain external nearest-neighbor data structures.

Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art performance on sentence-embedding and code-search tasks. The authors also report that GCBS is more computationally efficient than even minimal hard-negative mining approaches and needs only a few additional lines of code. The results make batch selection a consequential part of contrastive learning, with benefits demonstrated through both task performance and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: GCBS improves contrastive learning by optimizing batch assignments, reducing mining overhead while improving sentence-embedding and code-search results.

title: Global Selection of Contrastive Batches via Optimization on Sample Permutations

abstract: Co-training is a classical semi-supervised learning method which only requires a small number of labeled examples for learning, under reasonable assumptions. Despite extensive literature on the topic, very few hypothesis classes are known to be provably efficiently learnable via co-training, even under very strong distributional assumptions. In this work, we study the co-training problem in the stream-based active learning model. We show that a range of natural concept classes are efficiently learnable via co-training, in terms of both label efficiency and computational efficiency. We provide an efficient reduction of co-training under the standard assumption of weak dependence, in the stream-based active model, to online classification. As a corollary, we obtain efficient co-training algorithms with error independent label complexity for every concept class class efficiently learnable in the mistake bound online model. Our framework also gives co-training algorithms with label complexity $\tilde{O}(d\log (1/\epsilon))$ for any concept class with VC dimension $d$, though in general this reduction is not computationally efficient. Finally, using additional ideas from online learning, we design the first efficient co-training algorithms with label complexity $\tilde{O}(d^2\log (1/\epsilon))$ for several concept classes, including unions of intervals and homogeneous halfspaces.

paragraphs: Co-training aims to learn from few labeled examples under suitable assumptions, but proving both label efficiency and computational efficiency has been difficult. This paper studies co-training in a stream-based active-learning setting, where examples arrive in a stream and the learner can selectively request labels. Its results use the standard weak-dependence assumption.

The main construction reduces this co-training problem to online classification. Consequently, any concept class that is efficiently learnable in the mistake-bound online model receives an efficient co-training algorithm whose label complexity is independent of the target error. This transfers useful guarantees from online learning into the co-training setting.

Additional online-learning ideas yield efficient algorithms using approximately d² log(1/ε) labels for several classes, including unions of intervals and homogeneous halfspaces. The paper thus separates low label requirements from efficient computation and establishes settings where both can be achieved.
summary.tldr: A reduction to online classification yields provably label-efficient and computationally efficient co-training algorithms for several concept classes under weak dependence.

title: Fast Co-Training under Weak Dependence via Stream-Based Active Learning

abstract: Machine learning (ML) methods are having a huge impact across all of the sciences. However, ML has a strong ontology — in which only the data exist — and a strong epistemology — in which a model is considered good if it performs well on held-out training data. These philosophies are in strong conflict with both standard practices and key philosophies in the natural sciences. Here we identify some locations for ML in the natural sciences at which the ontology and epistemology are valuable. For example, when an expressive machine learning model is used in a causal inference to represent the effects of confounders, such as foregrounds, backgrounds, or instrument calibration parameters, the model capacity and loose philosophy of ML can make the results more trustworthy. We also show that there are contexts in which the introduction of ML introduces strong, unwanted statistical biases. For one, when ML models are used to emulate physical (or first-principles) simulations, they amplify confirmation biases. For another, when expressive regressions are used to label datasets, those labels cannot be used in downstream joint or ensemble analyses without taking on uncontrolled biases. The question in the title is being asked of all of the natural sciences; that is, we are calling on the scientific communities to take a step back and consider the role and value of ML in their fields; the (partial) answers we give here come from the particular perspective of physics.

paragraphs: This position paper asks how machine learning fits the goals and practices of natural science. The authors characterize ML as emphasizing data and judging models through performance on held-out data. They argue that these commitments can conflict with scientific approaches concerned with physical explanations and other standards of knowledge.

The paper identifies settings where ML's flexibility is valuable. In causal inference, expressive models can represent confounding effects such as foregrounds, backgrounds, and instrument calibration parameters. The authors argue that using model capacity for these effects can make scientific results more trustworthy. The usefulness of ML therefore depends partly on the role it plays within the inference.

The authors also identify harmful uses: emulating physical simulations can amplify confirmation bias, and labels produced by expressive regressions can introduce uncontrolled bias in downstream joint or ensemble analyses. Their answers come from a physics perspective and are explicitly partial. The broader invitation is for scientific communities to examine how ML changes the meaning and reliability of their conclusions.
summary.tldr: From a physics perspective, this position paper explains how ML can strengthen scientific inference in some roles and introduce serious biases in others.

title: Position: Is machine learning good or bad for the natural sciences?

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a powerful technique for enhancing the performance of neural networks while decoupling computational complexity from the number of parameters. However, despite this, scaling the number of experts requires adding more GPUs. In addition, the load imbalance in token load across experts causes unnecessary computation or straggler problems. We present ES-MoE, a novel method for efficient scaling MoE training. It offloads expert parameters to host memory and leverages pipelined expert processing to overlap GPU-CPU communication with GPU computation. It dynamically balances token loads across GPUs, improving computational efficiency. ES-MoE accelerates MoE training on a limited number of GPUs without degradation in model performance. We validate our approach on GPT-based MoE models, demonstrating 67$\times$ better scalability and up to 17.5$\times$ better throughput over existing frameworks.
originalAbstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a powerful technique for enhancing the performance of neural networks while decoupling computational complexity from the number of parameters. However, despite this, scaling the number of experts requires adding more GPUs. In addition, the load imbalance in token load across experts causes unnecessary computation or straggler problems. We present ES-MoE, a novel method for efficient scaling MoE training. It offloads expert parameters to host memory and leverages pipelined expert processing to overlap GPU-CPU communication with GPU computation. It dynamically balances token loads across GPUs, improving computational efficiency. ES-MoE accelerates MoE training on a limited number of GPUs without degradation in model performance. We validate our approach on GPT-based MoE models, demonstrating 67$\times$ better scalability and up to 17.5$\times$ better throughput over existing frameworks.

Uneven token assignments introduce another problem: some experts receive much more work than others, causing wasted computation or slow workers that hold up training.

ES-MoE addresses memory capacity and workload imbalance together. It stores expert parameters in host memory and processes experts through a pipeline that overlaps transfers between CPU and GPU with GPU computation. It also dynamically balances token loads across GPUs. These mechanisms target both the cost of moving expert parameters and the unequal distribution of work.

The authors validate the method on GPT-based MoE models, reporting faster training on a limited number of GPUs without degraded model performance. Compared with existing frameworks, they demonstrate 67 times better scalability and up to 17.5 times better throughput. These results support combining offloading, pipelining, and load balancing to expand feasible MoE training beyond GPU memory constraints in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: ES-MoE combines expert offloading, pipelined processing, and load balancing to scale MoE training beyond GPU memory limits.

title: Scaling Beyond the GPU Memory Limit for Large Mixture-of-Experts Model Training

abstract: In class-imbalanced learning, the scarcity of information about minority classes presents challenges in obtaining generalizable features for these classes. Leveraging large-scale pre-trained models with powerful generalization capabilities as teacher models can help fill this information gap. Traditional knowledge distillation transfers the label distribution $p(\boldsymbol{y}|\boldsymbol{x})$ predicted by the teacher model to the student model. However, this method falls short on imbalanced data as it fails to capture the class-conditional probability distribution $p(\boldsymbol{x}|\boldsymbol{y})$ from the teacher model, which is crucial for enhancing generalization. To overcome this, we propose Class-Conditional Knowledge Distillation (CCKD), a novel approach that enables learning of the teacher model’s class-conditional probability distribution during the distillation process. Additionally, we introduce Augmented CCKD (ACCKD), which involves distillation on a constructed class-balanced dataset (formed through data mixing) and feature imitation on the entire dataset to further facilitate the learning of features. Experimental results on various imbalanced datasets demonstrate an average accuracy improvement of 7.4% using our method.

paragraphs: When some classes have few training examples, a model may struggle to learn features that generalize for them. This paper uses a large pretrained teacher to help fill that information gap. It argues that conventional knowledge distillation misses an important part of the teacher's knowledge when transferring predictions to a student.

Standard distillation transfers the distribution of labels for a given input. Class-Conditional Knowledge Distillation, or CCKD, instead enables the student to learn the teacher's distribution of inputs conditioned on a class during distillation. This shifts attention toward the information associated with each class, which the paper identifies as crucial for generalization on imbalanced data.

These components combine balanced distillation with broader feature learning. Experiments on multiple imbalanced datasets report an average accuracy improvement of 7.4%. The findings support transferring class-conditional knowledge from pretrained teachers as a way to improve learning when minority-class information is scarce.
summary.tldr: CCKD transfers class-conditional teacher knowledge to improve imbalanced learning, with an augmented version adding balanced data mixing and feature imitation.

title: Enhancing Class-Imbalanced Learning with Pre-Trained Guidance through Class-Conditional Knowledge Distillation

abstract: The size of spatial receptive fields, from the early 3$\times$3 convolutions in VGGNet to the recent 7$\times$7 convolutions in ConvNeXt, has always played a critical role in architecture design. In this paper, we propose a Mixture of Receptive Fields (MoRF) instead of using a single receptive field. MoRF contains the combinations of multiple receptive fields with different sizes, e.g., convolutions with different kernel sizes, which can be regarded as experts. Such an approach serves two functions: one is to select the appropriate receptive field according to the input, and the other is to expand the network capacity. Furthermore, we also introduce two types of routing mechanisms, hard routing and soft routing to automatically select the appropriate receptive field experts. In the inference stage, the selected receptive field experts are merged via re-parameterization to maintain a similar inference speed compared to the single receptive field. To demonstrate the effectiveness of MoRF, we integrate the MoRF concept into multiple architectures, e.g., ResNet and ConvNeXt. Extensive experiments show that our approach outperforms the baselines in image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks without significantly increasing the inference time.

paragraphs: A convolutional network’s receptive field determines the spatial region involved in processing visual information. Its size is an important architectural choice. This paper introduces Mixture of Receptive Fields, or MoRF, which combines several receptive-field sizes and treats them as experts available to the network.

The contribution combines a broader set of spatial processing options with a mechanism for using those options efficiently during inference.
summary.tldr: MoRF routes inputs among receptive-field experts and merges selected experts for improved vision performance with little inference-time increase.

title: Receptive Fields As Experts in Convolutional Neural Architectures

abstract: Meta reinforcement learning sets a distribution over a set of tasks on which the agent can train at will, then is asked to learn an optimal policy for any test task efficiently. In this paper, we consider a finite set of tasks modeled through Markov decision processes with various dynamics. We assume to have endured a long training phase, from which the set of tasks is perfectly recovered, and we focus on regret minimization against the optimal policy in the unknown test task. Under a separation condition that states the existence of a state-action pair revealing a task against another, Chen et al. (2022) show that $O(M^2 \log(H))$ regret can be achieved, where $M, H$ are the number of tasks in the set and test episodes, respectively. In our first contribution, we demonstrate that the latter rate is nearly optimal by developing a novel lower bound for test-time regret minimization under separation, showing that a linear dependence with $M$ is unavoidable. Then, we present a family of stronger yet reasonable assumptions beyond separation, which we call strong identifiability, enabling algorithms achieving fast rates $\log (H)$ and sublinear dependence with $M$ simultaneously. Our paper provides a new understanding of the statistical barriers of test-time regret minimization and when fast rates can be achieved.

paragraphs: This paper studies adaptation to an unknown test task drawn from a finite set of Markov decision processes. It assumes a sufficiently long training phase has already recovered that task set perfectly. The remaining challenge is to minimize regret while learning which task is active and acting effectively within it.

Under a separation condition, each task can be distinguished from another through some state-action pair. The authors derive a lower bound showing that dependence at least linear in the number of tasks is unavoidable under this condition. This identifies a statistical barrier even when the possible tasks themselves are already known.

The paper then introduces stronger assumptions called strong identifiability. These enable algorithms with logarithmic dependence on the number of test episodes and sublinear dependence on the number of tasks simultaneously. The contribution explains how the information available for distinguishing tasks controls adaptation speed: fast test-time learning depends on more than merely having recovered the task collection during training.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes test-time regret barriers under task separation and stronger identifiability conditions that permit faster adaptation.

title: Test-Time Regret Minimization in Meta Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose Diffusion Inference-Time T-Optimization (DITTO), a general-purpose framework for controlling pre-trained text-to-music diffusion models at inference-time via optimizing initial noise latents. Our method can be used to optimize through any differentiable feature matching loss to achieve a target (stylized) output and leverages gradient checkpointing for memory efficiency. We demonstrate a surprisingly wide-range of applications for music generation including inpainting, outpainting, and looping as well as intensity, melody, and musical structure control – all without ever fine-tuning the underlying model. When we compare our approach against related training, guidance, and optimization-based methods, we find DITTO achieves state-of-the-art performance on nearly all tasks, including outperforming comparable approaches on controllability, audio quality, and computational efficiency, thus opening the door for high-quality, flexible, training-free control of diffusion models. Sound examples can be found at https://ditto-music.github.io/web/.

paragraphs: DITTO controls a pretrained text-to-music diffusion model by optimizing the initial noise from which generation begins. This moves control into inference time: the underlying model does not need fine-tuning for the demonstrated tasks. The target is expressed through a differentiable feature-matching loss, allowing optimization to steer the generated music toward desired properties.

The framework supports a wide range of musical edits and constraints. Demonstrations include filling missing passages, extending existing audio, creating loops, and controlling intensity, melody, or musical structure. These applications share the same basic mechanism of adjusting the starting latent noise according to a target loss. Gradient checkpointing helps make that optimization more memory efficient.

The authors compare DITTO with methods based on training, guidance, and optimization. They report state-of-the-art performance on nearly all evaluated tasks, including advantages over comparable approaches in controllability, audio quality, and computational efficiency. The findings suggest that optimizing a model’s starting point can provide flexible musical control while preserving the practical benefit of reusing an already trained generator.
summary.tldr: DITTO steers pretrained music diffusion models by optimizing their initial noise, enabling varied editing and control tasks without fine-tuning.

title: DITTO: Diffusion Inference-Time T-Optimization for Music Generation

abstract: This work proposes an algorithm improving the dimensionality dependence for gradient-free optimisation over cross-polytopes, which has many applications such as adversarial attacks, explainable AI and sparse regression. For bandit convex optimisation with two-point feedback over cross-polytopes, the state-of-the-art algorithms have a dimensionality dependence of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{d\log d})$, while the known lower bound is of the form $\Omega(\sqrt{d(\log d)^{-1}})$. We propose a mirror descent algorithm equipped with a symmetric version of the negative $\frac{1}{2}$-Tsallis entropy. Combined with an $\ell_1$-ellipsoidal smoothing-based gradient estimator, the proposed algorithm guarantees a dimensionality dependence on $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{d})$, which improves the state-of-the-art algorithms by a factor of $\sqrt{\log d}$. The idea can be further applied to optimising non-smooth and non-convex functions. We propose an algorithm with a convergence depending on $\mathcal{O}(d)$, which is the best-known dimensionality dependence.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization using function evaluations instead of directly available gradients. Its focus is optimization over cross-polytopes, where existing methods become more costly as dimension increases. The main question is how much of that dimensional dependence can be reduced while retaining theoretical guarantees for the optimization procedure.

These results matter for gradient-free problems in which dimension is a major source of difficulty, including the paper's motivating applications in adversarial attacks, explainable AI, and sparse regression.
summary.tldr: A mirror descent method improves the dimensional dependence of gradient-free convex optimization over cross-polytopes to O(sqrt(d)).

title: Improved Dimensionality Dependence for Zeroth-Order Optimisation over Cross-Polytopes

abstract: Large language models (LLM) have emerged as a powerful tool for AI, with the key ability of in-context learning (ICL), where they can perform well on unseen tasks based on a brief series of task examples without necessitating any adjustments to the model parameters. One recent interesting mysterious observation is that models of different scales may have different ICL behaviors: larger models tend to be more sensitive to noise in the test context. This work studies this observation theoretically aiming to improve the understanding of LLM and ICL. We analyze two stylized settings: (1) linear regression with one-layer single-head linear transformers and (2) parity classification with two-layer multiple attention heads transformers (non-linear data and non-linear model). In both settings, we give closed-form optimal solutions and find that smaller models emphasize important hidden features while larger ones cover more hidden features; thus, smaller models are more robust to noise while larger ones are more easily distracted, leading to different ICL behaviors. This sheds light on where transformers pay attention to and how that affects ICL. Preliminary experimental results on large base and chat models provide positive support for our analysis.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model use examples in its prompt without changing its parameters. This paper investigates why model size can change that behavior, particularly the observation that larger models tend to be more sensitive to noise in the test context. It seeks a theoretical explanation for that difference.

The authors analyze two simplified settings: linear regression with a one-layer, single-head linear Transformer, and parity classification with a two-layer Transformer using multiple attention heads. They derive closed-form optimal solutions in both. The solutions show smaller models emphasizing important hidden features, while larger models represent a broader collection of hidden features.

Within these settings, the broader coverage makes larger models easier to distract with noise, while the smaller models' focus provides greater robustness. This links differences in in-context behavior to which features the models attend to. Preliminary experiments on large base and chat models support the analysis. The theoretical conclusions come from the two stylized settings, with the practical experiments offering initial corroboration.
summary.tldr: In two stylized settings, larger Transformers cover more hidden features and become more noise-sensitive, with preliminary language-model experiments supporting the explanation.

title: Why Larger Language Models Do In-context Learning Differently?

abstract: A popular approach to the MAP inference problem in graphical models is to minimize an upper bound obtained from a dual linear programming or Lagrangian relaxation by (block-)coordinate descent. This is also known as convex/convergent message passing; examples are max-sum diffusion and sequential tree-reweighted message passing (TRW-S). Convergence properties of these methods are currently not fully understood. They have been proved to converge to the set characterized by local consistency of active constraints, with unknown convergence rate; however, it was not clear if the iterates converge at all (to any point). We prove a stronger result (conjectured before but never proved): the iterates converge to a fixed point of the method. Moreover, we show that the algorithm terminates within $\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ iterations. We first prove this for a version of coordinate descent applied to a general piecewise-affine convex objective. Then we show that several convex message passing methods are special cases of this method. Finally, we show that a slightly different version of coordinate descent can cycle.

paragraphs: Finding the most likely assignment in a graphical model is often approached through a relaxed optimization problem. Several message-passing algorithms improve an upper bound by updating one coordinate or block at a time. Although these methods are called convergent message passing, an important question remained: do their successive states actually settle at a single point?

Previous results established convergence toward a set described by local consistency conditions, without establishing convergence of the iterates themselves or a convergence rate. This paper proves the stronger fixed-point result for a particular coordinate-descent method on general piecewise-affine convex objectives. It also gives an iteration bound proportional to the inverse of the accuracy tolerance.

The authors then identify several convex message-passing algorithms as instances of this general method. This connects the abstract optimization result to established inference procedures. They also show that a slightly different coordinate-descent variant can cycle, demonstrating that the update rule matters: similar-looking procedures need not share the same convergence behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper proves fixed-point convergence and an inverse-tolerance iteration bound for a coordinate-descent method covering several convex message-passing algorithms.

title: Convergence of Some Convex Message Passing Algorithms to a Fixed Point

abstract: In this paper, we focus on distributed estimation and support recovery for high-dimensional linear quantile regression. Quantile regression is a popular alternative tool to the least squares regression for robustness against outliers and data heterogeneity. However, the non-smoothness of the check loss function poses big challenges to both computation and theory in the distributed setting. To tackle these problems, we transform the original quantile regression into the least-squares optimization. By applying a double-smoothing approach, we extend a previous Newton-type distributed approach without the restrictive independent assumption between the error term and covariates. An efficient algorithm is developed, which enjoys high computation and communication efficiency. Theoretically, the proposed distributed estimator achieves a near-oracle convergence rate and high support recovery accuracy after a constant number of iterations. Extensive experiments on synthetic examples and a real data application further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Quantile regression offers an alternative to least-squares regression that is useful for robustness to outliers and heterogeneous data. This paper studies its distributed, high-dimensional form, including both coefficient estimation and support recovery: identifying which variables have nonzero coefficients. The main obstacle is that the usual quantile-regression loss is nonsmooth, complicating distributed computation and its theoretical analysis.

The authors transform the original problem into a least-squares optimization and introduce a double-smoothing approach. This extends an earlier Newton-type distributed method while removing its restrictive assumption that the error term and covariates are independent. The resulting algorithm is designed to use both computation and communication efficiently.

The theoretical results establish a near-oracle convergence rate and high support-recovery accuracy after a constant number of iterations. These findings address both the accuracy of estimated effects and the identification of relevant variables. Experiments on synthetic examples and a real-data application further support the method's effectiveness, connecting the distributed optimization design to its statistical objectives.
summary.tldr: A double-smoothing method makes distributed high-dimensional quantile regression efficient while providing strong estimation and variable-selection guarantees.

title: Distributed High-Dimensional Quantile Regression: Estimation Efficiency and Support Recovery

abstract: Trustworthiness is an essential prerequisite for the real-world application of large language models. In this paper, we focus on the trustworthiness of language models with respect to retrieval augmentation. Despite being supported with external evidence, retrieval-augmented generation still suffers from hallucinations, one primary cause of which is the conflict between contextual and parametric knowledge. We deem that retrieval-augmented language models have the inherent capabilities of supplying response according to both contextual and parametric knowledge. Inspired by aligning language models with human preference, we take the first step towards aligning retrieval-augmented language models to a status where it responds relying merely on the external evidence and disregards the interference of parametric knowledge. Specifically, we propose a reinforcement learning based algorithm Trustworthy-Alignment, theoretically and experimentally demonstrating large language models’ capability of reaching a trustworthy status without explicit supervision on how to respond. Our work highlights the potential of large language models on exploring its intrinsic abilities by its own and expands the application scenarios of alignment from fulfilling human preference to creating trustworthy agents.

paragraphs: Giving a language model retrieved evidence does not automatically prevent hallucinations. This paper focuses on conflicts between the supplied context and information encoded in the model's parameters. A response may be influenced by internally stored knowledge even when external evidence is available to guide it.

Trustworthy-Alignment uses reinforcement learning to encourage the model to answer from external evidence while disregarding interference from parametric knowledge. The approach starts from the view that models already possess the capacity to respond using either source. Alignment is used to direct that capacity toward evidence reliance, extending the alignment objective beyond matching human preferences.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental evidence that models can reach the targeted trustworthy behavior without explicit supervision specifying how they should respond. Here, trustworthiness concerns reliance on the supplied evidence, the particular behavior the method is designed to elicit. The findings support reinforcement learning as a way to draw out and direct this existing capability, addressing one stated cause of hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation.
summary.tldr: Trustworthy-Alignment uses reinforcement learning to steer retrieval-augmented models toward external evidence when it conflicts with parametric knowledge.

title: Trustworthy Alignment of Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive performance across various tasks, but deploying them for inference poses challenges. Their high resource demands often necessitate complex, costly multi-GPU pipelines, or the use of smaller, less capable models. While quantization offers a promising solution utilizing lower precision for model storage, existing methods frequently experience significant performance drops at lower precision levels. Additionally, they typically provide only a limited set of solutions at specific bit levels, many of which are extensively manually tuned. To address these challenges, we propose a new method called SKIM: Scaled K-means clustering wIth Mixed precision. Our approach introduces two novel techniques: 1. A greedy algorithm to solve approximately optimal bit allocation across weight channels, and 2. A trainable scaling vector for non-differentiable K-means clustering. These techniques substantially improve the model performance and can be adapted to any given bit. Notably, in terms of perplexity, our method narrows the gap between quantized LLaMA models and their full precision counterparts by around 14% on average.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces the precision used to store a language model's weights, helping address its substantial deployment costs. At very low precision, however, model performance can deteriorate. Existing methods also tend to offer a restricted set of bit levels, with substantial manual tuning needed for particular configurations.

SKIM combines scaled K-means clustering with mixed precision. A greedy algorithm approximately optimizes how bits are allocated across weight channels. A trainable scaling vector complements the non-differentiable clustering procedure. Together, these techniques aim to improve the quality retained after quantization while adapting to a requested bit budget.

The reported evaluation finds that SKIM narrows the perplexity gap between quantized LLaMA models and their full-precision counterparts by around 14% on average. This is a reduction in that gap, rather than a claim of a 14% improvement on every task. The contribution connects flexible precision allocation with a trainable clustering adjustment, addressing both low-precision quality and the limited configuration choices of existing methods.
summary.tldr: SKIM combines mixed-precision bit allocation and scaled clustering, narrowing the reported LLaMA quantization perplexity gap by about 14% on average.

title: SKIM: Any-bit Quantization Pushing The Limits of Post-Training Quantization

abstract: Cardinality sketches are compact data structures that efficiently estimate the number of distinct elements across multiple queries while minimizing storage, communication, and computational costs. However, recent research has shown that these sketches can fail under adaptively chosen queries, breaking down after approximately $\tilde{O}(k^2)$ queries, where $k$ is the sketch size. In this work, we overcome this quadratic barrier by designing robust estimators with fine-grained guarantees. Specifically, our constructions can handle an exponential number of adaptive queries, provided that each element participates in at most $\tilde{O}(k^2)$ queries. This effectively shifts the quadratic barrier from the total number of queries to the number of queries sharing the same element, which can be significantly smaller. Beyond cardinality sketches, our approach expands the toolkit for robust algorithm design.

paragraphs: Cardinality sketches estimate the number of distinct elements while keeping only a compact summary of the data. Their small size reduces storage, communication, and computation. However, queries chosen adaptively can undermine their reliability: earlier research showed breakdown after roughly a quadratic number of queries in the sketch size k, up to logarithmic factors.

This paper designs robust estimators whose guarantees depend on how often individual elements recur across queries. The constructions can support exponentially many adaptive queries, provided each element appears in at most roughly k squared queries, again up to logarithmic factors. The key condition therefore concerns repeated participation by the same element, rather than the overall query count.

This distinction matters when a large collection of queries spreads its attention across many different elements. In that case, total query volume can be much larger than the participation count for any single element. The result moves the quadratic restriction to this finer measure of overlap, giving a more flexible robustness guarantee without claiming unrestricted resistance to every adaptive query sequence.
summary.tldr: New cardinality estimators support exponentially many adaptive queries when each element participates in only a bounded, roughly quadratic number of queries.

title: Breaking the Quadratic Barrier: Robust Cardinality Sketches for Adaptive Queries

abstract: Diffusion models, while powerful, can inadvertently generate harmful or undesirable content, raising significant ethical and safety concerns. Recent machine unlearning approaches offer potential solutions but often lack transparency, making it difficult to understand the changes they introduce to the base model. In this work, we introduce SAeUron, a novel method leveraging features learned by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to remove unwanted concepts in text-to-image diffusion models. First, we demonstrate that SAEs, trained in an unsupervised manner on activations from multiple denoising timesteps of the diffusion model, capture sparse and interpretable features corresponding to specific concepts. Building on this, we propose a feature selection method that enables precise interventions on model activations to block targeted content while preserving overall performance. Our evaluation shows that SAeUron outperforms existing approaches on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark for concepts and style unlearning, and effectively eliminates nudity when evaluated with I2P. Moreover, we show that with a single SAE, we can remove multiple concepts simultaneously and that in contrast to other methods, SAeUron mitigates the possibility of generating unwanted content under adversarial attack. Code and checkpoints are available at GitHub.

paragraphs: Removing unwanted concepts from a text-to-image diffusion model can be difficult to interpret: a method may change behavior without making the internal intervention clear. SAeUron addresses this by using sparse autoencoders to identify interpretable features associated with particular concepts and then intervening on those features.

The autoencoders are trained without supervision on model activations collected across multiple denoising timesteps. The authors show that they capture sparse features corresponding to specific concepts. A feature selection method then targets model activations to block unwanted content while preserving overall performance. This connects the removal procedure to identifiable internal representations.

A single sparse autoencoder can also support removal of multiple concepts simultaneously. Under adversarial attack, the method reduces the possibility of generating unwanted content compared with other methods. That result supports improved resistance in the evaluated attacks, rather than a universal guarantee that targeted content can never reappear.
summary.tldr: SAeUron uses interpretable sparse-autoencoder features to remove unwanted diffusion-model concepts while preserving performance and improving resistance to evaluated attacks.

title: SAeUron: Interpretable Concept Unlearning in Diffusion Models with Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: Decentralized learning has emerged as a powerful approach for handling large datasets across multiple machines in a communication-efficient manner. However, such methods often face scalability limitations, as increasing the number of machines beyond a certain point negatively impacts convergence rates. In this work, we propose Decentralized Anytime SGD, a novel decentralized learning algorithm that significantly extends the critical parallelism threshold, enabling the effective use of more machines without compromising performance. Within the stochastic convex optimization (SCO) framework, we establish a theoretical upper bound on parallelism that surpasses the current state-of-the-art, allowing larger networks to achieve favorable statistical guarantees and closing the gap with centralized learning in highly connected topologies.

paragraphs: Distributing learning across more machines does not always improve training. In decentralized methods, increasing the network beyond a critical size can worsen convergence rates. This paper studies that scalability barrier within stochastic convex optimization, asking how many machines can be used effectively while retaining favorable statistical performance.

The proposed algorithm, Decentralized Anytime SGD, extends the critical parallelism threshold. Its contribution is therefore about the range of useful parallel execution: it aims to let larger machine networks participate without sacrificing the performance guarantees under study. This connects the design of a decentralized learning algorithm directly to the question of how far its computation can be distributed.

The authors establish a theoretical upper bound on parallelism that improves on the existing state of the art. For highly connected network topologies, the result closes the gap with centralized learning. The topology qualification matters to that comparison: the stated centralized-level result concerns highly connected networks. Overall, the paper offers a theoretical route to greater decentralized scalability within the stochastic convex setting.
summary.tldr: Decentralized Anytime SGD expands theoretically supported parallelism and closes the gap with centralized learning in highly connected networks.

title: Enhancing Parallelism in Decentralized Stochastic Convex Optimization

abstract: We study memory-efficient optimization of neural networks (in particular language models) with linear gradient transformations, where the gradients are linearly mapped to a lower dimensional space than the full parameter space, thus saving memory required for gradient accumulation and optimizer state persistence. The model parameters are updated by first performing an optimization step in the lower dimensional space and then going back into the original parameter space via the linear map’s transpose. We show that optimizing the model in this transformed space is equivalent to reparameterizing the original model through a linear adapter that additively modifies the model parameters, and then only optimizing the adapter’s parameters. When the transformation is Kronecker-factored, this establishes an equivalence between GaLore and one-sided LoRA. We show that this duality between gradient transformations and adapter-based reparameterizations unifies existing approaches to memory-efficient training and suggests new techniques for improving training efficiency and memory use.

paragraphs: Training neural networks requires memory for accumulated gradients and persistent optimizer state. One way to reduce that cost is to map gradients linearly into a smaller space, perform optimization there, and map the update back using the transpose of the transformation. This paper examines what that procedure means in terms of the model being trained.

The authors show that this transformed-gradient optimization is equivalent to adding a linear adapter to the original parameters and optimizing only the adapter. The two descriptions therefore connect an optimizer-side change with a model-reparameterization change. This equivalence gives a common mathematical interpretation to approaches that can otherwise appear to operate at different parts of training.

For Kronecker-factored transformations, the result establishes an equivalence between GaLore and one-sided LoRA. The qualifier matters because the stated connection concerns that specific transformation structure and adapter form. More broadly, the duality unifies existing memory-efficient training methods and suggests ways to develop new ones. The contribution is an analytical relationship that can guide decisions about training efficiency and memory use.
summary.tldr: Optimization with linear gradient transformations is equivalent to training additive linear adapters, connecting GaLore and one-sided LoRA under a specific factorization.

title: On the Duality between Gradient Transformations and Adapters

abstract: Despite the success of distillation in large language models (LLMs), most prior work applies identical loss functions to both teacher- and student-generated data. These strategies overlook the synergy between loss formulations and data types, leading to a suboptimal performance boost in student models. To address this, we propose DistiLLM-2, a contrastive approach that simultaneously increases the likelihood of teacher responses and decreases that of student responses by harnessing this synergy. Our extensive experiments show that DistiLLM-2 not only builds high-performing student models across a wide range of tasks, including instruction-following and code generation, but also supports diverse applications, such as preference alignment and vision-language extensions. These findings highlight the potential of a contrastive approach to enhance the efficacy of LLM distillation by effectively aligning teacher and student models across varied data types.

paragraphs: Language-model distillation trains a student model using a teacher’s behavior. This paper argues that the origin of training responses should influence how they are used: responses generated by the teacher and responses generated by the student serve different roles. Applying the same loss function to both can miss a useful interaction between the data and the learning objective.

DistiLLM-2 introduces a contrastive approach that raises the likelihood of teacher responses while lowering the likelihood of student responses. The distinction between these two sources therefore becomes part of the training signal. The method aims to improve how effectively the student aligns with the teacher by matching the loss formulation to the type of response.

The authors report strong student performance across tasks including instruction following and code generation. Their experiments also cover preference alignment and extensions involving vision and language. These results support contrastive distillation as a useful approach across varied applications, with the central lesson that response provenance and loss design can be considered together when transferring model capabilities.
summary.tldr: DistiLLM-2 improves language-model distillation by increasing teacher-response likelihood and decreasing student-response likelihood through contrastive training.

title: DistiLLM-2: A Contrastive Approach Boosts the Distillation of LLMs

abstract: In applications with significant class imbalance or asymmetric costs, metrics such as the $F_\beta$-measure, AM measure, Jaccard similarity coefficient, and weighted accuracy offer more suitable evaluation criteria than standard binary classification loss. However, optimizing these metrics present significant computational and statistical challenges. Existing approaches often rely on the characterization of the Bayes-optimal classifier, and use threshold-based methods that first estimate class probabilities and then seek an optimal threshold. This leads to algorithms that are not tailored to restricted hypothesis sets and lack finite-sample performance guarantees. In this work, we introduce principled algorithms for optimizing generalized metrics, supported by $H$-consistency and finite-sample generalization bounds. Our approach reformulates metric optimization as a generalized cost-sensitive learning problem, enabling the design of novel surrogate loss functions with provable $H$-consistency guarantees. Leveraging this framework, we develop new algorithms, METRO (Metric Optimization), with strong theoretical performance guarantees. We report the results of experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of our methods compared to prior baselines.

paragraphs: Ordinary binary classification loss may poorly reflect the goal when classes are imbalanced or different mistakes carry different costs. Measures such as F-beta, Jaccard similarity, AM, and weighted accuracy can better match these needs, but directly optimizing them introduces computational and statistical challenges.

A common strategy estimates class probabilities and then searches for a decision threshold. The paper identifies a gap in such approaches: they are not tailored to restricted hypothesis classes and lack finite-sample guarantees. The authors instead reformulate generalized metric optimization as a generalized cost-sensitive learning problem, making the costs of decisions part of the optimization framework.

This reformulation supports new surrogate losses with H-consistency guarantees and leads to the METRO algorithms. The analysis includes finite-sample generalization bounds, connecting the training approach to performance with a limited dataset. Experimental comparisons demonstrate effectiveness against prior baselines. The contribution is a principled route from the chosen evaluation metric to trainable objectives, with guarantees that account for the hypothesis class used by the learner.
summary.tldr: METRO converts generalized classification metrics into cost-sensitive learning objectives with hypothesis-class-aware and finite-sample guarantees.

title: Principled Algorithms for Optimizing Generalized Metrics in Binary Classification

abstract: Contextual multi-armed bandits are a popular choice to model sequential decision-making. E.g., in a healthcare application we may perform various tests to asses a patient condition (exploration) and then decide on the best treatment to give (exploitation). When human design strategies, they aim for the exploration to be fast, since the patient’s health is at stake, and easy to interpret for a physician overseeing the process. However, common bandit algorithms are nothing like that: The regret caused by exploration scales with $\sqrt{H}$ over $H$ rounds and decision strategies are based on opaque statistical considerations. In this paper, we use an original classification view to meta learn interpretable and fast exploration plans for a fixed collection of bandits $\mathbb{M}$. The plan is prescribed by an interpretable decision tree probing decisions’ payoff to classify the test bandit. The test regret of the plan in the stochastic and contextual setting scales with $O (\lambda^{-2} C_{\lambda} (\mathbb{M}) \log^2 (MH))$, being $M$ the size of $\mathbb{M}$, $\lambda$ a separation parameter over the bandits, and $C_\lambda (\mathbb{M})$ a novel classification-coefficient that fundamentally links meta learning bandits with classification. Through a nearly matching lower bound, we show that $C_\lambda (\mathbb{M})$ inherently captures the complexity of the setting.

paragraphs: The paper treats exploration in a bandit problem as a classification task: use observed payoffs to identify which member of a fixed collection of environments is being encountered. This changes the purpose of exploratory actions. They become informative tests within a learned plan, rather than decisions driven only by general statistical rules.

The plan takes the form of an interpretable decision tree. Its branches describe how payoff observations guide subsequent probes and ultimately identify the test environment. Learning this structure across the collection connects meta learning to classification while making the exploration strategy easier to inspect.

For stochastic and contextual settings, the authors bound test regret using a separation parameter, the collection size, the time horizon, and a new classification coefficient. The horizon enters through a squared logarithm, with other factors reflecting how difficult the environments are to distinguish. A nearly matching lower bound shows that the coefficient captures an inherent difficulty of this setting. The guarantee therefore depends on the structure of the fixed collection, rather than establishing uniformly fast exploration for arbitrary bandit problems.
summary.tldr: The paper learns interpretable exploration trees by treating identification of a bandit environment as classification within a fixed collection.

title: A Classification View on Meta Learning Bandits

abstract: Coreset, as a summary of training data, offers an efficient approach for reducing data processing and storage complexity during training. In the emerging vertical federated learning (VFL) setting, where scattered clients store different data features, it directly reduces communication complexity. In this work, we introduce coresets construction for regularized logistic regression both in centralized and VFL settings. Additionally, we improve the coreset size for regularized linear regression in the VFL setting. We also eliminate the dependency of the coreset size on a property of the data due to the VFL setting. The improvement in the coreset sizes is due to our novel coreset construction algorithms that capture the reduced model complexity due to the added regularization and its subsequent analysis. In experiments, we provide extensive empirical evaluation that backs our theoretical claims. We also report the performance of our coresets by comparing the models trained on the complete data and on the coreset.

paragraphs: A coreset summarizes training data so that learning can use less data processing and storage. In vertical federated learning, clients hold different features of the data, so smaller summaries also reduce communication. This paper develops coreset constructions for regularized logistic regression in both centralized and vertically federated settings, and improves coreset sizes for regularized linear regression under vertical federation.

The key idea is to make the construction reflect the reduction in model complexity caused by regularization. The algorithms and their analysis exploit that reduced complexity to obtain smaller summaries. The authors also remove a coreset-size dependence on a data property introduced by the vertically federated setting, strengthening the resulting size guarantees.

Extensive experiments are reported to support the theoretical claims. The evaluation also compares models trained on complete datasets with models trained on the coresets, connecting the summary-size results to actual learning performance. The contribution matters because the value of a smaller coreset extends beyond storage: when features are distributed across clients, it can directly reduce the information that training needs to communicate.
summary.tldr: New coreset constructions exploit regularization to shrink data summaries and reduce communication in vertically federated regression.

title: Improved Coresets for Vertical Federated Learning: Regularized Linear and Logistic Regressions

abstract: This paper studies meta-reinforcement learning with adaptation from human feedback. It aims to pre-train a meta-model that can achieve few-shot adaptation for new tasks from human preference queries without relying on reward signals. To solve the problem, we propose the framework adaptation via Preference-Order-preserving EMbedding (POEM). In the meta-training, the framework learns a task encoder, which maps tasks to a preference-order-preserving task embedding space, and a decoder, which maps the embeddings to the task-specific policies. In the adaptation from human feedback, the task encoder facilitates efficient task embedding inference for new tasks from the preference queries and then obtains the task-specific policy. We provide a theoretical guarantee for the convergence of the adaptation process to the task-specific optimal policy and experimentally demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance with substantial improvement over baseline methods.
