paragraphs: The paper studies how a pretrained reinforcement learning system can adapt to new tasks using a small amount of human preference feedback. The adaptation stage does not depend on reward signals. This makes the central challenge one of translating preference queries into a task-specific policy efficiently, using knowledge acquired during meta-training.

POEM learns two connected components. A task encoder maps tasks into an embedding space designed to preserve preference ordering. A decoder maps those embeddings into policies. When a new task arrives, human preference queries help infer its embedding, and the decoder then produces the corresponding task-specific policy.

The approach concentrates adaptation on identifying the task within a learned representation that connects preferences to behavior. The authors provide a theoretical convergence guarantee for adaptation to the task-specific optimal policy. Experiments also report state-of-the-art performance with substantial gains over baseline methods. Together, these contributions support preference-preserving task representations as a route to few-shot adaptation from human feedback.
summary.tldr: POEM learns preference-preserving task embeddings that enable few-shot policy adaptation from human feedback without reward signals.

title: Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Adaptation from Human Feedback via Preference-Order-Preserving Task Embedding

abstract: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) seeks to localize the anomaly mask of an input image with respect to normal samples. Either by reconstructing normal counterparts (reconstruction-based) or by learning an image feature embedding space (embedding-based), existing approaches fundamentally rely on image-level or feature-level matching to derive anomaly scores. Often, such a matching process is inaccurate yet overlooked, leading to sub-optimal detection. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of cost filtering, borrowed from classical matching tasks, such as depth and flow estimation, into the UAD problem. We call this approach CostFilter-AD. Specifically, we first construct a matching cost volume between the input and normal samples, comprising two spatial dimensions and one matching dimension that encodes potential matches. To refine this, we propose a cost volume filtering network, guided by the input observation as an attention query across multiple feature layers, which effectively suppresses matching noise while preserving edge structures and capturing subtle anomalies. Designed as a generic post-processing plug-in, CostFilter-AD can be integrated with either reconstruction-based or embedding-based methods. Extensive experiments on MVTec-AD and VisA benchmarks validate the generic benefits of CostFilter-AD for both single- and multi-class UAD tasks. Code and models will be released at https://github.com/ZHE-SAPI/CostFilter-AD.

paragraphs: Image anomaly detection identifies regions that differ from normal examples. Existing methods often reconstruct a normal version of an image or compare learned features with normal samples. Both approaches rely on matching, and inaccurate matches can distort the resulting anomaly scores. CostFilter-AD targets this intermediate source of error.

The method first builds a matching cost volume: a structure with two image-location dimensions and another dimension representing possible matches. A filtering network then refines these costs. It uses the input image as an attention query across multiple feature layers, aiming to suppress matching noise while retaining boundaries and detecting small or subtle abnormalities.

CostFilter-AD is designed as a post-processing component that can be added to either reconstruction-based or embedding-based detectors. Experiments on MVTec-AD and VisA report benefits for both single-class and multi-class detection. The stated findings support improving the reliability of the matching stage as a useful route to better anomaly localization, with applicability across both major detector families.
summary.tldr: CostFilter-AD improves image anomaly detection by filtering noisy matching costs while preserving boundaries and subtle abnormalities.

title: CostFilter-AD: Enhancing Anomaly Detection through Matching Cost Filtering

abstract: Despite advances in learning-based methods, finding valid Lyapunov functions for nonlinear dynamical systems remains challenging. Current neural network approaches face two main issues: challenges in scalable verification and limited interpretability. To address these, we propose an end-to-end framework using transformers to construct analytical Lyapunov functions (local), which simplifies formal verification, enhances interpretability, and provides valuable insights for control engineers. Our framework consists of a transformer-based trainer that generates candidate Lyapunov functions and a falsifier that verifies candidate expressions and refines the model via risk-seeking policy gradient. Unlike Alfarano et al. (2024), which utilizes pre-training and seeks global Lyapunov functions for low-dimensional systems, our model is trained from scratch via reinforcement learning (RL) and succeeds in finding local Lyapunov functions for high-dimensional and non-polynomial systems. Given the symbolic nature of the Lyapunov function candidates, we employ efficient optimization methods for falsification during training and formal verification tools for the final verification. We demonstrate the efficiency of our approach on a range of nonlinear dynamical systems with up to ten dimensions and show that it can discover Lyapunov functions not previously identified in the control literature. Full implementation is available on Github.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the problem of finding analytical Lyapunov functions for nonlinear dynamical systems. Existing approaches that represent these functions with neural networks can be difficult to interpret and formally verify. The authors instead generate symbolic mathematical expressions, making the resulting candidates more accessible to control engineers and better suited to formal checking.

Their framework pairs a transformer that proposes expressions with a falsifier that checks candidates during training. Feedback from these checks improves the generator through a risk-seeking policy-gradient method. Training starts from scratch using reinforcement learning. Efficient optimization methods support falsification during learning, while separate formal verification tools check the final expressions.

The reported experiments cover nonlinear systems with up to ten dimensions, including non-polynomial systems. The method finds local Lyapunov functions, so its demonstrated scope concerns local rather than global behavior. The authors also report discovering functions not previously identified in the control literature. Together, these findings support symbolic generation as a route toward interpretable, verifiable results for challenging dynamical systems.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement-learning transformer generates symbolic local Lyapunov functions that can be formally verified for nonlinear systems with up to ten dimensions.

title: Analytical Lyapunov Function Discovery: An RL-based Generative Approach

abstract: Reliable watermarking of panoramic imagery is fundamentally challenged by arbitrary 3D rotations. As panoramas are defined on the sphere, they naturally transform under the action of $SO(3)$, rendering conventional planar representations and augmentation-based robustness strategies inadequate and devoid of theoretical guarantees. To address this, we formulate panoramas as spherical signals and leverage $SO(3)$ representation theory to derive provably rotation-invariant descriptors. While spherical harmonic coefficients transform equivariantly under rotations, the natural invariant constructions are typically limited to zeroth-order statistics which eliminate directional information and severely constrain embedding capacity. In this work, we introduce a principled third-order invariant construction by coupling higher-order $SO(3)$ irreducible representations via tensor products and projecting onto the trivial representation. This yields a spherical invariant bispectrum that preserves phase information while remaining strictly rotation-invariant. Leveraging this property, we embed watermarks into higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients and recover them from invariant bispectral scalars, enabling reliable extraction under arbitrary 3D rotations. We provide a theoretical proof of $SO(3)$ invariance for it and demonstrate experimentally its near-perfect robustness to continuous rotations while maintaining high visual fidelity.

paragraphs: Rotating a panoramic image in three dimensions changes how its content is represented, making embedded watermarks difficult to recover reliably. This paper treats panoramas as signals on a sphere and builds descriptors whose values remain unchanged under the rotation group SO(3). The goal is to obtain rotation robustness from mathematical structure.

Spherical harmonic coefficients change predictably under rotation, but simple invariant summaries can discard directional information and constrain watermark capacity. The proposed construction couples higher-order representations through tensor products and projects the result onto the rotation-invariant component. This produces a third-order spherical bispectrum that preserves phase information while remaining strictly invariant to rotation.

The method embeds watermarks in higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients and reads them through invariant bispectral scalars. These are complementary claims: the proof establishes an invariant representation, and the experiments show how effectively the watermarking system uses it. The approach connects richer spherical information with reliable extraction under arbitrary three-dimensional rotations.
summary.tldr: A provably rotation-invariant spherical bispectrum enables panoramic watermark extraction with near-perfect experimental robustness to continuous 3D rotations.

title: Rotation-Invariant Spherical Watermarking via Third-Order SO(3) Representation Coupling

abstract: Sparse Mixture of Experts (SMoE) architectures improve the training efficiency of Large Language Models (LLMs) by routing input tokens to a selected subset of specialized experts. Despite their remarkable success, both training and inference in SMoE models suffer from the expert collapse issue (Chi et al., 2022a), which degrades model performance. Prior studies primarily focus on improving the router; however, such methods rely on training from scratch or fine-tuning, which requires high computational and data-processing costs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, despite these efforts, the issue persists when advancing well-pretrained SMoE models, as evidenced by both theoretical and empirical results. To fill that gap, we analyze the advanced SMoE models and observe that the eigenvectors of expert weight matrices encode rich semantic information, pointing to an effective alternative to conventional routing strategies. Building on this insight, we propose Singular Value Decomposition SMoE (SSMoE), a novel and training-free framework that leverages spectral properties of the expert weights to address the collapse issue and enhance model performance. Extensive experiments across diverse language and vision tasks, under both clean and corrupt data settings, demonstrate the strong generalization and robustness of SSMoE. Our findings highlight how a deeper understanding of model internals can guide the development of more effective SMoE architectures.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models process each token with only a selected subset of their experts. This makes expert selection central to efficiency and performance. The paper investigates expert collapse, a routing problem that degrades these models during training and inference. It presents theoretical and empirical evidence that the issue persists even when advancing well-pretrained models with existing approaches.

The authors look inside the experts themselves for an alternative routing signal. They observe that eigenvectors of expert weight matrices contain useful semantic information. Their SSMoE framework uses spectral properties of these weights to address collapse without additional training. This changes where routing information comes from: the framework draws on structure already present in the expert parameters.

Experiments cover language and vision tasks with both clean and corrupted data, reporting strong generalization and robustness. The practical appeal is improving routing without the computational and data-processing costs of retraining or fine-tuning a router. The findings also suggest that examining learned weight structure can reveal information useful for coordinating the experts.
summary.tldr: SSMoE uses spectral information already present in expert weights to improve routing and address expert collapse without additional training.

title: Eigenvectors of Experts are Training-free Non-collapsing Routers

abstract: Language models with recurrent depth, also referred to as universal or looped when considering transformers, are defined by the capacity to increase their computation through the repetition of layers. Recent efforts in pretraining have demonstrated that these architectures can scale to modern language modeling tasks while exhibiting advantages in reasoning tasks. In this work, we examine the relationship between recurrent-depth models and diffusion language models. Building on their similarities, we develop a new diffusion forcing sampler for these models to accelerate generation. The sampler advances by decoding new tokens at every forward pass of the model, while the latent states of these tokens can be further refined in parallel through recurrence. Theoretically, under a fixed wall-clock budget, generation with our sampler is strictly more expressive than baseline autoregressive generation as it preserves the same recurrent depth while updating a strictly wider front of token positions in parallel, enabling more computation at equal serial depth. Moreover, this sampler, based on principles from diffusion literature, can be directly applied to existing 3.5B recurrent-depth transformers without any tuning, leading to up to a 5x speedup.

paragraphs: Recurrent-depth language models increase computation by applying layers repeatedly. This gives them an opportunity to refine internal representations through additional passes. The paper studies their relationship to diffusion language models and uses that connection to design a generation procedure that better exploits parallel computation.

The proposed diffusion forcing sampler decodes new tokens on every forward pass while continuing to refine token latent states through recurrence. Multiple positions can therefore receive updates in parallel. Under a fixed wall-clock budget, the authors prove greater expressivity than baseline autoregressive generation: the sampler maintains recurrent depth while updating a strictly wider set of token positions at equal serial depth.

The sampler applies directly to existing 3.5-billion-parameter recurrent-depth transformers without tuning, and the authors report speedups of up to five times. The result shows that the generation schedule itself can unlock additional efficiency from an already trained architecture. Its theoretical advantage is specifically tied to the budgeted comparison, while the measured speedup describes the evaluated model applications.
summary.tldr: A diffusion-inspired sampler generates new tokens while refining multiple positions in parallel, speeding existing recurrent-depth transformers by up to five times.

title: Efficient Parallel Samplers for Recurrent-Depth Models and Their Connection to Diffusion Language Models

abstract: LLM-based agents solve complex tasks through iterative reasoning, tool use, and environment interaction, where each intermediate thought directly shapes subsequent actions. Small deviations in these thoughts can therefore propagate into unsafe behaviors, yet existing guardrails typically operate only on final outputs or require intrusive model modifications. We introduce Thought-Aligner, a lightweight plug-in safety model that performs causal correction on unsafe thoughts before action execution, without altering the underlying agent. The corrected thoughts are fed back into the agent, steering its decision process and tool use toward safer trajectories. Because it operates solely at the thought level, Thought-Aligner is model-agnostic and can be integrated into diverse agent frameworks. We train Thought-Aligner via two-stage contrastive learning on paired safe and unsafe thoughts generated across ten risk scenarios. Experiments on diverse agent-safety benchmarks and six LLMs show that Thought-Aligner increases behavioral safety from about 50% without protection to around 90% on average, exceeding state-of-the-art guardrails by roughly 23%, while also improving helpfulness by about 5%. The method incurs low per-step latency and minimal overhead, enabling scalable and practical deployment. We publicly release Thought-Aligner-7B at https://huggingface.co/WhitzardAgent/Thought-Aligner-7B.

paragraphs: Thought-Aligner intervenes between an agent’s intermediate reasoning and its next action. The paper’s motivation is that small deviations in a thought can influence later tool use and propagate into unsafe behavior. Checking only the final output can therefore miss the point where a consequential action is being selected.

The method uses a separate safety model to correct unsafe thoughts before execution, then feeds the corrected version back into the agent. It leaves the underlying agent unchanged and is designed to work across agent frameworks. These results show that intervening in the reasoning that guides actions can improve both safety and usefulness in the evaluated agent settings.
summary.tldr: Thought-Aligner corrects unsafe intermediate thoughts before agents act, substantially improving reported behavioral safety while also increasing helpfulness.

title: Think Twice Before You Act: Enhancing Agent Behavioral Safety with Thought Correction

abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to interpret large language models by decomposing activations into sparse, human-understandable features, but scaling to large dictionaries exposes fundamental challenges. Systematic studies reveal pervasive feature splitting that fragments coherent concepts into non-atomic latents and widespread feature absorption that creates arbitrary exceptions in general features, severely compromising latent reliability. These issues stem from inconsistent latent assignment across samples: without cross-sample constraints, per-sample optimization often allows a single underlying concept to be inconsistently distributed across multiple redundant or interfering latents. To address this, we introduce C$^2$R (Cross-sample Consistency Regularization). C$^2$R explicitly encourages that each semantic feature is consistently represented by a unified latent across the batch by penalizing the co-activation of directionally similar latents. Comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that C$^2$R effectively mitigates both splitting and absorption while, crucially, preserving reconstruction fidelity, providing a principled solution that enhances latent interpretability without degrading model performance. Source code is available[https://github.com/hr-jin/Cross-sample-Consistency-Regularization].

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders aim to explain language-model activations using a small number of active, interpretable features. As their feature dictionaries grow, a coherent concept can become fragmented across several latents, while a broad feature can acquire arbitrary exceptions. These problems, called splitting and absorption, make an individual latent less dependable as an explanation.

The paper links both failures to inconsistent assignments across examples. Optimizing each example separately can allow the same concept to be represented by different redundant or interfering latents. Cross-sample Consistency Regularization, or C²R, adds a batch-level constraint by penalizing co-activation among latents with similar directions. This encourages a semantic feature to use a unified latent across samples.

The evaluations show that the regularizer mitigates both splitting and absorption while preserving reconstruction fidelity. That combination matters because clearer features would be less useful if they stopped accurately representing the original activations. The reported results support cross-sample consistency as a way to improve interpretability without sacrificing the autoencoder’s reconstruction performance.
summary.tldr: A cross-sample regularizer makes sparse autoencoder features more consistent while preserving reconstruction fidelity.

title: C$^2$R: Cross-sample Consistency Regularization Mitigates Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: Graph structure learning is a core problem in graph-based machine learning, essential for uncovering latent relationships and ensuring model interpretability. However, most existing approaches are ill-suited for large-scale and dynamically evolving graphs, as they often require complete re-learning of the structure upon the arrival of new nodes and incur substantial computational and memory costs. In this work, we propose GraphFLEx—a unified and scalable framework for Graph Structure Learning in Large and Expanding Graphs. GraphFLEx mitigates the scalability bottlenecks by restricting edge formation to structurally relevant subsets of nodes identified through a combination of clustering and coarsening techniques. This dramatically reduces the search space and enables efficient, incremental graph updates. The framework supports 48 flexible configurations by integrating diverse choices of learning paradigms, coarsening strategies, and clustering methods, making it adaptable to a wide range of graph settings and learning objectives. Extensive experiments across 26 diverse datasets and graph neural network architectures demonstrate that GraphFLEx achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly improved scalability. Our implementation is publicly available here: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Scaling_Graph_Learning-CB67/README.md.

paragraphs: Learning a graph’s structure means deciding which nodes should be connected so that the graph captures useful relationships. That becomes expensive for large graphs, especially when new nodes arrive and existing methods require the structure to be learned again. GraphFLEx targets both the initial search cost and the cost of maintaining a graph as it expands.

The framework combines clustering and coarsening to identify structurally relevant subsets of nodes. It restricts possible edge formation to those subsets, sharply reducing the search space and enabling incremental updates. This makes the selection of candidate connections a central part of scaling graph structure learning, rather than treating every potential connection as equally relevant.

GraphFLEx offers 48 configurations through different combinations of learning paradigms, coarsening strategies, and clustering methods. Evaluations across 26 datasets and graph neural network architectures report state-of-the-art performance with significantly improved scalability. The framework therefore provides several ways to adapt the same search-reduction principle to different graph settings and learning objectives.
summary.tldr: GraphFLEx makes graph structure learning more scalable by restricting candidate edges and supporting incremental updates as graphs grow.

title: GraphFLEx: Unsupervised Structure Learning $\underline\textF$ramework for $\underline\textL$arge $\underline\textEx$panding $\underline\textGraph$s

abstract: Dataset distillation, a training-aware data compression technique, has recently attracted increasing attention as an effective tool for mitigating costs of optimization and data storage. However, progress remains largely empirical. Mechanisms underlying the extraction of task-relevant information from the training process and the efficient encoding of such information into synthetic data points remain elusive. In this paper, we theoretically analyze practical algorithms of dataset distillation applied to the gradient-based training of two-layer neural networks with width $L$. By focusing on a non-linear task structure called multi-index model, we prove that the low-dimensional structure of the problem is efficiently encoded into the resulting distilled data. This dataset reproduces a model with high generalization ability for a required memory complexity of $\tilde \Theta(r^2d+L)$, where $d$ and $r$ are the input and intrinsic dimensions of the task. To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the first theoretical works that include a specific task structure, leverage its intrinsic dimensionality to quantify the compression rate and study dataset distillation implemented solely via gradient-based algorithms.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses training information into synthetic data designed for a learning procedure. Although it has shown practical promise, understanding what these synthetic examples capture remains difficult. This paper develops a theoretical account of how practical gradient-based distillation algorithms extract and encode task-relevant structure.

The analysis studies gradient-based training of two-layer neural networks with width L on nonlinear tasks described by a multi-index model. Within this setting, the authors prove that the distilled data efficiently encode the problem's low-dimensional structure. The important distinction is between the full input dimension d and the intrinsic task dimension r, which describes the smaller structure relevant to learning.

The distilled dataset can reproduce a model with high generalization ability at a required memory complexity of approximately r²d + L, with logarithmic factors suppressed in the stated bound. This makes the compression result explicitly dependent on task structure and network width. The contribution is a theoretical explanation for a specified nonlinear setting, linking gradient-based distillation to the efficient storage of low-dimensional representations.
summary.tldr: For a specified nonlinear task family, the paper proves that gradient-based dataset distillation efficiently stores low-dimensional structure while preserving strong generalization.

title: Dataset Distillation Efficiently Encodes Low-Dimensional Representations from Gradient-Based Learning of Non-Linear Tasks

abstract: Frozen self-supervised representations often transfer well with only a few labels across many semantic tasks. We argue that a single geometric quantity, directional CDNV (decision-axis variance), sits at the core of two favorable behaviors: strong few-shot transfer within a task, and low interference across many tasks. We show that both emerge when variability along class-separating directions is small. First, we prove sharp non-asymptotic multiclass generalization bounds for downstream classification whose leading term is the directional CDNV. The bounds include finite-shot corrections that cleanly separate intrinsic decision-axis variability from centroid-estimation error. Second, we link decision-axis collapse to multitask geometry: for independent balanced labelings, small directional CDNV across tasks forces the corresponding decision axes to be nearly orthogonal, helping a single representation support many tasks with minimal interference. Empirically, across SSL objectives, directional CDNV collapses during pretraining even when classical CDNV remains large, and our bounds closely track few-shot error at practical shot sizes. Additionally, on synthetic multitask data, we verify that SSL learns representations whose induced decision axes are nearly orthogonal.

paragraphs: The paper asks why frozen representations learned without labels can support classification with very few labeled examples. Its central quantity, directional CDNV, measures variability along the directions that separate classes. The key idea is that variation matters differently depending on its direction: substantial overall variation can coexist with little variation along the axes used for classification.

The authors prove multiclass generalization bounds whose leading term is directional CDNV. Additional terms account for having only a finite number of labeled examples, separating intrinsic variability from errors in estimating class centers. They also show that, for independent balanced labelings, small directional CDNV across tasks forces their decision axes to be nearly orthogonal, helping explain low interference between tasks.

Across self-supervised objectives, directional CDNV decreases during pretraining even when its classical counterpart remains large. The bounds closely follow observed classification error at practical label counts. Synthetic multitask experiments also show nearly orthogonal decision axes. Together, these findings connect useful transfer to a specific geometry of class separation, with the multitask theoretical claim depending on the stated labeling assumptions.
summary.tldr: Low representation variability along class-separating directions helps explain few-shot transfer and, under stated labeling assumptions, reduced interference across tasks.

title: Directional Neural Collapse Explains Few-Shot Transfer in Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: We introduce FrontierCS, a benchmark of 240 open-ended problems across diverse areas of computer science, designed and reviewed by experts, including CS PhDs and top-tier competitive programming participants and problem setters. Unlike existing benchmarks that focus on tasks with known optimal solutions, FrontierCS targets problems where the optimal solution is unknown, but the quality of a solution can be objectively evaluated. Models solve these tasks by implementing executable programs rather than outputting a direct answer. FrontierCS includes algorithmic problems, which are often NP-hard variants of competitive programming problems with objective partial scoring, and research problems with the same property. For each problem, we provide an expert reference solution and an automatic evaluator. Combining open-ended design, measurable progress, and expert curation, FrontierCS provides a benchmark at the frontier of computer-science difficulty. Empirically, we find that frontier reasoning models still lag far behind human experts, and that simply increasing reasoning budgets does not close this gap on open-ended challenges. Moreover, these models struggle to identify internal equivalence classes, and existing agentic frameworks also exhibit brittleness on such problems due to overfitting. FrontierCS thus offers a new lens into model capabilities on real frontier computer science problems.

paragraphs: FrontierCS evaluates computer-science problem solving where the best possible solution is unknown but candidate solutions can still be scored objectively. Models must implement executable programs, making solution quality measurable through what their code accomplishes. This permits evaluation of progress on open-ended problems without requiring a known optimum.

The benchmark contains 240 problems designed and reviewed by experts, including computer-science PhDs and experienced competitive programmers and problem setters. It covers algorithmic challenges, often NP-hard variants of programming problems, and research problems with objective partial scoring. Each task includes an expert reference solution and an automatic evaluator, providing both a comparison point and a repeatable assessment procedure.

The experiments find a large gap between frontier reasoning models and human experts, which simply increasing reasoning budgets does not close. Models also struggle to recognize internal equivalence classes, while existing agent frameworks show brittleness attributed to overfitting. Together, these observations suggest that open-ended, graded programming challenges expose weaknesses that are not resolved merely by allocating more reasoning effort.
summary.tldr: FrontierCS uses objectively scored, open-ended programming problems to reveal a substantial gap between frontier models and human experts.

title: FrontierCS: Evolving Challenges for Evolving Intelligence

abstract: This work proposes a novel method for solving learning from label proportion problems. For this purpose, we learn a classifier that minimizes three key objectives: (i) a bag-level loss, which quantifies the discrepancy between true and predicted label proportions in bags, (ii) an instance-level loss, inspired from domain adaptation, which leverages anchor samples with known labels and trainable supports and (iii) a distribution discrepancy that aims at aligning anchor’s learned support with those of the bag samples. The problem is formulated as an alternating optimization process, iteratively updating the classifier and aligning distributions via a particle flow method. The flow of anchor samples is governed by a vector field designed to minimize the anchor loss while ensuring alignment between anchor and bag distributions. We provide a theoretical analysis, guaranteeing the convergence of the flow and identifying conditions under which the method achieves effective alignment. Our analysis highlights that gap and diversity in label proportions within bags is a critical factor for learnability. Empirical results on tabular and image datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.

The problem is formulated as an alternating optimization process, iteratively updating the classifier and aligning distributions via a particle flow method. The flow of anchor samples is governed by a vector field designed to minimize the anchor loss while ensuring alignment between anchor and bag distributions. We provide a theoretical analysis, guaranteeing the convergence of the flow and identifying conditions under which the method achieves effective alignment. Our analysis highlights that gap and diversity in label proportions within bags is a critical factor for learnability. Empirical results on tabular and image datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Learning from label proportions means training with groups of examples whose class mixtures are known, even when individual labels are not. This paper combines that group-level information with labeled anchor samples. The aim is to learn an individual classifier while making the anchors’ learned support align with the samples found in the groups.

Training balances three objectives: matching the known group proportions, fitting labeled anchors through an instance-level loss, and reducing distributional mismatch between anchors and group samples. The method alternates classifier updates with particle-flow updates. A vector field moves the anchors to reduce their loss while also encouraging alignment with the group distributions.

The theoretical analysis guarantees convergence of the flow and gives conditions for effective alignment. It also identifies separation and diversity among group label proportions as critical factors for learnability. Experiments on tabular and image datasets outperform state-of-the-art approaches. Together, the analysis and results explain how aggregate labels and a set of labeled anchors can jointly support classification, while highlighting the importance of informative variation between groups.
summary.tldr: Alternating classifier training with anchor particle flows improves learning from group label proportions, with theory linking learnability to proportion diversity.

title: Particle Flow for Learning from Label Proportions

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly advanced, with Gemini-3-Pro setting a new performance milestone. In this work, we explore collective intelligence as an alternative to monolithic scaling, and demonstrate that open-source LLMs’ collaboration can surpass Gemini-3-Pro. We first revisit LLM routing and aggregation at scale and identify three key bottlenecks: (1) current train-free routers are limited by a query-based paradigm focusing solely on textual similarity; (2) recent aggregation methods remain largely static, failing to select appropriate aggregators for different tasks; (3) the complementarity of routing and aggregation remains underutilized. To address these problems, we introduce JiSi, a novel framework designed to release the full potential of LLMs’ collaboration through three innovations: (1) Query-Response Mixed Routing capturing both semantic information and problem difficulty; (2) Support-Set-based Aggregator Selection jointly evaluating the aggregation and domain capacity of aggregators; (3) Adaptive Routing-Aggregation Switch dynamically leveraging the advantages of routing and aggregation. Comprehensive experiments on nine benchmarks demonstrate that JiSi can surpass Gemini-3-Pro with only 47% costs by orchestrating ten open-source LLMs, while outperforming mainstream baselines. It suggests that collective intelligence represents a novel path towards Artificial General Intelligence (AGI).

paragraphs: This paper studies whether coordinating several language models can provide a practical alternative to relying on one increasingly capable model. It identifies weaknesses in how existing systems choose a model for a question, select a model to combine answers, and decide when combining answers is worthwhile.

The proposed framework, JiSi, makes these choices more adaptive. Its routing method considers information from both queries and responses to capture meaning and problem difficulty. It selects an aggregator using a support set that evaluates both answer-combining ability and domain competence. A further mechanism switches between routing and aggregation according to their respective advantages.

Across nine benchmarks, the authors report that orchestrating ten open-source models can surpass Gemini-3-Pro at 47% of its cost, while also outperforming mainstream baselines. These findings support collaboration as a promising way to improve capability and cost together in the evaluated setting. The broader connection to artificial general intelligence is presented as a possible research direction.
summary.tldr: JiSi adaptively routes questions and combines answers from ten open-source models, surpassing Gemini-3-Pro at 47% of its cost in the reported evaluation.

title: Beyond Gemini-3-Pro: Revisiting LLM Routing and Aggregation at Scale

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) improves sample efficiency by leveraging learned dynamics models, but often suffers from unstable training due to dynamics model learning mismatch: models are trained on data from historical policies while being queried under the continually updated current policy. This mismatch can cause policy-relevant local model error to remain large even as global prediction error decreases, leading to oscillatory updates. We present a finite-horizon performance analysis that decomposes the policy performance gap into global model error, policy-induced distribution shift, and historical policy mixture effects, showing that minimizing global error alone is insufficient for stable optimization. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Prioritized Model Experience Replay (PMER), a lightweight replay mechanism that prioritizes high-error transitions during dynamics model training. PMER implicitly emphasizes policy-relevant regions without explicit policy distance estimation and integrates seamlessly into Dyna-style MBRL frameworks. Experiments on MuJoCo benchmarks demonstrate improved stability, faster convergence, and higher sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned dynamics model to improve sample efficiency. A mismatch arises because that model learns from experience collected by older policies while the current policy continues changing. Prediction error can fall overall yet remain large in regions important to current decisions, producing unstable policy updates.

The paper analyzes this issue over a finite horizon. It separates the policy performance gap into global model error, policy-induced distribution shift, and effects from the mixture of historical policies. The analysis shows why minimizing aggregate prediction error alone is insufficient for stable optimization. It motivates directing more model-training effort toward transitions where predictions remain inaccurate.

Prioritized Model Experience Replay implements that idea through a lightweight replay mechanism that favors high-error transitions. This implicitly emphasizes policy-relevant regions without explicitly estimating distances between policies and fits into Dyna-style frameworks. On MuJoCo benchmarks, the authors report greater stability, faster convergence, and improved sample efficiency. The contribution links a diagnosis of model-training mismatch to a practical change in experience selection.
summary.tldr: PMER prioritizes high-error transitions when training dynamics models, improving stability and sample efficiency in model-based reinforcement learning experiments.

title: Prioritized Model Experience Replay

abstract: One-shot prediction enables rapid adaptation of pretrained foundation models to new tasks using only one labeled example, but lacks principled uncertainty quantification. While conformal prediction provides finite-sample coverage guarantees, standard split conformal methods are inefficient in the one-shot setting due to data splitting and reliance on a single predictor. We propose Conformal Aggregation of One-Shot Predictors (CAOS), a conformal framework that adaptively aggregates multiple one-shot predictors and uses a leave-one-out calibration scheme to fully exploit scarce labeled data. Despite violating classical exchangeability assumptions, we prove that CAOS achieves valid marginal coverage using a monotonicity-based argument. Experiments on one-shot facial landmarking and RAFT text classification tasks show that CAOS produces substantially smaller prediction sets than split conformal baselines while maintaining reliable coverage.

paragraphs: A pretrained model can adapt to a task using one labeled example, but that prediction alone does not express uncertainty with a statistical guarantee. Standard split conformal prediction offers coverage guarantees, yet dividing scarce labels between fitting and calibration wastes valuable information in this setting. Relying on a single predictor also limits what the available examples can contribute.

CAOS combines multiple one-shot predictors adaptively and calibrates their outputs with a leave-one-out procedure. This lets the framework make fuller use of the labeled data. The resulting construction violates classical exchangeability assumptions used in familiar conformal arguments, so the authors establish valid marginal coverage through a different proof based on monotonicity.

Experiments on facial landmarking and RAFT text classification produce substantially smaller prediction sets than split conformal baselines while preserving reliable coverage. Smaller sets mean the uncertainty output is more specific at the maintained coverage level. The guarantee is marginal, describing coverage across cases rather than promising correctness for every individual prediction. The contribution connects efficient use of scarce labels with principled uncertainty quantification.
summary.tldr: CAOS aggregates one-shot predictors and reuses scarce labels for calibration, producing smaller prediction sets with valid marginal coverage.

title: CAOS: Conformal Aggregation of One-Shot Predictors

abstract: Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning (SPML) studies learning from incomplete supervision, where each instance is annotated with only one positive label despite potentially belonging to multiple categories. While existing methods assume the annotated labels are randomly distributed, real-world annotations are often biased toward the most salient category. We formalize this realistic scenario as Salient Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning (SalSPML). This salient annotation bias poses a challenge to conventional SPML methods, as the missing labels often correspond to less salient and harder-to-recognize categories. Fortunately, we find that salient annotations are typically more representative and informative. Motivated by this insight, we propose Prototype-Guided Rejection for Salient Annotation (PiSA), which constructs reliable class-wise prototypes from salient labels and leverages them to guide embedding learning for non-salient labels recognition. We theoretically demonstrate that SalSPML is harder than Random SPML due to irreducible annotation bias, and under SalSPML, more accurate prototypes facilitate false-negative label detection. Experiments on multiple benchmarks, together with two newly constructed real-world SalSPML datasets, demonstrate that PiSA consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving an average mAP improvement of 3.16%.

paragraphs: An example may belong to several categories even when only one is annotated. Many methods for this setting assume that the observed positive label is chosen randomly. This paper instead studies annotations biased toward the most noticeable category, calling the setting Salient Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning. Such bias leaves less obvious, harder-to-recognize categories disproportionately unannotated.

The authors identify a useful counterpart to that difficulty: salient labels tend to provide representative and informative examples. PiSA uses them to construct reliable prototypes for each class. These prototypes guide representation learning so that the model can better recognize non-salient categories whose labels are missing.

The theoretical analysis shows that salient annotation makes the problem harder than random annotation because of irreducible bias. It also shows that more accurate prototypes help identify false-negative labels in this setting. Across multiple benchmarks and two newly constructed real-world datasets, PiSA consistently outperforms existing methods, with an average mAP improvement of 3.16%. The method therefore uses information carried by annotation bias to help address the recognition difficulty that the bias creates.
summary.tldr: PiSA uses representative salient labels to build class prototypes that help recover less obvious missing labels, improving results under biased single-positive annotation.

title: One Coin Has Two Sides: Single Positive Multi Label Learning from Salient Annotations

abstract: While reinforcement learning has achieved impressive progress in language model reasoning, it is constrained by the requirement for verifiable rewards. Recent verifier-free RL methods address this limitation by utilizing the probabilities that LLMs generate reference answers as reward signals. However, these approaches typically sample reasoning traces conditioned only on the question. This design decouples reasoning-trace sampling from answer information, leading to inefficient exploration and incoherence between traces and final answers. In this paper, we propose Coupled Variational Reinforcement Learning (CoVRL), which bridges variational inference and reinforcement learning by coupling prior and posterior distributions through a hybrid sampling strategy. By constructing and optimizing a composite distribution that integrates these two distributions, CoVRL enables efficient exploration while preserving strong thought-answer coherence. Extensive experiments on mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks show that CoVRL improves performance by 12.4% over the base model and achieves an additional 2.3% improvement over state-of-the-art verifier-free RL baselines, providing a principled framework for enhancing the general reasoning capabilities of language models.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for reasoning often depends on rewards that can verify whether an answer is correct. Verifier-free methods offer another route: they use the model’s probability of producing a reference answer as a reward. However, sampling reasoning from the question alone leaves useful answer information disconnected from the search for reasoning traces.

Coupled Variational Reinforcement Learning, or CoVRL, connects these pieces through variational inference. It combines prior and posterior distributions in a hybrid sampling strategy, then optimizes a composite distribution incorporating both. The intended benefit is to explore useful reasoning more efficiently while keeping the sampled reasoning consistent with the resulting answer.

Experiments on mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks report a 12.4% performance improvement over the base model and a further 2.3% improvement over leading verifier-free reinforcement learning baselines. These results support coupling answer information with reasoning exploration during training. Here, verifier-free learning still uses reference answers for its reward signal; the contribution concerns how that information informs the reasoning process.
summary.tldr: CoVRL couples reasoning sampling with answer information to improve verifier-free reinforcement learning on mathematical and general reasoning tasks.

title: Coupled Variational Reinforcement Learning for Language Model General Reasoning

abstract: Codebook-based generators built on masked language model (MLM) transformers have become highly effective in text and vision, yet remain underused for tabular data. This is because codebooks typically act as information bottlenecks, whereas synthetic tabular generation requires a code space larger than the training sample, with additional codes trained to support new tabular rows. We address this gap with Q-Tab, a codebook-based tabular generator that uses lookup-free quantization (LFQ) with residual corruption to jointly tokenize numerical variables, categorical variables are directly one-hot tokenized. A BERT-style MLM captures dependencies in the token space and can then be sampled from. Corruption propagates reconstruction supervision across the numerical code space, but under joint encoder–decoder training induces a moving-target regression problem whose difficulty depends on the corruption structure. This motivates residual LFQ as the quantization mechanism, balancing broader supervision with locality. Q-Tab achieves state-of-the-art predictive utility and label prediction, while matching the distributional fidelity of diffusion-based generators.

paragraphs: Generating synthetic table rows requires capturing relationships among numerical and categorical variables. Q-Tab explores code-based generation with a masked-language-model transformer. The paper identifies a difficulty with conventional codebooks: useful tabular generation needs a code space larger than the training sample, including codes that can support new rows.

Q-Tab jointly tokenizes numerical variables with lookup-free quantization and residual corruption, while categorical variables receive direct one-hot tokenization. A BERT-style masked model learns dependencies among these tokens and supports sampling. Corruption spreads reconstruction supervision across the numerical code space, helping train codes beyond those directly represented by the original examples.

That broader supervision introduces a complication: when encoder and decoder learn together, reconstruction targets move, and the corruption structure affects how difficult this regression becomes. Residual quantization balances coverage with locality to address this issue. The authors report state-of-the-art predictive utility and label prediction while matching diffusion generators in distributional fidelity. These results indicate that the token-based approach can produce useful synthetic tables while preserving their statistical resemblance to the data.
summary.tldr: Q-Tab combines residual lookup-free quantization with masked token modeling to generate statistically faithful and predictively useful synthetic tables.

title: Q-Tab: Quantized Tabular Data Generator

abstract: Current research on video hallucination mitigation primarily focuses on isolated error types, leaving compositional hallucinations—arising from incorrect reasoning over multiple interacting spatial and temporal factors largely underexplored. We introduce OmniVCHall, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate both isolated and compositional hallucinations in Video Large Language Models (VLLMs). OmniVCHall spans diverse video domains, introduces a novel camera-based hallucination type, and defines a fine-grained taxonomy, together with adversarial answer options (e.g., “All are correct” and “None of the above”) to prevent shortcut reasoning. The evaluations of 39 representative VLLMs reveal that even advanced models (e.g., Qwen3-VL and GPT-5) exhibit substantial performance degradation. We propose TriCD, a contrastive decoding framework with a triple-pathway calibration mechanism. An adaptive perturbation controller dynamically selects distracting operations to construct negative video variants, while a saliency-guided enhancement module adaptively reinforces grounded token-wise visual evidences. These components are optimized via reinforcement learning to encourage precise decision-making under compositional hallucination settings. Experimental results show that TriCD consistently improves performance across two representative backbones, achieving an average accuracy improvement of over 10%. The data and code are released at https://github.com/BMRETURN/OmniVCHall.

paragraphs: This paper studies video hallucinations caused by incorrectly combining several spatial and temporal factors. Such errors go beyond a single mistaken detail. The authors introduce OmniVCHall to evaluate both isolated and compositional hallucinations across diverse video domains, including a new category involving cameras and a detailed taxonomy of errors.

The benchmark includes adversarial answer choices such as options asserting that every answer, or no answer, is correct. These are designed to discourage shortcut reasoning. Evaluations of 39 video language models reveal substantial degradation even in advanced systems. The results motivate TriCD, a contrastive decoding framework that calibrates generation through three pathways.

TriCD adaptively creates distracting video variants and strengthens visual evidence relevant to individual output tokens using saliency guidance. Reinforcement learning optimizes these components for decisions involving compositional hallucinations. Across two representative backbones, the method consistently improves performance, with average accuracy gains above 10%. The findings support combining challenging evaluation with decoding mechanisms that explicitly distinguish distracting inputs from grounded visual evidence.
summary.tldr: OmniVCHall tests interacting video hallucinations, while TriCD improves decoding by contrasting distractions with reinforced visual evidence.

title: Learning to Decode Against Compositional Hallucination in Video Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) are discrete autoencoders that compress images into discrete tokens. However, they are difficult to train due to discretization. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective technique dubbed Gaussian Quant (GQ), which first trains a Gaussian VAE under certain constraints and then converts it into a VQ-VAE without additional training. For conversion, GQ generates random Gaussian noise as a codebook and finds the closest noise vector to the posterior mean. Theoretically, we prove that when the logarithm of the codebook size exceeds the bits-back coding rate of the Gaussian VAE, a small quantization error is guaranteed. Practically, we propose a heuristic to train Gaussian VAEs for effective conversion, named the target divergence constraint (TDC). Empirically, we show that GQ outperforms previous VQ-VAEs, such as VQGAN, FSQ, LFQ, and BSQ, on both UNet and ViT architectures. Furthermore, TDC also improves previous Gaussian VAE discretization methods, such as TokenBridge. The source code is provided in https://github.com/tongdaxu/VQ-VAE-from-Gaussian-VAE.

paragraphs: Gaussian Quant offers a different route to image autoencoders that produce discrete tokens. Directly training a vector-quantized variational autoencoder is difficult because of discretization. The proposed method first trains a Gaussian VAE under suitable constraints, then converts it to a discrete model without further training. The training-free claim applies specifically to this conversion step.

For conversion, the method creates a codebook from random Gaussian noise vectors and selects the vector closest to the encoder's posterior mean. The authors prove a sufficient condition for small quantization error: the logarithm of the codebook size must exceed the Gaussian VAE's bits-back coding rate. They also propose a target divergence constraint as a practical training heuristic for making the initial model suitable for conversion.

Experiments on UNet and ViT architectures show Gaussian Quant outperforming VQGAN, FSQ, LFQ, and BSQ. The target divergence constraint also improves earlier Gaussian VAE discretization methods, including TokenBridge. These results support separating continuous-model training from discrete conversion while shaping the initial representation for that conversion.
summary.tldr: Gaussian Quant converts a suitably trained Gaussian VAE into a discrete image autoencoder using a random codebook without additional training.

title: Training-Free Vector Quantization via Gaussian VAEs

abstract: Knowledge-intensive Visual Question Answering (KI-VQA) frequently suffers from severe knowledge conflicts caused by the inherent limitations of open-domain retrieval. However, existing paradigms face critical limitations, including the lack of generalizable conflict detection and intra-model constraint mechanisms to handle conflicting evidence. To address these challenges, we propose the REAL (Reasoning-Pivot Alignment) framework centered on the novel concept of the Reasoning-Pivot. Distinct from reasoning steps that prioritize internal self-derivation, a reasoning-pivot serves as an atomic unit (node or edge) in the reasoning chain that emphasizes knowledge linkage, and it typically relies on external evidence to complete the reasoning. Supported by our constructed REAL-VQA dataset, our approach integrates Reasoning-Pivot Aware SFT (RPA-SFT) to train a generalizable discriminator by aligning conflicts with pivot extraction, and employs Reasoning-Pivot Guided Decoding (RPGD), an intra-model decoding strategy that leverages these pivots for targeted conflict mitigation. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that REAL significantly enhances discrimination accuracy and achieves superior performance, validating our pivot-driven resolution paradigm.

paragraphs: Answering an image-based question may require outside knowledge, but retrieved material can conflict with other evidence. REAL addresses both recognizing those conflicts and controlling how they affect the answer. Its organizing concept is a reasoning-pivot: a small unit in a reasoning chain where a knowledge connection typically depends on external evidence.

A pivot can be a node or an edge in the chain. This focuses attention on the particular connection that needs support, rather than treating every reasoning step alike. Using the constructed REAL-VQA dataset, the authors train a discriminator through Reasoning-Pivot Aware supervised fine-tuning, connecting conflict identification with extraction of these evidence-dependent units.

During answer generation, Reasoning-Pivot Guided Decoding uses the pivots to target conflicting information within the model's own decoding process. Experiments across diverse datasets report significantly improved discrimination accuracy and superior overall performance. The findings support connecting conflict detection to the precise knowledge links used in reasoning, so that detecting a disagreement can directly inform how the answer is generated.
summary.tldr: REAL detects and mitigates conflicting evidence by identifying the specific knowledge links that visual-question reasoning depends on.

title: REAL: Resolving Knowledge Conflicts in Knowledge-Intensive Visual Question Answering via Reasoning-Pivot Alignment

abstract: Recent test-time defenses for CLIP claim to preserve zero-shot clean accuracy while improving adversarial robustness. However, we find the reported robustness of six recent proposed state-of-the-art methods substantially overestimated: they fail under basic adaptive attacks. We further observe that these defenses share a common reliance on an indicative measurement that is assumed to capture the distributional difference between clean and adversarial samples and to determine whether the defense should preserve or alter the static model’s prediction. We argue that this assumption is the fundamental weakness, and we propose CLIP-MAD (Manipulating Assumed Difference), an adaptive attack strategy designed to break it. CLIP-MAD efficiently expands the adversarial distribution without costly full gradient calculations and can be flexibly combined with existing attack baselines to further boost attack strength. Experiments across 13 datasets demonstrate that CLIP-MAD produces strong adversarial samples that markedly reduce the robustness of diverse test-time defenses, revealing a false sense of security in CLIP’s zero-shot robustness. Code will be available at https://github.com/rzzhang222/CLIP-MAD.

paragraphs: Test-time defenses for CLIP aim to preserve performance on clean inputs while resisting adversarial ones. This paper finds that the reported robustness of six recent methods is substantially overestimated under basic adaptive attacks. It identifies a shared dependency: a measurement intended to distinguish clean from adversarial inputs determines whether a defense changes the original model’s prediction.

The authors argue that this assumed distinction is a fundamental weakness and introduce CLIP-MAD to exploit it. The attack targets the premise behind the defense’s decision signal, efficiently expanding the adversarial distribution without costly full gradient calculations. It can also be combined with existing attack baselines to increase attack strength.

Across 13 datasets, CLIP-MAD produces adversarial examples that markedly reduce the robustness of diverse test-time defenses. The findings show that a defense’s apparent success can depend on whether its clean-versus-adversarial indicator remains informative against attacks designed around it. They therefore challenge the evaluated robustness claims by testing the assumption that controls when protection is activated.
summary.tldr: CLIP-MAD undermines test-time defenses by attacking the assumed distinction used to decide whether an input needs protection.

title: You Don’t Protect if You Don’t Expect: Breaking the Key Assumption behind CLIP’s Test-Time Defenses

abstract: This position paper argues that prompting intent should be audited in LLM-assisted peer review, moving beyond the sole detection or disclosure of LLM usage. As major conferences increasingly allow LLM assistance and deploy mechanisms for detecting LLM-generated text, a critical gap remains: usage alone does not determine risk. A more consequential variable is prompting intent, the objective or stance encoded in how an LLM is instructed, which can systematically shape review framing and tone. We advocate an intent-centric auditing perspective that treats prompting intent as latent and infers relevant signals from the review text. Because intent is unobservable in real deployments, we train an intent detector using synthetically labeled LLM-generated reviews. Among ICLR 2026 reviews previously flagged for substantial LLM usage, we apply our detector to infer prompting intent and find coherent linguistic and structural signatures associated with directional prompting, along with systematic associations with review ratings, confidence, and paper acceptance decisions. We conclude with practical considerations for auditing LLM-assisted peer review, with an emphasis on procedural transparency and human-in-the-loop oversight.
originalAbstract: This position paper argues that prompting intent should be audited in LLM-assisted peer review, moving beyond the sole detection or disclosure of LLM usage. As major conferences increasingly allow LLM assistance and deploy mechanisms for detecting LLM-generated text, a critical gap remains: usage alone does not determine risk. A more consequential variable is prompting intent, the objective or stance encoded in how an LLM is instructed, which can systematically shape review framing and tone. We advocate an intent-centric auditing perspective that treats prompting intent as latent and infers relevant signals from the review text. Because intent is unobservable in real deployments, we train an intent detector using synthetically labeled LLM-generated reviews. Among ICLR 2026 reviews previously flagged for substantial LLM usage, we apply our detector to infer prompting intent and find coherent linguistic and structural signatures associated with directional prompting, along with systematic associations with review ratings, confidence, and paper acceptance decisions. We conclude with practical considerations for auditing LLM-assisted peer review, with an emphasis on procedural transparency and human-in-the-loop oversight.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that detecting AI assistance in peer review does not fully describe its risks. The objective or stance embedded in a prompt can shape a review’s framing and tone. The authors therefore propose auditing prompting intent, focusing on how assistance was directed rather than treating all language-model use as equivalent.

Because real prompting intent is unobserved, they train a detector using generated reviews with synthetic intent labels. They then apply it to ICLR 2026 reviews previously flagged for substantial language-model use. The analysis finds coherent linguistic and structural patterns associated with directional prompting, together with systematic associations involving review ratings, reviewer confidence, and paper acceptance.

These results concern inferred intent and observed associations, so their meaning depends on that distinction from directly inspecting prompts. The practical proposal is to use review text as evidence for an intent-focused auditing process. The authors emphasize transparent procedures and human oversight, positioning the detector as part of a broader examination of how AI assistance influences scientific assessment.
summary.tldr: The authors infer prompting intent from AI-assisted reviews and argue that audits should examine directional influence alongside whether AI was used.

title: Position: Prompting Intent Should Be Audited in LLM-Assisted Peer Review

abstract: The scores returned by support vector machines are often used as a confidence measures in the classification of new examples. However, there is no theoretical argument sustaining this practice. Thus, when classification uncertainty has to be assessed, it is safer to resort to classifiers estimating conditional probabilities of class labels. Here, we focus on the ambiguity in the vicinity of the boundary decision. We propose an adaptation of maximum likelihood estimation, instantiated on logistic regression. The model outputs proper conditional probabilities into a user-defined interval and is less precise elsewhere. The model is also sparse, in the sense that few examples contribute to the solution. The computational efficiency is thus improved compared to logistic regression. Furthermore, preliminary experiments show improvements over standard logistic regression and performances similar to support vector machines.

paragraphs: Classification scores are often interpreted as confidence, but the paper questions that interpretation for support vector machines because it lacks a theoretical justification. When uncertainty matters, the authors favor estimating conditional class probabilities. They focus particularly on ambiguity near the decision boundary, where examples are difficult to assign confidently to one class.

The proposed method adapts maximum likelihood estimation within logistic regression. It produces proper conditional probabilities within an interval chosen by the user, accepting lower precision outside that interval. This concentrates the model's probability-estimation effort in the region of interest instead of demanding the same precision everywhere.

The resulting classifier is also sparse: only a small number of training examples contribute to the solution. The paper reports improved computational efficiency relative to logistic regression. Preliminary experiments show improvements over standard logistic regression and performance similar to support vector machines. Together, these findings suggest a way to combine focused uncertainty estimation with a compact classifier, while retaining the explicitly limited probability precision outside the selected interval.
summary.tldr: A sparse logistic-regression adaptation estimates class probabilities precisely within a user-selected interval while improving computational efficiency.

title: Sparse probabilistic classifiers
